editorialDecl.p: EEBO-TCP is a partnership between the Universities of Michigan and Oxford and the publisher ProQuest to create accurately transcribed and encoded texts based on the image sets published by ProQuest via their Early English Books Online (EEBO) database (http://eebo.chadwyck.com). The general aim of EEBO-TCP is to encode one copy (usually the first edition) of every monographic English-language title published between 1473 and 1700 available in EEBO.

EEBO-TCP aimed to produce large quantities of textual data within the usual project restraints of time and funding, and therefore chose to create diplomatic transcriptions (as opposed to critical editions) with light-touch, mainly structural encoding based on the Text Encoding Initiative (http://www.tei-c.org).

The EEBO-TCP project was divided into two phases. The 25,363 texts created during Phase 1 of the project have been released into the public domain as of 1 January 2015. Anyone can now take and use these texts for their own purposes, but we respectfully request that due credit and attribution is given to their original source.
Users should be aware of the process of creating the TCP texts, and therefore of any assumptions that can be made about the data.

Text selection was based on the New Cambridge Bibliography of English Literature (NCBEL). If an author (or for an anonymous work, the title) appears in NCBEL, then their works are eligible for inclusion. Selection was intended to range over a wide variety of subject areas, to reflect the true nature of the print record of the period. In general, first editions of a works in English were prioritized, although there are a number of works in other languages, notably Latin and Welsh, included and sometimes a second or later edition of a work was chosen if there was a compelling reason to do so.

Image sets were sent to external keying companies for transcription and basic encoding. Quality assurance was then carried out by editorial teams in Oxford and Michigan. 5% (or 5 pages, whichever is the greater) of each text was proofread for accuracy and those which did not meet QA standards were returned to the keyers to be redone. After proofreading, the encoding was enhanced and/or corrected and characters marked as illegible were corrected where possible up to a limit of 100 instances per text. Any remaining illegibles were encoded as <gap>s. Understanding these processes should make clear that, while the overall quality of TCP data is very good, some errors will remain and some readable characters will be marked as illegible. Users should bear in mind that in all likelihood such instances will never have been looked at by a TCP editor.
The texts were encoded and linked to page images in accordance with level 4 of the TEI in Libraries guidelines.

Copies of the texts have been issued variously as SGML (TCP schema; ASCII text with mnemonic sdata character entities); displayable XML (TCP schema; characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or text strings within braces); or lossless XML (TEI P5, characters represented either as UTF-8 Unicode or TEI g elements).
Keying and markup guidelines are available at the Text Creation Partnership web site.
This file is the EEBO-TCP transcription with editorial layers added inline; nothing of the transcription has been removed.

choice/orig holds the text as printed; choice/reg holds the modern reading. reg/@resp says who decided it (#auto = machine, #editor = reviewed by hand); reg/@type is spelling, case, punctuation, spacing, grammar (an archaic form modernized: thou, hath, -eth), reference (a scripture reference in the modern style: Heb. xii. 5 as Heb 12:5) or emendation (another word, or a word added or removed). Where the editor overrode the machine, the editor's reg comes first and the machine's proposal follows as a second reg[@resp='#auto'].
choice/abbr + choice/expan: macron abbreviations (e.g. frō = from) and superscript contractions (yᵉ = the).
supplied: letters or words lost to illegible print, with @cert and a comment giving the evidence; the TCP gap element is kept inside.

Spelling regularized: u/v, i/j, silent final e, doubled consonants, -ie to -y, -nesse to -ness, and a word list. Grammatical forms (hath, doth, thou, thee, thy, ye, shalt, wilt, art, hast, dost) are retained. Footnote text is left in original spelling.
list[@change='#review']: run-in enumerations (I. ... II. ...) set out as numbered lists; the printed numerals are kept in label.
head[@type='edition']: section title used by this edition; the printed heading is kept in the preceding head. @change='#review' points at the revisionDesc entry for these structural changes.
Line breaks are those of the TCP transcription (newlines in the text; g[@ref='char:EOLhyphen'] marks a word hyphenated at line end). pb/@n is the printed page, pb/@facs the page image.
reg[@type='spacing']: a space this edition adds (empty orig) or removes (empty reg) between words.
@prev/@next link blocks this edition runs together into one paragraph; they stay separate elements as printed.
p[@rend='levelN']: a paragraph this edition sets in by its place in the author's numbered outline (level N).
seg[@rend='smallcaps'][@type='opening']: the first word of a division, printed in capitals after a drop cap, which this edition sets in small capitals.

seg[@type='transcription']: words the transcription misread or left out, set as printed (read on the page image); a comment inside gives the transcription's reading and the evidence, and @change points at the revisionDesc entry.

div.head: THE PREFACE.
div.p: THEREThere is no Questionquestion whatsoever, that is of greater Importanceimportance to Mankindmankind, and that it more concerns every individual Personperson to be well resolved in, than this, What are the distinguishing Qualificationsqualifications of those that are in Favourfavorfavour with God, and entitled to his eternal Rewardsrewards? Or, which comes to the same Thingthing, What is the Naturenature of true Religionreligion? andAnd wherein do lie the distinguishing Notesnotes of that Vertuevirtue and Holinessholiness, that is acceptable in the Sightsight of God. But tho'though it be of such Importanceimportance, and tho'though we have clear and abundant Lightlight in the Wordword of God to direct us in this Mattermatter, yet there is no one Pointpoint, wherein professing Christians do more differ one from another. It would be endless to reckon up the Varietyvariety of Opinionsopinions in this Pointpoint, that divide the christian Worldworld; making manifest the Truthtruth of that of our SaviourSavior, Strait is the Gategate, and narrow is the Wayway, that leads to Lifelife, and few there be that find it.

The Considerationconsideration of these Thingsthings has long engaged me to attend to this Mattermatter, with the utmost Diligencediligence and Carecare, and Exactnessexactness of Searchsearch and Enquiryinquiryenquiry, that I have been capable of: Itit is a Subjectsubject on which my Mindmind has been peculiarly intent, ever since I first entredentered on the Studystudy of Divinitydivinity.—Butbut as to the Successsuccess of my Enquiriesinquiriesenquiries, it must be left to the Judgmentjudgment of the Readerreader of the following Treatisetreatise.

I am sensible it is much more difficult to judge impartially of that which is the Subjectsubject of this Discoursediscourse, in the midst of the Dustdust and Smokesmoke of such a Statestate of Controversycontroversy, as this Landland is now in, about Thingsthings of this Naturenature: Asas it is more difficult to write impartially, so
it is more difficult to read impartially.—Manymany will probably be hurt in their Spiritsspirits, to find so much that appertains to religious Affectionaffection, here condemned: Andand perhaps Indignationindignation and Contemptcontempt will be excited in others, by finding so much here justified and approved. And it may be, some will be ready to charge me with Inconsistenceinconsistencyinconsistence with my self, in so much approving some Thingsthings, and so much condemning others; as I have found, this has always been objected to me by some, ever since the Beginningbeginning of our late Controversiescontroversies about Religionreligion. 'Tis a hard Thingthing to be a hearty zealous Friendfriend of what has been good and glorious, in the late extraordinary Appearancesappearances, and to rejoice much in it; and at the same Timetime, to see the evil and pernicious Tendencytendency of what has been bad, and earnestly to oppose that. But yet, I am humbly, but fully perswadedpersuaded, we shall never be in the Wayway of Truthtruth, nor go on in a Wayway acceptable to God, and tending to the Advancementadvancement of Christ's Kingdomkingdom, 'tilltill we do so. There is indeed something very mysterious in it, that so much Goodgood, and so much Badbad, should be mix'dmixed together in the Churchchurch of God: Asas 'tis a mysterious Thingthing, and what has puzzled and amazed many a good Christian, that there should be that which is so divine and precious, as the saving Gracegrace of God, and the new and divine Naturenature, dwelling in the same Heartheart, with so much Corruptioncorruption, Hypocrisyhypocrisy and Iniquityiniquity, in a particular Saintsaint. Yet neither of these, is more mysterious than real. And neither of 'emthem is a new or rare Thingthing. 'Tis no new Thingthing, that much false Religionreligion should prevail, at a Timetime of great reviving of true Religionreligion; and that at such a Timetime, Multitudesmultitudes of Hypocriteshypocrites should spring up among true Saintssaints. It was so in that great Reformationreformation, and Revivalrevival of Religionreligion, that was in Josiah's Timetime; as appears by Jer.Jeremiah 3.: 10. andAnd 4. 3, 4. andAnd also by the great Apostacyapostasyapostacy that there was in the Landland, so soon after his Reignreign. So it was in that great Outout-pouring of the Spirit upon the Jews, that was in the Daysdays of John the Baptist; as appears by the great Apostacyapostasyapostacy of that Peoplepeople, so soon after so general an Awakeningawakening, and the temporary religious Comfortscomforts and Joysjoys of many; John 5.: 35. Ye were willing, for a Seasonseason, to rejoice in his Lightlight. So it was in those great Commotionscommotions that were among the Multitudemultitude, occasion'doccasioned by the Preachingpreaching of Jesus Christ: Of the many that were then called, but few were chosen; of the Multitudemultitude that were roused and affected by his Preachingpreaching, and at one Timetime or other appeared mightily engaged, full of Admirationadmiration of Christ, and elevated with Joyjoy, but few were true Disciplesdisciples, that stood the Shockshock of the great Trialstrials that came afterwards, and endured to the Endend: Manymany were like the stony Groundground, or thorny Groundground; and but few, comparatively, like the good Groundground: Ofof the whole Heapheap that was gathered, great Partpart was Chaffchaff, that the Windwind afterwards drove away; and the Heapheap of Wheatwheat that was left, was comparatively small; as appears abundantly, by the Historyhistory of
the new Testament. So it was in that great Outout-pouring of the Spirit that was in the Apostle'sapostle's Daysdays; as appears by Matth.Matthew 24.: 10, 11, 12, 13. Gal. 3.: 1. andAnd 4. 11, 15. Phil. 2.: 21. andAnd 3. 18, 19. And the two Epistlesepistles to the Corinthians, and many other Partsparts of the new Testament. And so it was in the great Reformationreformation from Popery.—Itit appears plainly to have been in the visible Churchchurch of God, in Timestimes of great reviving of Religionreligion, from Timetime to Timetime, as it is with the Fruitfruit Treestrees in the Springspring; there are a Multitudemultitude of Blossomsblossoms; all which appear fair and beautiful, and there is a promising Appearanceappearance of young Fruitsfruits; but many of 'emthem are but of short Continuancecontinuance, they soon fall off, and never come to Maturitymaturity.

Not that it is to be supposed that it will always be so: • Forfor tho'though there never will, in this Worldworld, be an entire Puritypurity; either in particular Saintssaints, in a perfect Freedomfreedom from Mixturesmixtures of Corruptioncorruption; or in the Churchchurch of God, without any Mixturemixture of Hypocriteshypocrites with Saintssaints, and counterfeit Religionreligion, and false Appearancesappearances of Gracegrace, with true Religionreligion and real Holinessholiness: Yetyet, 'tis evident, that there will come a Timetime of much greater Puritypurity in the Churchchurch of God, than has been in Agesages past: it is plain by those Textstexts of Scripture. Isai.Isa 52.: 1. Ezek. 44.: 6, 7, 9. Joel 3.: 17. Zech. 14.: 21. Psal.Ps 69.: 32, 35, 36. Isai.Isa 35.: 8, 10. Chap. 4. 3, 4. Ezek. 20.: 38. Psal.Ps 37 • .: 9, 10, 11, 29 • . And one great Reasonreason of it will be, that at that Timetime, God will give much greater Lightlight to his Peoplepeople, to distinguish between true Religionreligion and its Counterfeitscounterfeits; Mal. 3.: 3. And he shall sit as a Refinerrefiner, and Purifierpurifier of Silversilver; and he shall purify the Sonssons of Levi 〈◊〉 , and purge them 〈◊〉 as Goldgold and Silversilver; that they 〈◊◊〉 may offer 〈◊〉 to the Lord 〈◊〉 an Offeringoffering in Righteousnessrighteousness. With Verseverse 18, which is a Continuationcontinuation of the Prophecyprophecy of the same happy Timestimes, then shall ye return, and discern between the Righteousrighteous and the Wickedwicked, between him that serveth God, and him that serveth him not.

'Tis by the Mixturemixture of counterfeit Religionreligion with true, not discern'ddiscerned and distinguished, that the Devildevil has had his greatest Advantageadvantage against the Causecause and Kingdomkingdom of Christ, all along, hitherto. 'Tis plainly by this Meansmeans, principally, that he has prevail'dprevailed against all Revivingsrevivings of Religionreligion, that ever have been, since the first founding of the christian Churchchurch. By this, he hurt the Causecause of Christianity, in, and after the apostolic Ageage, much more than by all the Persecutionspersecutions of both Jews and Heathensheathens: Thethe Apostlesapostles, in all their Epistlesepistles, shewshow themselves much more concerned at the former Mischiefmischief, than the latter. By this, Satan prevail'dprevailed against the Reformationreformation, begun by Luther, Zuinglius, &c. toTo put a Stopstop to its Progressprogress, and bring it into Disgracedisgrace; ten Timestimes more, than by all those bloody, cruel, and before, unheard of Persecutionspersecutions of the Churchchurch of Rome. By
this principally, has he prevail'dprevailed against Revivalsrevivals of Religionreligion, that have been in our Nationnation since the Reformationreformation. By this he prevail'dprevailed against New-England, to quench the Lovelove, and spoil the Joyjoy of her Espousalsespousals, about an hundred Yearsyears ago. And I think, I have had Opportunityopportunity enough to see plainly, that by this, the Devildevil has prevail'dprevailed against the late, great Revivalrevival of Religionreligion in New-England, so happy and promising in its Beginningbeginning: Herehere most evidently has been the main Advantageadvantage Satan has had against us; by this he has foil'dfoiled us; 'tis by this Meansmeans, that the Daughterdaughter of Zion in this Landland, now lies on the Groundground, in such piteous Circumstancescircumstances, as we now behold her; with her Garmentsgarments rent, her Faceface disfigur'ddisfigured, her Nakednessnakedness expos'dexposed, her Limbslimbs broken, and weltringweltering in the Bloodblood of her own Woundswounds, and in no wise able to arise; and this, so quickly after her late great Joysjoys and Hopeshopes. Lam. 1.: 17. Zion spreadeth 〈◊〉 forth her Handshands, and there is none to comfort her: Thethe Lord hath commanded concerning Jacob, that his Adversariesadversaries shall be round about him: Jerusalem is as a menstruous Womanwoman among them. I have observ'd the Devildevil prevail the same Wayway, against two great Revivingsrevivings of Religionreligion in this Countrycountry.—Satan goes on with Mankindmankind, as he began with them: Hehe prevail'dprevailed against our first Parentsparents, and cast 'emthem out of Paradiseparadise, and suddenly brought all their Happinesshappiness and Gloryglory to an Endend, by appearing to be a Friendfriend to their happy Paradisaicparadisaic Statestate, and pretending to advance it to higher Degreesdegrees. So the same cunning Serpentserpent, that beguiled Eve 〈◊〉
thro'through his Subtiltysubtletysubtilty, by perverting us from the Simplicitysimplicity that is in Christ, hath suddenly prevail'dprevailed to deprive us of that fair Prospectprospect, we had a little while ago, of a Kindkind of paradisaic Statestate of the Churchchurch of God in New-England.

After Religionreligion has revived in the Churchchurch of God, & Enemiesenemies appear, Peoplepeople that are engaged to defend it'sits Causecause, are commonly most exposed, where they are least sensible of Dangerdanger. While they are wholly intent upon the Oppositionopposition that appears openly before 'emthem, to make Headhead against that, and do neglect carefully to look all round 'emthem, the Devildevil comes behind 'emthem, and gives a fatal Stabstab unseen; and has Opportunityopportunity to give a more home Strokestroke, and wound the deeper, because he strikes at his Leisureleisure, and according to his Pleasurepleasure, being obstructed by no Guardguard or Resistanceresistance.

And so it is likely ever to be in the Churchchurch, whenever Religionreligion revives remarkably, 'tilltill we have learned well to distinguish between true and false Religionreligion, between saving Affectionsaffections and Experiencesexperiences, and those manifold fair Shewsshows, and glistering Appearancesappearances, by which they are counterfeited; the Consequencesconsequences of which, when they are not distinguished, are often inexpressibly dreadful. By this Meansmeans, the Devildevil gratifies himself, by bringing it to pass, that Thatthat should be offered
to God, by Multitudesmultitudes, under a Notionnotion of a pleasing acceptable Sacrificesacrifice to him, that is indeed above all Thingsthings abominable to him. By this Meansmeans, he deceives great Multitudesmultitudes about the Statestate of their Soulssouls; making them think they are something, when they are nothing; and so eternally undoes 'emthem: Andand not only so, but establishes many, in a strong Confidenceconfidence of their eminent Holinessholiness, who are in God's Sightsight, some of the vilest of Hypocriteshypocrites. By this Meansmeans, he many Waysways, damps and wounds Religionreligion in the Heartshearts of the Saintssaints, obscures and deforms it by corrupt Mixturesmixtures, causes their religious Affectionsaffections wofullywoefully to degenerate, and sometimes for a considerable Timetime, to be like the Manna 〈◊〉 manna, that bred Wormsworms and stank; and dreadfully ensnares and confounds the Mindsminds of others of the Saintssaints, and brings 'emthem into great Difficultiesdifficulties and Temptationstemptations, and entangles 'emthem in a Wildernesswilderness, out of which they can by no Meansmeans extricate themselves. By this Meansmeans, Satan mightily encourages the Heartshearts of open Enemiesenemies of Religionreligion, and strengthens their Handshands, and fills them with Weaponsweapons, and makes strong their Fortressesfortresses; when at the same Timetime, Religionreligion and the Churchchurch of God lie exposed to 'emthem, as a Citycity without Wallswalls. By this Meansmeans, he brings it to pass, that Menmen work Wickednesswickedness under a Notionnotion of doing God Serviceservice, and so sin without Restraintrestraint yea 〈◊〉 with earnest Forwardnessforwardness and Zealzeal, and with all their Mightmight. By this Meansmeans, he brings in, even the Friendsfriends of Religionreligion, insensibly to themselves, to do the Workwork of Enemiesenemies, by destroying Religionreligion, in a far more effectual Mannermanner, than open Enemiesenemies can do, under a Notionnotion of advancing it. By this Meansmeans the Devildevil scatters the Flockflock of Christ, and sets 'emthem one against another, and that with great Heatheat of Spiritspirit, under a Notionnotion of Zealzeal for God; and Religionreligion by Degreesdegrees, degenerates into vain Janglingjangling; and during the Strifestrife, Satan leads both Partiesparties far out of the right Wayway, driving each to great Extremesextremes, one on the right Handhand, and the other on the Leftleft, according as he finds they are most inclined, or most easily moved and sway'dswayed, 'tilltill the right Pathpath in the Middlemiddle, is almost wholly neglected. And in the midst of this Confusionconfusion, the Devildevil has great Opportunityopportunity to advance his own Interestinterest, and make it strong in Waysways innumerable, and get the Governmentgovernment of all into his own Handshands, and work his own Willwill. And by what is seen of the terrible Consequencesconsequences of this counterfeit Religionreligion, when not distinguished from true Religionreligion, God's Peoplepeople in general have their Mindsminds unhinged and unsettled, in Thingsthings of Religionreligion, and know not where to set their Footfoot, or what to think or do; and many are brought into Doubtsdoubts, whether there be any Thingthing at all in Religionreligion; and Heresyheresy, and Infidelityinfidelity and Atheismatheism greatly prevail.

Therefore, it greatly concerns us to use our utmost Endeavoursendeavorsendeavours, clearly to discern, and have it well settled and established, wherein
true Religionreligion does consist. 'Tilltill this be done, it may be expected that great Revivingsrevivings of Religionreligion, will be but of short Continuancecontinuance: 'Tilltill'till this 〈◊〉 be done, there is but little Goodgood to be expected, of all our warm Debatesdebates, in Conversationconversation and from the Presspress, not knowing clearly and distinctly, what we ought to contend for.

My Designdesign is to contribute my Mitemite, and use my best (however feeble) Endeavoursendeavorsendeavours to this Endend, in the ensuing Treatisetreatise: Whereinwherein it must be noted, that my Designdesign is somewhat diverse from the Designdesign of what I have formerly published, which was to shewshow the distinguishing Marksmarks of a Workwork of the Spirit of God, including both his common, and saving Operationsoperations; but what I aim at now, is to shewshow the Naturenature and Signssigns of the gracious Operationsoperations of God's Spirit, by which they are to be distinguished from all Thingsthings whatsoever that the Mindsminds of Menmen are the Subjectssubjects of, which are not of a saving Naturenature. If I have succeeded in this my Aimaim, in any tolerable Measuremeasure, I hope it will tend to promote the Interestinterest of Religionreligion. And whether I have succeeded to bring any Lightlight to this Subjectsubject, or no and however my Attemptattempt may be reproach'dreproached, in these captious, censorious Timestimes, I hope in the Mercymercy of a gracious and righteous God, for the Acceptanceacceptance of the Sinceritysincerity of my Endeavoursendeavorsendeavours, and hope also, for the Candorcandor and Prayersprayers of the true Followersfollowers of the Meekmeek and charitable Lamb of God.

div.head: PART I.
Concerning the Nature of the Affections, and their Importance in Religion.
1 PETER i. 8.
Whom having not seen, ye love: Inin whom, though now ye see him not, yet believing, ye rejoice with Joyjoy unspeakable, and full of Gloryglory.
div.p: INIn these Wordswords, the Apostleapostle represents the Statestate of the Mindsminds of the Christians he wrote to, under the Persecutionspersecutions they were then the Subjectssubjects of. These Persecutionspersecutions are what he has Respectrespect to, in the two preceedingpreceding Versesverses, when he speaks of the Trialtrial of their Faithfaith, and of their being in Heavinessheaviness through manifold Temptationstemptations.

Such Trialstrials are of threefold Benefitbenefit to true Religionreligion: Herebyhereby the Truthtruth of it is manifested, and it appears to be indeed true Religionreligion: Theythey, above all other Thingsthings, have a Tendencytendency to distinguish between true Religionreligion and false, and to cause the Differencedifference between them evidently to appear. Hence they are called by the Namename of Trialstrials, in the Verseverse nextly preceedingpreceding the Texttext, and in innumerable other Placesplaces: Theythey try the Faithfaith and Religionreligion of Professorsprofessors, of what Sortsort it is, as apparent Goldgold is tried in the Firefire, and manifested,
whether it be true Goldgold or no. And the Faithfaith of true Christians being thus tried and proved to be true, is found to Praisepraise, and Honourhonorhonour, and Gloryglory; as in that preceedingpreceding Verseverse.

And then, Thesethese Trialstrials are of further Benefitbenefit to true Religionreligion; they not only manifest the Truthtruth of it, but they make it'sits genuine Beautybeauty and Amiablenessamiableness remarkably to appear. True Vertuevirtue never appears so lovely, as when it is most oppressed: Andand the divine Excellencyexcellency of real Christianity, is never exhibited with such Advantageadvantage, as when under the greatest Trialstrials: Thenthen it is that true Faithfaith appears much more precious than Goldgold; and upon this Accountaccount, is found 〈◊〉 to Praisepraise, and Honourhonorhonour, and Gloryglory.

And again, Anotheranother Benefitbenefit that such Trialstrials are of to true Religionreligion, is, that they purify and increase it. They not only manifest it to be true, but also tend to refine it, and deliver it from those Mixturesmixtures of that which is false, which incumberencumber and impede it; that nothing may be left but that which is true. They tend to cause the Amiablenessamiableness of true Religionreligion to appear to the best Advantageadvantage, as was before observed; and not only so, but they tend to increase it'sits Beautybeauty, by establishing and confirming it, and making it more lively and vigourousvigorous, and purifying it from those Thingsthings that obscured it'sits Lustrelusterlustre and Gloryglory. As Goldgold that is tried in the Firefire, is purged from it'sits Alloyalloy, and all Remaindersremainders of Drossdross, and comes forth more solid and beautiful; so true Faithfaith being tried as Goldgold is tried in the Firefire, becomes more precious; and thus also is found unto Praisepraise, and Honourhonorhonour, and Gloryglory. The Apostleapostle seems to have Respectrespect to each of these Benefitsbenefits, that Persecutionspersecutions are of to true Religionreligion, in the Verseverse preceedingpreceding the Texttext.

And in the Texttext, the Apostleapostle observes how true Religionreligion operated in the Christians he wrote to, under their Persecutionspersecutions, whereby these Benefitsbenefits of Persecutionpersecution appeared in them; or what manner of Operationoperation of true Religionreligion, in them, it was, whereby their Religionreligion, under Persecutionpersecution, was manifested to be true Religionreligion, and eminently appeared in the genuine Beautybeauty and Amiablenessamiableness of true Religionreligion, and also appeared to be increased and purified, and so was like to be found unto Praisepraise, and Honourhonorhonour, and Gloryglory, at the Appearingappearing of Jesus Christ. DOCT. True Religionreligion, in great Part, consists in holy Affectionsaffections.

Here I would,

I. It may be enquiredinquired, what the Affectionsaffections of the Mindmind are?
I answer, Thethe Affectionsaffections are no other, than the more vigorous and sensible Exercisesexercises of the Inclinationinclination and Willwill of the Soulsoul.

God has induedendued the Soulsoul with two Facultiesfaculties: Oneone is that by which it is capable of Perceptionperception and Speculationspeculation, or by which it discerns and views and judges of Thingsthings; which is called the Understandingunderstanding. The Exercisesexercises of this Facultyfaculty are of two Sortssorts; either those by which the Soulsoul is carried out towards the Thingsthings that are in view, in approving of them, being pleased with them, and inclined to them; or those in which the Soulsoul opposes the Thingsthings that are in view, in disapproving them, and in being displeased with them, averse from them, and rejecting them.

And as the Exercisesexercises of the Inclinationinclination and Willwill of the Soulsoul are various in their Kindskinds, so they are much more various in their Degreesdegrees. to act vigorously and sensibly, and the Actingsactings of the Soulsoul are with that Strengthstrength that (thro'through the Lawslaws of the Unionunion which the Creator has fix'dfixed between Soulsoul and Bodybody) the Motionmotion of the Bloodblood and animal Spiritsspirits begins to be sensibly alter'daltered; whence oftentimes arises some bodily Sensationsensation, especially about the Heartheart and Vitalsvitals, that are the Fountainfountain of the Fluidsfluids of the Bodybody: Fromfrom whence it comes to pass, that the Mindmind, with regard to the Exercisesexercises of this Facultyfaculty, perhaps in all Nationsnations and Agesages, is called the Heartheart. And it is to be noted, that they are these more rigorousvigorous and sensible Exercisesexercises of this Facultyfaculty, that are called the Affectionsaffections.

The Willwill, and the Affectionsaffections of the Soulsoul, are not two Facultiesfaculties; the Affectionsaffections are not essentially distinct from the Willwill, nor do they differ from the meermere Actingsactings of the Willwill and Inclinationinclination of the Soulsoul, but only in the Livelinessliveliness, and Sensiblenesssensibleness of Exerciseexercise.

It must be confessed, that Languagelanguage is here somewhat imperfect, and the Meaningmeaning of Wordswords in a considerable Measuremeasure looselose and unfixed, and not precisely limited by Customcustom, which governs the Useuse of Languagelanguage. In some Sensesense, the Affectionaffection of the Soulsoul differs nothing at all from the Willwill and Inclinationinclination, and the Willwill never is in any Exerciseexercise any further than it is affected; it is not moved out of a Statestate of perfect Indifferenceindifference, any otherwise than as it is affected one Wayway or other, and acts nothing voluntarily any further. In every Actact of the Willwill whatsoever, the Soulsoul either likes or dislikes, is either inclined or disinclined to what is in view: Thesethese are not essentially different from those Affectionsaffections of Lovelove and Hatredhatred: Thatthat Likingliking or Inclinationinclination of the Soulsoul to a Thingthing, if it be in a high Degreedegree, and be vigorous and lively, is the very same Thingthing with the Affectionaffection of Lovelove: Andand that Dislikingdisliking and Disincliningdisinclining, if in a great Degreedegree, is the very same with Hatredhatred. In every Actact of the Willwill for, or towards something not present, the Soulsoul is in some Degreedegree inclined to that Thingthing; and that Inclinationinclination, if in a considerable Degreedegree, is the very same with the Affectionaffection of Desiredesire. Such seems to be our Naturenature, and such the Lawslaws of the Unionunion of Soulsoul and Bodybody, that there never is in any Casecase whatsoever, any lively and vigorous Exerciseexercise of the Willwill or Inclinationinclination of the Soulsoul, without some Effecteffect upon the Bodybody, in some Alterationalteration of the Motionmotion of it'sits Fluidsfluids, and especially of the animal Spiritsspirits. 8. The Religionreligion of Heavenheaven consists very much in Affectionaffection.

There is doubtless true Religionreligion in Heavenheaven, and true Religionreligion in it'sits utmost Puritypurity and Perfectionperfection. But according to the Scripture Representationrepresentation of the heavenly Statestate, the Religionreligion of Heavenheaven consists chiefly in holy and mighty Lovelove and Joyjoy, and the Expressionexpression of these in most fervent and exalted Praisespraises. So that the Religionreligion of the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven, consists in the same Thingsthings with that Religionreligion of the Saintssaints on Earthearth, which is spoken of in our Texttext, viz.Love, and Joy unspeakable, and full of Gloryglory. Now it would be very foolish to pretend, that because the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven ben't united to Fleshflesh and Bloodblood, and have no animal Fluidsfluids to be moved, (through the Lawslaws of Unionunion of Soulsoul and Bodybody) with those great Emotionsemotions of their Soulssouls, that therefore their exceeding Lovelove and Joyjoy are no Affectionsaffections.—Wewe are not speaking of the Affectionsaffections of the Bodybody, but of the Affectionsaffections of the Soulsoul, the chief of which are Lovelove and Joyjoy. When these are in the Soulsoul, whether that be in the Bodybody or out of it, the Soulsoul is affected and moved. And when they are in the Soulsoul, in that Strengthstrength in which they are in the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven, the Soulsoul is mightily affected and moved, or, which is the same Thingthing, has great Affectionsaffections. 'Tis true, we don't experimentally know what Lovelove and Joyjoy are in a Soulsoul out of a Bodybody, or in a glorified Bodybody; i. eE. weWe han't had Experienceexperience of Lovelove and Joyjoy in a Soulsoul in these Circumstancescircumstances; but the Saintssaints on Earthearth do know what divine Lovelove and Joyjoy in the Soulsoul are & they know what Lovelove & Joyjoy are of the same Kindkind, with the Lovelove and Joyjoy which are in Heavenheaven, in separate Soulssouls there. The Lovelove and Joyjoy of the Saintssaints on Earthearth, is the Beginningbeginning and Dawningdawning of the Lightlight, Lifelife, and Blessednessblessedness of Heavenheaven, and is like their Lovelove and Joyjoy there; or rather, the same in Naturenature, tho'though not the same with it, or like to it, in Degreedegree and Circumstancescircumstances. This is
evident by many Scriptures, as Prov. 4.: 18. John 4.: 14. andAnd Chapchap. 6. 40, 47, 50, 51, 54, 58. 1 John 3.: 15. 1 Cor. 13.: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. 'Tis unreasonable therefore to suppose, that the Lovelove and Joyjoy of the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven, not only differ in Degreedegree and Circumstancescircumstances, from the holy Lovelove and Joyjoy of the Saintssaints on Earthearth, but is so entirely different in Naturenature, that they are no Affectionsaffections; and meerlymerely because they have no Bloodblood and animal Spiritsspirits to be set in Motionmotion by them, which Motionmotion of the Bloodblood and animal Spiritsspirits is not of the Essenceessence of these Affectionsaffections, in Menmen on the Earthearth, but the Effecteffect of them; altho'although by their Reactionreaction they may make some circumstantial Differencedifference in the Sensationsensation of the Mindmind. There is a Sensationsensation of the Mindmind which loves and rejoices, that is antecedent to any Effectseffects on the Fluidsfluids of the Bodybody; and this Sensationsensation of the Mindmind, therefore don't depend on these Motionsmotions in the Bodybody, and so may be in the Soulsoul without the Bodybody. And wherever there are the Exercisesexercises of Lovelove and Joyjoy, there is that Sensationsensation of the Mindmind, whether it be in the Bodybody, or out; and that inward Sensationsensation, or kind of spiritual Sensesense, or Feelingfeeling, and Motionmotion of the Soulsoul, is what is called Affectionaffection; Thethe Soulsoul when it thus feels, (if I may so say) and is thus moved, is said to be affected, and especially when this inward Sensationsensation and Motionmotion, are to a very high Degreedegree, as they are in the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven. If we can learn any thing of the Statestate of Heavenheaven from the Scripture, the Lovelove and Joyjoy that the Saintssaints have there, is exceeding great and vigorous; impressing the Heartheart with the strongest and most lively Sensationsensation, of inexpressible Sweetnesssweetness, mightily moving, animating, and engaging them, making them like to a Flameflame of Firefire. And if such Lovelove and Joyjoy ben't Affectionsaffections, then the Wordword Affectionaffection is of no Useuse in Languagelanguage.—Willwill any say, that the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven, in beholding the Faceface of their Father, and the Gloryglory of their Redeemer, and contemplating his wonderful Worksworks, and particularly his laying down his Lifelife for them, have their Heartshearts nothing moved and affected, by all which they behold or consider?

Hence therefore the Religionreligion of Heavenheaven, consisting chiefly in holy Lovelove and Joyjoy, consists very much in Affectionaffection: Andand therefore undoubtedly, true Religionreligion consists very much in Affectionaffection. The Wayway to learn the true Naturenature of any Thingthing, is to go where that Thingthing is to be found in it'sits Puritypurity and Perfectionperfection. If we would know the Naturenature of true Goldgold, we must view it, not in the Oaroar, but when it is refined. If we would learn what true Religionreligion is, we must go where there is true Religionreligion, and nothing but true Religionreligion, and in it'sits highest Perfectionperfection, without any Defectdefect or Mixturemixture. All who are truelytruly religious are not of this Worldworld, they are Strangersstrangers here, and belong to Heavenheaven; they are born from above, Heavenheaven is their native Countrycountry, and the Naturenature which they receive by this heavenly Birthbirth, is an heavenly Naturenature, they receive an Anointinganointing from Aboveabove; that Principleprinciple of true Religionreligion which is in them, is a Communicationcommunication
of the Religionreligion of Heavenheaven; their Gracegrace is the Dawndawn of Gloryglory; and God fits them for that Worldworld by conforming them to it.
9. This appears from the Naturenature and Designdesign of the Ordinancesordinances and Dutiesduties, which God hath appointed, as Meansmeans and Expressionsexpressions of true Religionreligion.

To instance in the Dutyduty of Prayerprayer: 'Tis'tis manifest, we are not appointed, in this Dutyduty, to declare God's Perfectionsperfections, his Majestymajesty, Holinessholiness, Goodnessgoodness, and Allsufficiencyall-sufficiencyallsufficiency, and our own Meannessmeanness, Emptinessemptiness, Dependencedependence, and Unworthinessunworthiness, and our Wantswants and Desiresdesires, to inform God of these Thingsthings, or to incline his Heartheart, and prevail with him to be willing to shewshow us Mercymercy; but suitably to affect our own Heartshearts with the Thingsthings we express, and so to prepare us to receive the Blessingsblessings we ask. And the Dutyduty of singing Praisespraises to God, seems to be appointed wholly to excite and express religious Affectionsaffections. No other Reasonreason can be assigned, why we should express our selves to God in Verseverse, rather than in Proseprose, and do it with Musickmusicmusick, but only, that such is our Naturenature and Frameframe, that these Thingsthings have a Tendencytendency to move our Affectionsaffections.

The same thing appears in the Naturenature and Designdesign of the Sacramentssacraments, which God hath appointed. And the impressing divine Thingsthings on the Heartshearts and Affectionsaffections of Menmen, is evidently one great and main Endend for which God has ordained, that his Wordword delivered in the holy Scriptures, should be opened, applied, and set home upon Menmen, in Preachingpreaching. And therefore it don't answer the Aimaim which God had in this Institutioninstitution, meerlymerely for Menmen to have good Commentariescommentaries and Expositionsexpositions on the Scripture, and other good Booksbooks of Divinitydivinity; because, altho'although these may tend, as well as Preachingpreaching, to give Menmen a good doctrinal or speculative Understandingunderstanding of the Workthings of the wordwork of God, yet they have not an equal Tendencytendency to impress them on Men'smen's Heartshearts and Affectionsaffections. God hath appointed a particular, and lively Applicationapplication of his Wordword, to Menmen, in the Preachingpreaching of it, as a fit Meansmeans to affect Sinnerssinners, with the Importanceimportance of the Thingsthings of Religionreligion, and their own Miserymisery, and Necessitynecessity of a Remedyremedy, and the Gloryglory and Sufficiencysufficiency of a Remedyremedy
provided; and to stir up the pure Mindsminds of the Saintssaints, and quicken their Affectionsaffections, by often bringing the great Thingsthings of Religionreligion to their Remembranceremembrance, and setting them before them in their proper Colourscolorscolours, tho'though they know them, and have been fully instructed in them already; 2 Pet. 1.: 12, 13. And particularly, to promote those two Affectionsaffections in them, which are spoken of in the Texttext, Lovelove and Joy: Christ gave same Apostlesapostles, and some Prophetsprophets, and some Evangelistsevangelists, and some Pastorspastors and Teachersteachers, that the Bodybody of Christ might be edified in Lovelove, Eph. 4.: 11, 12, 16. And another Affectionaffection which God has appointed Preachingpreaching as a Meansmeans to promote in the Saintssaints, is Joyjoy; and therefore Ministersministers are called Helpershelpers of their Joyjoy, 2 Cor. 1.: 24.

10. 'Tis an Evidenceevidence that true Religionreligion, or Holinessholiness of Heartheart, lies very much in the Affectionaffection of the Heartheart, that the Scriptures place the Sinsin of the Heartheart very much in Hardnesshardness of Heartheart.
