But the Househouse of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: Forfor all the Househouse of Israel are impudent and hard-hearted. The Wickednesswickedness of that perverse rebellious Generationgeneration in the Wildernesswilderness, is ascribed to the Hardnesshardness of their Heartshearts; Psal.Ps 95.: 7,—10, To Dayday, if ye will hear my Voicevoice, harden not your Heartheart, as in the Provocationprovocation, and as in the Dayday of Temptationtemptation in the Wildernesswilderness; when your Fathersfathers tempted me, proved me, and saw my Workwork: Fortyforty Yearsyears long was I grieved with this Generationgeneration, and said it is a Peoplepeople that do err in their Heartheart, &c.—Thisthis is spoken of as what prevented Zedekiah's turning to the Lord, 2 Chron.Chr 36.: 13. He stiffened his Neckneck, and hardnedhardened his Heartheart, from turning to the Lord God of Israel. This Principleprinciple is spoken of, as that from whence Menmen are without the Fearfear of God, and depart from God's Ways: • Isai.Isa 63.: 17. O Lord, why hast thou made us to err from thy Waysways, and hardnedhardened our Heartheart from thy Fearfear? And Men'smen's rejecting Christ, and opposing Christ anityChristianity, is laid to this Principleprinciple; Acts 19.: 9. But when divers were hardnedhardened, and believed not, but spake Evilevil of that Wayway before the Multitudemultitude;—God's leaving Menmen to the Powerpower of the Sinsin and
Corruptioncorruption of the Heartheart, is often express'dexpressed by God's hardening 〈◊〉 their Heartshearts; Rom. 9,: 18. Therefore hath he Mercymercy on whom 〈…〉 he will have 〈◊〉 Mercymercy, and whom he will he hardeneth. John 12.: 40. He hath blinded 〈◊〉 their Mindsminds, and hardened their Heartshearts. And the Apostleapostle seems to speak of an evil Heartheart, that departs from the living God, and a hard Heartheart, as the same Thingthing. Heb. 3.: 8. Harden not your Heartheart, as in the Provocationprovocation, &c. Verse 12, 13. Take heed Brethrenbrethren, lest there be in any of you an evil Heartheart of Unbeliefunbelief in departing from the living God, but exhort one another daily, while it is called to Dayday; lest any of you be hardened through the Deceitfulnessdeceitfulness of Sinsin. And that great Workwork of God in Conversionconversion, which consists in delivering a Personperson from the Powerpower of Sinsin, and mortifying Corruptioncorruption, is express'dexpressed, once and again, by God's taking away the Heartheart of Stonestone, and giving an Heartheart of Fleshflesh, Ezek. 11.: 19. andAnd Chapchchap. 36.: 26.

Now by a hard Heartheart, is plainly meant an unaffected Heartheart, or a Heartheart not easy to be moved with vertuousvirtuous Affectionsaffections, like a Stonestone, insensible, stupid, unmoved and hard to be impressed. Hence the hard Heartheart is called a stony 〈◊〉 Heartheart, and is opposed to an Heartheart of Fleshflesh, that has feeling, and is sensibly touch'dtouched and moved. We read in Scripture of a hard Heartheart, and a tender Heartheart: Andand doubtless we are to understand these, as contrary the one to the other. But what is a tender Heartheart, but a Heartheart which is easily impressed with what ought to affect it? God commends Josiah, because his Heartheart was tender; and 'tis evident by those Thingsthings which are mention'dmentioned as Expressionsexpressions and Evidencesevidences of this Tendernesstenderness of Heartheart, that by his Heartheart being tender is meant, his Heartheart being easily moved with religious and pious Affectionaffection; 2 KingsKgs 22.: 19. Because thine Heartheart was tender, and thou hast humbled thy self before the Lord, when thou heardstheardest what I spake against this Placeplace, and against the Inhabitantsinhabitants thereof, that they should become a Desolationdesolation, and a Cursecurse, and hast rent thy Clothesclothes, and hast wept before me; I also have heard thee, saith the Lord. And this is one thing, wherein it is necessary we should become as little Childrenchildren, in order to our entringentering into the Kingdomkingdom of God, even that we should have our Heartshearts tender, and easily affected and moved in spiritual and divine Thingsthings, as little Childrenchildren have in other Thingsthings.

'Tis very plain in some Placesplaces, in the Textstexts themselves, that by Hardnesshardness of Heartheart is meant a Heartheart void of Affectionaffection. So to signify the Ostrich's being without natural Affectionaffection to her Youngyoung, it is said, Job 39.: 16. She hardeneth her Heartheart against her young Onesones, as though they were not hers. So a Personperson having a Heartheart unaffected in Timetime of Dangerdanger, is express'dexpressed by his hardening his Heartheart, Prov. 28.: 14 Happy is the Manman that feareth alwayalways; but he that hardneth his Heartheart shall fall into Mischiefmischief.

Now therefore since it is so plain, that by a hard Heartheart, in Scripture, is meant a Heartheart destitute of pious Affectionsaffections, and since also
the Scriptures do so frequently place the Sinsin and Corruptioncorruption of the Heartheart in Hardnesshardness of Heartheart; it is evident, that the Gracegrace and Holinessholiness of the Heartheart, on the contrary, must, in a great Measuremeasure, consist in its having pious Affectionsaffections, and being easily susceptive of such Affectionaffection. Divines are generally agreed, that Sinsin radically and fundamentally consists in what is negative, or privative, having its Rootroot and Foundationfoundation in a Privationprivation or Wantwant of Holinessholiness. And therefore undoubtedly, if it be so that Sinsin does very much consist in Hardnesshardness of Heartheart, and so in the Wantwant of pious Affectionsaffections of Heartheart; Holinessholiness does consist very much in those pious Affectionsaffections.

I am far from supposing that all Affe • ctionsaffections do shewshow a tender Heartheart: Hatredhatred, Angeranger, Vain-glory, and other selfish and self-exalting Affectionsaffections, may greatly prevail in the hardest Heartheart. But yet it is evident that Hardnesshardness of Heartheart, and Tendernesstenderness of Heartheart, are Expressionsexpressions that relate to the Affectionsaffections of the Heartheart, and denote the Heart'sheart's being susceptible of, or shut up against, certain Affectionsaffections, of which I shall have Occasionoccasion to speak more afterwards.

Upon the Wholewhole, I think it clearly and abundantly evident, that true Religionreligion lies very much in the Affectionsaffections. Not that I think these Argumentsarguments prove, that Religionreligion in the Heartshearts of the truly Godlygodly, is ever in exact Proportionproportion to the Degreedegree of Affectionaffection, and present Emotionemotion of the Mindmind. For undoubtedly, there is much Affectionaffection in the true Saintssaints which is not spiritual: Theirtheir religious Affectionsaffections are often mixed; all is not from Gracegrace, but much from Naturenature. And tho'though the Affectionsaffections have not their Seatseat in the Bodybody, yet the Constitutionconstitution of the Bodybody, may very much contribute to the present Emotionemotion of the Mindmind. And the Degreedegree of Religionreligion is rather to be judged of by the Fixednessfixedness and Strengthstrength of the Habithabit that is exercised in Affectionaffection, whereby holy Affectionaffection is habitual, than by the Degreedegree of the present Exerciseexercise: Andand the Strengthstrength of that Habithabit is not always in Proportionproportion to outward Effectseffects and Manifestationsmanifestations, or inward Effectseffects, in the Hurryhurry and Vehemencevehemence, and sudden Changeschanges of the Coursecourse of the Thoughtsthoughts of the Mindmind. But yet it is evident, that Religionreligion consists so much in Affectionaffection, as that without holy Affectionaffection there is no true Religionreligion▪: Andand no Lightlight in the Understandingunderstanding is good, which don't produce holy Affectionaffection in the Heartheart; no Habithabit or Principleprinciple in the Heartheart is good, which has no such Exerciseexercise; and no external Fruitfruit is good, which don't proceed from such Exercisesexercises.
Having thus considered the Evidenceevidence of the Propositionproposition laid down, I proceed to some Inferencesinferences.
1. We may hence learn how great their Errorerror is, who are for discarding all religious Affectionsaffections, as having nothing solid or substantial in them.

There seems to be too much of a Dispositiondisposition this Wayway, prevailing in this Landland at this Timetime. Because many who, in the late extraordinary Seasonseason, appeared to have great religious Affectionsaffections, did not manifest a right Tempertemper of Mindmind, and run into many Errorserrors, in the Timetime of their Affectionaffection, and the Heatheat of their Zealzeal; and because the high Affectionsaffections of many seem to be so soon come to nothing, and some who seemed to be mightily raised and swallowed with Joyjoy and Zealzeal, for a Whilewhile, seem to have returned like the Dogdog to his Vomitvomit: Hencehence religious Affectionsaffections in general are grown out of Creditcredit, with great Numbersnumbers, as tho'though true Religionreligion did not at all consist in them. Thus we easily, and naturally run from one Extremeextreme to another. A little while ago we were in the other Extremeextreme; there was a prevalent Dispositiondisposition to look upon all high religious Affectionsaffections, as eminent Exercisesexercises of true Gracegrace, without much inquiring into the Naturenature and Sourcesource of those Affectionsaffections, and the Mannermanner in which they arose: Ifif Personspersons did but appear to be indeed very much moved and raised, so as to be full of religious Talktalk, and express themselves with great Warmthwarmth and Earnestnessearnestness, and to be fill'dfilled, or to be very full, as the Phrasesphrases were; it was too much the Mannermanner, without further Examinationexamination, to conclude such Personspersons were full of the Spirit of God, and had eminent Experienceexperience of his gracious Influencesinfluences. This was the Extremeextreme which was prevailing three or four Yearsyears ago. But of late, instead of esteeming and admiring all religious Affectionsaffections, without Distinctiondistinction, it is a Thingthing much more prevalent, to reject and discard all without Distinctiondistinction. Herein appears the Subtiltysubtletysubtilty of Satan. While he saw that Affectionsaffections were much in Voguevogue, knowing the greater Partpart of the Landland were not versed in such Thingsthings, and had not had much Experienceexperience of great religious Affectionsaffections, to enable them to judge well of 'emthem, and distinguish between true and false; then he knew he could best play his Gamegame, by sowing Tarestares amongst the Wheatwheat, and mingling false Affectionsaffections with the Worksworks of God's Spirit: Hehe knew this to be a likely Wayway to delude and eternally ruin many Soulssouls, and greatly to wound Religionreligion in the Saintssaints, and entangle them in a dreadful Wildernesswilderness, and by and by, to bring all Religionreligion into Disreputedisrepute. But now, when the ill Consequencesconsequences of these false Affectionsaffections appear, and 'tis become very apparent, that some of those Emotionsemotions which made a glaring Shewshow, and were by many greatly admired, were in Realityreality Nothingnothing; the Devildevil sees it to be for his Interestinterest to go another Wayway to work, and to endeavourendeavor to his utmost to propagate and establish a Perswasionpersuasion, that all Affectionsaffections and sensible Emotionsemotions of the Mindmind, in Thingsthings of Religionreligion, are nothing at all to be regarded, but are rather to be avoided, and carefully guarded against, as Thingsthings of a pernicious Tendencytendency. This he knows is the Wayway to bring all Religionreligion to a meermere lifeless Formalityformality, and effectually shut out the Powerpower of Godlinessgodliness, and every Thingthing which is spiritual, and to have all true
Christianity turn'dturned out of Doorsdoors. For altho'although to true Religionreligion, there must indeed be something else besides Affectionaffection; yet true Religionreligion consists so much in the Affectionsaffections, that there can be no true Religionreligion without them. He who has no religious Affectionaffection, is in a Statestate of spiritual Deathdeath, and is wholly destitute of the powerful, quickening, saving Influencesinfluences of the Spirit of God upon his Heartheart. As there is no true Religionreligion, where there is nothing else but Affectionaffection; so there is no true Religionreligion where there is no religious Affectionaffection. As on the one Handhand, there must be Lightlight in the Understandingunderstanding, as well as an affected fervent Heartheart, where there is Heatheat without Lightlight, there can be nothing divine or heavenly in that Heartheart; so on the other Handhand, where there is a Kindkind of Lightlight without Heatheat, a He • adhead stored with Notionsnotions and Speculationsspeculations, with a cold and una • ffected Heartheart, there can be nothing divine in that Lightlight, that Knowledgeknowledge is no true spiritual Knowledgeknowledge of divine Thingsthings. If the great Thingsthings of Religionreligion are rightly understood, they will affect the Heartheart. The Reasonreason why Menmen are not affected by such infinitely great, important, glorious, and wonderful Thingsthings, as they often hear and read of, in the Wordword of God, is undoubtedly because they are blind; if they were not so, it would be impossible, and utterly inconsistent with human Naturenature, that their Heartshearts should be otherwise, than strongly impress'dimpressed, and greatly moved by such Thingsthings.

This Mannermanner of slighting all religious Affectionsaffections, is the Wayway exceedingly to harden the Heartshearts of Menmen, and to encourage 'emthem in their Stupiditystupidity and Senselessnesssenselessness, and to keep 'emthem in a Statestate of spiritual Deathdeath as long as they live, and bring 'emthem at last to Deathdeath eternal. The prevailing Prejudiceprejudice against religious Affectionsaffections at this Dayday, in the Landland, is apparently of awful Effecteffect, to harden the Heartshearts of Sinnerssinners, and damp the Gracesgraces of many of the Saintssaints, and stundstun the Lifelife and Powerpower of Religionreligion, and preclude the Effecteffect of Ordinancesordinances, and hold us down in a Statestate of Dulnessdullnessdulness and Apathyapathy, and undoubtedly causes many Personspersons greatly to offend God, in entertaining mean and low Thoughtsthoughts of the extraordinary Workwork he has lately wrought in this Landland.

And for Personspersons to despise and cry down all religious Affectionsaffections, is the Wayway to shut all Religionreligion out of their own Heartshearts, and to make thorough Workwork in ruining their Soulssouls.

They who condemn high Affectionsaffections in others, are certainly not likely to have high Affectionsaffections themselves. And let it be considered 〈◊〉 be consideredbe consider’d, that they who have but little religious Affectionaffection, have certainly but little Religionreligion. And they who condemn others for their religious Affectionsaffections, and have none themselves, have no Religionreligion.

There are false Affectionsaffections, and there are true. A Man'sman's having much Affectionaffection, don't prove that he has any true Religionreligion: Butbut if he has no Affectionaffection, it proves that he has no true Religionreligion. The right
Wayway, is not to reject all Affectionsaffections, nor to approve all; but to distinguish between Affectionsaffections, approving some, and rejecting others; separating between the Wheatwheat and the Chaffchaff, the Goldgold and the Drossdross, the Preciousprecious and the Vilevile.

2. If it be so, that true Religionreligion lies much in the Affectionsaffections, hence we may infer, that such Meansmeans are to be desired, as have much of a Tendencytendency to move the Affectionsaffections. Such Booksbooks, and such a Wayway of Preachingpreaching the Wordword, and Administrationadministration of Ordinancesordinances, and such a Wayway of worshipping God in Prayerprayer, and singing Praisespraises, is much to be desired, as has a Tendencytendency deeply to affect the Heartshearts of those who attend these Meansmeans.

Such a Kindkind of Meansmeans, would formerly have been highly approved of and applauded by the Generalitygenerality of the Peoplepeople of the Landland, as the most excellent and profitable, and having the greatest Tendencytendency to promote the Endsends of the Meansmeans of Gracegrace. But the prevailing Tastetaste seems of late strangely to be alter'daltered: Thatthat pathetical Mannermanner of Prayingpraying and Preachingpreaching, which would formerly have been admir'dadmired and extolled 〈◊〉 extolledextoll’d, and that for this Reasonreason, because it had such a Tendencytendency to move the Affectionsaffections, now, in great Multitudesmultitudes, immediately excites Disgustdisgust, and moves no other Affectionsaffections, than those of Displeasuredispleasure and Contemptcontempt.

Perhaps, formerly the Generalitygenerality (at least of the common Peoplepeople) were in the Extremeextreme, of looking too much to an affectionate Addressaddress, in publickpublic Performancesperformances: Butbut now, a very great Partpart of the Peoplepeople, seem to have gone far into a contrary Extremeextreme. Indeed there may be such Meansmeans, as may have a great Tendencytendency to stir up the Passionspassions of weak and ignorant Personspersons, and yet have no great Tendencytendency to Benefitbenefit their Soulssouls. For tho'though they may have a Tendencytendency to excite Affectionsaffections, they may have little or none to excite gracious Affectionsaffections, or any Affectionsaffections tending to Gracegrace. But undoubtedly, if the Thingsthings of Religionreligion, in the Meansmeans used, are treated according to their Naturenature, and exhibited truly, so as tends to convey just Apprehensionsapprehensions, and a right Judgmentjudgment of them; the more they have a Tendencytendency to move the Affectionsaffections, the better.

3. If true Religionreligion lies much in the Affectionsaffections, hence we may learn, what great Causecause we have to be ashamed and confounded before God 〈◊〉 , that we are no more affected with the great Thingsthings of Religionreligion. It appears from what has been said, that this arises from our having so little true Religionreligion.

God has given to Mankindmankind Affectionsaffections, for the same Purposepurpose which he has given all the Facultiesfaculties and Principlesprinciples of the human Soulsoul for, viz. thatThat they might be subservient to Man'sman's chief Endend, and the great Businessbusiness for which God has created him, that is the Businessbusiness of Religionreligion.
And yet how common is it among Mankindmankind, that their Affectionsaffections are much more exercised and engaged in other Mattersmatters, than in Religionreligion! In Thingsthings which concern Men'smen's worldly Interestinterest, their outward Delightsdelights, their Honourhonorhonour and Reputationreputation, and their natural Relationsrelations, they have their Desiresdesires eager, their Appetitesappetites vehement, their Lovelove warm and affectionate, their Zealzeal ardent; in these Thingsthings their Heartshearts are tender and sensible, easily moved, deeply impress'dimpressed, much concerned, very sensibly affected, and greatly engaged; much depress'ddepressed with Griefgrief at worldly Losseslosses, and highly raised with Joyjoy at worldly Successessuccesses and Prosperityprosperity. But how insensible and unmov'dunmoved are most Menmen, about the great Thingsthings of another Worldworld! How dull are their Affectionsaffections! How heavy and hard their Heartshearts in these Mattersmatters! Here their Lovelove is cold, their Desiresdesires languid, their Zealzeal low, and their Gratitudegratitude small. How they can sit and hear of the infinite Heightheight and Depthdepth and Lengthlength and Breadthbreadth of the Lovelove of God in Christ Jesus, of his giving his infinitely dear Son, to be offered up a Sacrificesacrifice for the Sinssins of Menmen, and of the unparallel'dunparalleled Lovelove of the innocent, holy and tender Lamb of God, manifested in his dying Agoniesagonies, his bloody Sweatsweat, his loud and bitter Criescries, and bleeding Heartheart, and all this for Enemiesenemies, to redeem them from deserved, eternal Burningsburnings, and to bring to unspeakable and everlasting Joyjoy and Gloryglory; and yet be cold, and heavy, insensible, and regardless! Where are the Exercisesexercises of our Affectionsaffections proper, if not here? What is it that does more require them? And what can be a fit Occasionoccasion of their lively and vigorous Exerciseexercise, if not such an one as this? Can any Thingthing be set in our Viewview, greater and more important? Any Thingthing more wonderful and surprising? Or more nearly concerning our Interestinterest? Can we suppose the wise Creator implanted such Principlesprinciples in the human Naturenature as the Affectionsaffections, to be of Useuse to us, and to be exercised on certain proper Occasionsoccasions, but to lie still on such an Occasionoccasion as this? Can any Christian, who believes the Truthtruth of these Thingsthings, entertain such Thoughtsthoughts?

If we ought ever to exercise our Affectionsaffections at all, and if the Creator han't unwisely constituted the human Naturenature, in making these Principlesprinciples a Partpart of it, when they are vain and useless; then they ought to be exercised about those Objectsobjects which are most worthy of them. But is there any Thingthing, which Christians can find in Heavenheaven or Earthearth, so worthy to be the Objectsobjects of their Admirationadmiration and Lovelove, their earnest and longing Desiresdesires, their Hopehope, and their Rejoicingrejoicing, and their fervent Zealzeal, as those Thingsthings that are held forth to us in the Gospelgospel of Jesus Christ? In which, not only are Thingsthings declared most worthy to affect us, but they are exhibited in the most affecting Mannermanner. The Gloryglory and Beautybeauty of the blessed Jehovah, which is most worthy in it self, to be the Objectobject of our Admirationadmiration and Lovelove, is there exhibited in the most affecting Mannermanner that can be conceived of, as
it appears shining in all its Lustrelusterlustre, in the Faceface of an incarnate, infinitely loving, meek, compassionate, dying Redeemer. All the Vertuesvirtues of the Lamb of God, his Humilityhumility, Patiencepatience, Meeknessmeekness, Submissionsubmission, Obedienceobedience, Lovelove & Compassioncompassion, are exhibited to our Viewview, in a manner the most tending to move our Affectionsaffections, of any that can be imagined; as they all had their greatest Trialtrial, and their highest Exerciseexercise, and so their brightest Manifestationmanifestation, when he was in the most affecting Circumstancescircumstances; even when he was under 〈◊〉 his last Sufferingssufferings, those unutterable and unparallel'dunparalleled Sufferingssufferings, he endured, from his tender Lovelove and Pitypity to us. There also, the hateful Naturenature of our Sinssins is manifested in the most affecting Mannermanner possible; as we see the dreadful Effectseffects of them, in what our Redeemer, who undertook to answer for us, suffered for them. And there we have the most affecting Manifestationsmanifestations of God's Hatredhatred of Sinsin, and his Wrathwrath and Justicejustice in punishing it; as we see his Justicejustice in the Strictnessstrictness and Inflexiblenessinflexibleness of it, and his Wrathwrath in its Terriblenessterribleness, in so dreadfully punishing our Sinssins, in Oneone who was infinitely dear to him, and loving to us. So has God disposed Thingsthings, in the Affairaffair of our Redemptionredemption, and in his glorious Dispensationsdispensations, revealed to us in the Gospelgospel, as tho'though every Thingthing were purposely contrived in such a Mannermanner, as to have the greatest, possible Tendencytendency to reach our Heartshearts in the most tender Partpart, and move our Affectionsaffections most sensibly and strongly. How great Causecause have we therefore to be humbled to the Dustdust, that we are no more affected!

div.head: PART II.
ShewingShowing what are no certain Signs that religious Affections are truly gracious, or that they are not.
div.p: IFIf any one, on the Readingreading of what has been just now said, is ready to acquit himself, and say, I am not one of those who have no religious Affectionsaffections; I am often greatly moved with the Considerationconsideration of the great Thingsthings of Religionreligion; Letlet him not content himself with this, that he has religious Affectionsaffections. For (as was observed before) as we ought not to reject and condemn all Affectionsaffections, as tho'though true Religionreligion did not at all consist in Affectionaffection; so on the other Handhand, we ought not to approve of all, as tho'though every one that was religiously affected, had true Gracegrace, and was therein the Subjectsubject of the saving Influencesinfluences of the Spirit of God: and that therefore the right Wayway is to distinguish among religious Affectionsaffections, between one sort and another. Therefore let us now endeavourendeavor to do this: Andand in order to it, I would do two Thingsthings.

I. I would mention some Thingsthings, which are no Signssigns one Wayway or the other, either that Affectionsaffections are such as true Religionreligion consists in, or that they are otherwise; that we may be guarded against judging of Affectionsaffections by false Signssigns.
II. I would observe some Thingsthings, wherein those Affectionsaffections which are spiritual and gracious, differ from those which are not so, and may be distinguished and known.
FIRST, I would take Noticenotice of some Thingsthings, which are no Signssigns that Affectionsaffections are gracious, or that they are not.
I. 'Tis no Signsign one Wayway or the other, that religious Affectionsaffections are very great, or raised very high.

Some are ready to condemn all high Affectionsaffections: Ifif Personspersons appear to have their religious Affectionsaffections raised to an 〈◊◊〉 raised to anrais'd to an extraordinary Pitchpitch, they are prejudiced against them, and determine that they are Delusionsdelusions, without further Enquiryinquiryenquiry. But if it be as has been proved, that true Religionreligion lies 〈◊〉 very much in religious Affectionsaffections, then it follows, that if there be a great deal 〈◊〉 of true Religionreligion, there will be great religious Affectionsaffections; if true Religionreligion in the Heartshearts of Menmen, be raised to a great Heightheight, divine and holy Affectionsaffections will be raised to a great Heightheight.

Love is an Affectionaffection; but will any Christian say, Menmen ought not to love God and Jesus Christ in a high Degreedegree? And will any say, we ought not to have a very great Hatredhatred of Sinsin, and a very deep Sorrowsorrow for it? Or that we ought not to exercise a high Degreedegree of Gratitudegratitude to God, for the Merciesmercies we receive of him, and the great Thingsthings he has done for the Salvationsalvation of fallen Menmen? Or that we should not have very great and strong Desiresdesires after God and Holinessholiness? Is there any who will profess, that his Affectionsaffections in Religionreligion are great enough; and will say, I have no Causecause to be humbled, that I am no more affected with the Thingsthings of Religionreligion than I am, I have no Reasonreason to be ashamed, that I have no greater Exercisesexercises of Lovelove to God, and Sorrowsorrow for Sinsin, and Gratitudegratitude for the Merciesmercies which I have received? Who is there that will go and bless God, that he is affected enough with what he has read and heard, of the wonderful Lovelove of God to Wormsworms and Rebelsrebels, in giving his only begotten Son to die for them, and of the dying Lovelove of Christ; and will pray that he mayn't be affected with them in any higher Degreedegree, because high Affectionsaffections are improper, and very unlovely in Christians, being enthusiastical, and ruinous to true Religionreligion?

Our Texttext plainly speaks of great and high Affectionsaffections, when it speaks of rejoicing with Joyjoy unspeakable and full of Gloryglory: Herehere the most suparlativesuperlative Expressionsexpressions are used, which Languagelanguage will afford. And the Scriptures often require us to exercise very high Affectionsaffections: Thusthus in the first and great Commandmentcommandment of the Lawlaw, there is an Accumulationaccumulation of Expressionsexpressions, as tho'though Wordswords were wanting to express the Degreedegree, in which we ought to love God; Thou shalt love the Lord thy God, with all thy Heartheart, with all thy Soulsoul, with all thy Mindmind, and with all thy Strengthstrength. So the Saintssaints are called upon to exercise high Degreesdegrees of Joyjoy: Rejoicerejoice, says Christ to his Disciplesdisciples, and be exceeding glad, Matth.Matt 5.: 12. So it is said, Psal.Ps 68.: 3. Let the Righteousrighteous be glad; let them rejoice before God; yea, let them exceedingly
rejoice. So in the same Bookbook of Psalms, the Saintssaints are often called upon to shout 〈◊〉 for Joyjoy; and in Luke to 6. 23. leap 〈◊〉 Leap for Joyjoy. So they are abundantly called upon to exercise 〈◊〉 high Degreesdegrees of Gratitudegratitude for Merciesmercies, to Praise God with all their Heartshearts, with Heartshearts lifted up in the Waysways of the Lord, and their Soulssouls magnifying the Lord, singing his praises, talking of his wondrous Workwork, declaring 〈◊〉 his Doingsdoings. &c.

And we find the most eminent Saints 〈◊◊〉 in Scripture, often professing high Affectionsaffections. Thus the Psalmistpsalmist speaks of his Lovelove, as if it were unspeakable; Psal.Ps 119.: 97 • . Oh how love 〈◊◊〉 I thy Lawlaw! So he expresses a great Degreedegree of Hatred 〈◊〉 hatred of Sinsin; Psal.Ps 139 • .: 21, 22. Do I not hate them, O Lord, that have thee? And am I not grieved with them that rise 〈◊〉 up against thee? I hate them with 〈◊〉 perfect Hatredhatred. He also expresses a high Degreedegree of Sorrowsorrow for Sinsin: Hehe speaks of his Sinssins going over his Headhead, as an heavy Burden, that was too 〈…〉 heavy for him; and of his rearingroaring all the Dayday, and his Moisture’s 〈◊〉 being turned 〈◊〉 into the Droughtdrought of Sum •• summer, and his Bonesbones being as it were broken with Sorrowsorrow. So he often expresses great Degreesdegrees of spiritual Desiresdesires, in a Multitudemultitude of the strongest Expressionsexpressions which can be conceived of; such as his longing, his Soulssouls thirsting as a 〈◊◊〉 dry and thirsty Landland where no Waterwater is, his Pantingspantings, his Fleshflesh and Heartheart crying out, his Soulsoul breaking 〈◊〉 for the Longinglonging it hath 〈◊〉 , &c. He expresses the Exercisesexercises of great and extreme Griefgrief for the Sinssins of others. Psal.Ps 119.: 136. Rivers of Waterwater run down mine Eyeseyes, because they keep not thy Lawlaw. And Verseverse 53. Horror hath taken hold upon me, because of the Wickedwicked that forsake thy Lawlaw. He expresses high Exercisesexercises of Joyjoy, Psal.Ps 21.: 1. The King shall joy 〈◊〉 in thy Strengthstrength; and in thy Salvationsalvation, how greatly shall he rejoice. Psal.Ps 71.: 23. My Lipslips shall greatly rejoice, when I sing unto thee. Psal.Ps 73.: 3 ---7 〈◊〉 . Because thy loving Kindnesskindness is better than Lifelife, my Lipslips shall praise thee. Thus will I bless thee, while I live: I will lift up my Handshands in thy Namename: Mymy Soulsoul shall be satisfied as with Marrowmarrow and Fatnessfatness, and my Mouthmouth shall praise thee with joyful Lipslips: Whenwhen I remember thee 〈◊〉 upon my Bedbed, and meditate on thee in the Nightnight Watches. 〈◊〉 ; because thou Lastlast been my Helphelp, therefore in the Shadowshadow of thy Wingswings will I rejoice.

The Apostleapostle Paul expresses high Exercisesexercises of Affectionaffection. Thus he expresses the Exercisesexercises of Pitypity and Concernconcern for others Goodgood, even to Anguish of Heartheart; a great, fervent and abundant Lovelove, and earnest and longing Desiresdesires, and exceeding Joyjoy; and speaks of the Exultation 〈◊〉 exultation and Triumphstriumphs of his Soulsoul, and his earnest Expectationexpectation and Hopehope, and his abundant Tearstears, and the Travailstravails of his Soulsoul, in Pitypity, Griefgrief, earnest Desiresdesires, godly Jealousyjealousy and fervent Zealzeal, in many Placesplaces that have been cited already, and which therefore I need not repeat. John the Baptist expressed great Joyjoy, John 3.: 3929. Those blessed Womenwomen that anointed the Bodybody of Jesus are 〈◊〉 represented as in a very high Exerciseexercise of religious Affectionaffection, on Occasionoccasion of Christ's Resurrectionresurrection; Matth, 28. 8. And they departed from the Sepulchresepulchersepulchre, with Fearfear and great Joyjoy.

'Tis often foretold of the Churchchurch of God, in her future happy Seasonsseasons here on Earthearth, that they shall exceedingly rejoice; Psal.Ps 89 • .: 15, 16 • . They shall walk, O Lord, in the Lightlight of thy Countenance 〈◊〉 countenance: Inin thy Namename shall they rejoice all the Day, and in thy Righteousness shall they be exalted. Zech. 〈…〉 9. 9. Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion, shout, O 〈…〉 shall they rejoice all the Day, and in thy Righteousness shall they be exalted. Zech 9:9. Rejoice greatly, O Daughter of Zion, shout, O Daughterdaughter of Jerusalem: Beholdbehold thy King cometh 〈◊〉 . &c. The same is represented in innumerable other Placesplaces. And because high Degreesdegrees of Joyjoy are the proper and genuine Fruits 〈◊◊〉 of the Gospelgospel of Christ, therefore the Angelangel calls 〈◊〉 this Gospelgospel, good 〈◊〉 Tydingstidingstydings of great Joyjoy, that should be to all 〈◊◊〉 Peoplepeople.

The Saintssaints and Angelsangels in Heavenheaven, that have Religionreligion in it'sits highest Perfectionperfection, are exceedingly affected with what they behold and contemplate, of God's Perfectionsperfections and Worksworks. They are all as a pure heavenly Flameflame of Firefire, in their Lovelove, and in the Greatnessgreatness and Strengthstrength of their Joyjoy and Gratitudegratitude: Theirtheir Praisespraises are represented, as the Voice 〈◊〉 voice of many Waterswaters, and as the Voice 〈◊〉 voice of a great Thunderthunder. Now the only Reasonreason why their Affectionsaffections are so much higher than the holy Affectionsaffections of Saintssaints on Earthearth, is, they see the Thingsthings they are affected by, more according to their Truthtruth, and have their Affectionsaffections more conformed to the Naturenature of Thingsthings. And therefore, if religious Affectionsaffections in Menmen here below, are but of the same Naturenature and Kindkind with their's, the higher they are, and the nearer they are to their's in Degreedegree, the better; because therein they will be so much the more conformed to Truthtruth, as their's are.

From these Thingsthings it certainly appears, that religious Affectionsaffections being in a very high Degreedegree, is no Evidenceevidence that they are not such as have the Naturenature of true Religionreligion. Therefore they do greatly err, who condemn Personspersons as Enthusiastsenthusiasts, meerlymerely because their Affectionsaffections are very high.

And on the other Handhand, 'Tis'tis no Evidenceevidence that religious Affectionsaffections are of a spiritual and gracious Naturenature, because they are great. 'Tis very manifest by the holy Scripture, our sure and infallible Rulerule to judge of Thingsthings of this Naturenature, that there are religious Affectionsaffections which are very high, that are not spiritual and saving. The Apostleapostle Paul speaks of Affectionsaffections in the Galatians, which had been exceedingly elevated, and which yet he manifestly speaks of, as fearing that they were vain, and had come to nothing. Gal. 4.: 15. Where is the Blessednessblessedness you spake of 〈◊〉 ? For I bear you Recordrecord, that if it had been possible, you would have plucked 〈◊〉 out your own Eyeseyes, and have given them to me. And in the 11th Verseverse he tells them, he was afraid of 'emthem, lest he had bestowed upon them Labourlaborlabour in vain. So the Childrenchildren of Israel were greatly affected with God's Mercymercy to 'emthem, when they had seen how wonderfully he wrought for them at the Red Sea, where they sang God's Praisepraise; tho'though they soon forgat his Worksworks. So they were greatly affected again, at Mountmount Sinai, when they saw the marvelous
Manifectationsmanifestationsmanifectations God made of himself there; and seemed mightily engaged in their Mindsminds, and with great Forwardnessforwardness made Answeranswer, when God proposed his holy Covenantcovenant to them, saying, All that the Lord hath spoken will 〈◊〉 we do, and be obedient 〈◊〉 . But how soon was there an Endend to all this mighty Forwardnessforwardness and Engagednessengagedness of Affectionaffection? How quickly were they turned aside after other Godsgods, rejoicing and shouting around their golden Calfcalf? So great Multitudesmultitudes who were affected with the Miraclemiracle of raising Lazarus from the Deaddead, were elevated to a high Degreedegree, and made a mighty ado, when Jesus presently after enter'dentered into Jerusalem, exceedingly magnifying Christ, as tho'though the Groundground were not good enough for the Assass he rode to tread upon; and therefore cut down Branchesbranches of Palm-trees, and st •• rawedstrewed them in the Wayway; yea pull'dpulled off their Garmentsgarments, and spread them in the Wayway; and cried with loud Voicesvoices, Hosanna to the Son of David, Blessed is he that cometh in the Namename of the Lord, Hosanna in the Highesthighest; so as to make the whole Citycity ring again, and put all into an Uproaruproar. We learn by the Evangelistevangelist John, that the Reasonreason why the Peoplepeople made this ado, was because they were affected with the Miraclemiracle of raising Lazarus; John 12.: 18. Here was a vast Multitudemultitude crying Hosanna on this Occasionoccasion, so that it gave Occasionoccasion to the Pharisees to say, Behold the Worldworld is gone after him, John 12.: 19. butBut Christ had at that Timetime but few true Disciplesdisciples. And how quickly was this ado at an Endend? All of this Naturenature is quell'dquelled and dead, when this Jesus stands bound, with a mock Roberobe and a Crowncrown of Thornsthorns, to be derided, spit upon, scoarg'dscourged, condemn'dcondemned and executed. Indeed there was a great and loud Outout cry concerning him, among the Multitudemultitude then, as well as before; but of a very different Kindkind: 'Tis'tis not then, Hosanna, Hosanna, but Crucifycrucify, Crucifycrucify.

And it is the concurring Voicevoice of all orthodox Divinesdivines, that there may be religious Affectionsaffections, which are raised to a very high Degreedegree, and yet there be nothing of true Religionreligion. Mr. Stoddard observes, Thatthat common Affectionsaffections are sometimes stronger than saving. Guide to Christ. pP. 21.
II. 'Tis no Signsign that Affectionsaffections have the Naturenature of true Religionreligion, or that they have not, that they have great Effectseffects on the Bodybody.

All Affectionsaffections whatsoever, have in some Respectrespect or Degreedegree, an Effecteffect on the Bodybody. As was observed before, such is our Naturenature, and such are the Lawslaws of Unionunion of Soulsoul and Bodybody, that the Mindmind can have no lively or vigorous Exerciseexercise, without some Effecteffect upon the Bodybody. So subject is the Bodybody to the Mindmind, and so much do its Fluidsfluids, especially the animal Spiritsspirits, attend the 〈◊〉 Motionsmotions and Exercisesexercises of the Mindmind, that there can't be so much as an intense Thoughtthought,
without an Effecteffect upon them. Yea, 'tis questionable, whether an embodied Soulsoul ever so much as thinks one Thoughtthought, or has any Exerciseexercise at all, but that there is some corresponding Motionmotion or Alterationalteration of Motionmotion, in some Degreedegree, of the Fluidsfluids, in some Partpart of the Bodybody. But universal Experienceexperience shewsshows, that the Exerciseexercise of the Affectionsaffections, have in a special Mannermanner a Tendencytendency, to some sensible Effecteffect upon the Bodybody. And if • this be so, that all Affectionsaffections have some Effecteffect on the Bodybody, we may then well suppose, the greater those Affectionsaffections be, and the more vigorous their Exerciseexercise (other Circumstancescircumstances being equal) the greater will be the Effecteffect on the Bodybody. Hence it is not to be wondered at, that very great and strong Exercisesexercises of the Affectionsaffections, should have great Effectseffects on the Bodybody. And therefore, seeing there are very great Affectionsaffections, both common and spiritual; hence it is not to be wondered at, that great Effectseffects on the Bodybody, should arise from both these Kindskinds of Affectionsaffections. And consequently these Effectseffects are no Signssigns, that the Affectionsaffections they arise from, are of one Kindkind or the other.

Great Effectseffects on the Bodybody certainly are no sure Evidencesevidences that Affectionsaffections are spiritual; for we see that such Effectseffects oftentimes arise from great Affectionsaffections about temporal Thingsthings, and when Religionreligion is no Wayway concerned in them. And if great Affectionsaffections about secular Thingsthings,, that are purely natural, may have these Effectseffects, I know not by what Rulerule we should determine, that high Affectionsaffections about religious Thingsthings, which arise in like Mannermanner from Naturenature, can't have the like Effecteffect.

Nor on the other Handhand, do I know of any Rulerule any have to determine, that gracious and holy Affectionsaffections, when raised as high as 〈◊〉 any natural Affectionsaffections, and have equally strong and vigorous Exercisesexercises, can't have a great Effecteffect on the Bodybody. No such Rulerule can be drawn from Reasonreason: I know of no Reasonreason, why a being affected with a Viewview of God's Gloryglory should not cause the Bodybody to faint, as well as a being affected with a Viewview of Solomon's Gloryglory. And no such Rulerule has as yet been produced from the Scripture: Nonenone has ever been found in all the late Controversiescontroversies which have been about Thingsthings of this Naturenature. There is a great Powerpower in spiritual Affectionsaffections; we read of the Powerpower which worketh in Christians, Eph. 3.: 7. and of the Spirit of God being in them, as the Spirit of Powerpower, 2 Tim. 1.: 7. and of the effectual working of his Powerpower in them Ibid v. 7. Ibid. v. 19. yea of the working of God's mighty Powerpower in them. Eph. 1.: 19. But Man'sman's Naturenature is weak: Fleshflesh and Bloodblood are represented in Scripture as exceeding weak; and particularly with Respectrespect to it'sits Unfitnessunfitness for great spiritual and heavenly Operationsoperations and Exercisesexercises, Matth.Matt 26.: 41. 1 Cor. 15.: 43, & 50.
The Texttext we are upon speaks of Joy unspeakable, and full of Gloryglory. And who that considers what Man'sman's Naturenature is, and what the Naturenature of the Affectionsaffections are, can reasonably doubt but that such unutterable and glorious Joysjoys, may be too great and mighty for weak Dustdust and Ashesashes, so as to be considerably overbearing to it? It is evident by the Scripture, that true divine Discoveriesdiscoveries, or Ideasideas of God's Gloryglory, when given in a great Degreedegree, have a Tendencytendency, by affecting the Mindmind, to overbear the Bodybody; because the Scripture teaches us often, that if these Ideasideas or Viewsviews should be given to such a Degreedegree, as they are given in Heavenheaven, the weak Frameframe of the Bodybody could not subsist under it, and that no Manman can, in that Mannermanner, see God and live. The Knowledgeknowledge which the Saintssaints have of God's Beautybeauty and Gloryglory in this Worldworld, and those holy Affectionsaffections that arise from it, are of the same Naturenature and Kindkind with what the Saintssaints are the Subjectssubjects of in Heavenheaven, differing only in Degreedegree and Circumstancescircumstances: Whatwhat God gives them here, is a Foretasteforetaste of heavenly Happinesshappiness, and an Earnestearnest of their future Inheritanceinheritance. And who shall limit God in his giving this Earnestearnest, or say he shall give so much of the Inheritanceinheritance, such a Partpart of the future Rewardreward, as an Earnestearnest of the Wholewhole, and no more? And seeing God has taught us in his Wordword, that the whole Rewardreward is such, that it would at once destroy the Bodybody, is it not too bold a Thingthing for us, so to set Boundsbounds to the sovereign God, as to say, that in giving the Earnestearnest of this Rewardreward in this Worldworld, he shall never give so much of it, as in the least to diminish the Strengthstrength of the Bodybody, when God has no where thus limited himself?

The Psalmistpsalmist speaking of vehement religious Affectionsaffections he had, speaks of an Effecteffect in his Fleshflesh or Bodybody, besides what was in his Soulsoul, expressly distinguishing one from the other, once and again, Psal.Ps 84.: 2. My Soulsoul longeth, yea even fainteth for the Courtscourts of the Lord, my Heartheart and my Fleshflesh crieth out for the living God. Here is a plain Distinctiondistinction between the Heartheart and the Fleshflesh, as being each affected. So Psal.Ps 63.: 1. My Soulsoul thirsteth for thee, my Fleshflesh longeth for thee, in a dry and thirsty Landland, where no Waterwater is. Here also is an evident designed Distinctiondistinction between the Soulsoul and the Fleshflesh.

The Prophetprophet Habakkuk speaks of his Body's being over-born, by a Sensesense of the Majestymajesty of God, Hab. 3.: 16. When I heard, my Bellybelly trembled, my Lipslips quivered at the Voicevoice, Rottennessrottenness enter'dentered into my Bonesbones, and I trembled in myself. Nothing hinders but that all these Thingsthings may meet together in Menmen, and yet they be without a Sparkspark of Gracegrace in their Heartshearts. And these Affectionsaffections may come after great Awakeningsawakenings and Convictionsconvictions of Conscienceconscience; and there may be great Appearancesappearances of a Workwork of Humiliationhumiliation; and counterfeit Lovelove and Joyjoy, and other Affectionsaffections may seem to follow these, and one another, just in the same Orderorder, that is commonly observable in the holy Affectionsaffections of true Convertsconverts.
And these religious Affectionsaffections may be carried to a great Heightheight, and may cause Abundanceabundance of Tearstears, yea, may overcome the Naturenature of those who are the Subjectssubjects of them, and may make them affectionate, and fervent, and fluent in speaking of the Thingsthings of God, and dispose them to be abundant in it; and may be attended with many sweet Textstexts of Scripture, and precious Promisespromises, brought with great Impressionimpression on their Mindsminds; and may dispose them with their Mouthsmouths to praise and glorify God, in a very ardent Mannermanner, and fervently to call upon others to praise him, crying out of their Unworthinessunworthiness, and extolling free Gracegrace. And may, moreover, dispose them to abound in the external Dutiesduties of Religionreligion, such as Prayerprayer, hearing the Wordword preached, Singingsinging, and religious Conferenceconference: and these Thingsthings attended with a great Resemblanceresemblance of a christian Assuranceassurance, in its greatest Heightheight, when the Saintssaints mount on Eagleseagles Wingswings, above all Darknessdarkness and Doubtingdoubting. I think it has been made plain, that there may be all these Thingsthings, and yet there be nothing more than the common Influencesinfluences of the Spirit of God, join'djoined with the Delusionsdelusions of Satan, and the wicked and deceitful Heartheart. To which I may add, that all these Thingsthings may be attended with a sweet natural Tempertemper, and a good doctrinal Knowledgeknowledge of Religionreligion, and a long Acquaintanceacquaintance with the Saintssaints Wayway of talking and of expressing their Affectionsaffections and Experiencesexperiences, and a natural Abilityability and Subtiltysubtletysubtilty in accommodating their Expressionsexpressions & Mannermanner of speaking to the Dispositionsdispositions & Notionsnotions of the Hearershearers, and a taking Decencydecency of Expressionexpression and Behaviourbehaviorbehaviour, formed by a good Educationeducation. How great therefore may the Resemblanceresemblance be, as to all outward Expressionsexpressions and Appearancesappearances, between an Hypocritehypocrite and a true Saintsaint! Doubtless 'tis the glorious Prerogativeprerogative of the omniscient God, as the great Searchersearcher of Heartshearts, to be able well to separate between Sheepsheep and Goatsgoats. And what an indecent, Selfself-Exaltationexaltation, and Arrogancearrogance is it, in poor fallible dark Mortalsmortals, to pretend that they can determine and know, who are really sincere and upright before God, and who are not!

Many seem to lay great Weightweight on that, and to suppose it to be what may determine them with respect to others real Pietypiety, when they not only tell a plausible Storystory, but when, in giving an Accountaccount of their Experiencesexperiences, they make such a Representationrepresentation, and speak after such a Mannermanner, that they feel their Talktalk; that is to say, when their Talktalk seems to harmonize with their own Experienceexperience, and their Heartshearts are to • uched and affected and delighted, by what they hear them say, and drawn out by it, in dear Lovelove to them. But there is not that Certaintycertainty in such Thingsthings, and that full Dependancedependencedependance to be had upon them, which many imagine. A true Saintsaint greatly delights in Holinessholiness: Itit is a most beautiful Thingthing in his Eyeseyes; Andand God's Workwork, in savingly renewing and making holy and happy, a poor, and before perishing Soulsoul, appears to him a most glorious Workwork. No wonder
therefore, that his Heartheart is touch'dtouched, and greatly affected, when he hears another give a probable Accountaccount of this Workwork, wrought on his own Heartheart, and when he sees in him probable Appearancesappearances of Holinessholiness; whether those pleasing Appearancesappearances have any Thingthing real to answer them, or no. And if he uses the same Wordswords, which are commonly made use of, to express the Affectionsaffections of true Saintssaints, and tells of many Thingsthings following one another in an Orderorder, agreeable to the Methodmethod of the Experienceexperience of him that hears him, and also speaks freely and boldly, and with an Airair of Assuranceassurance: Nono wonder that the other thinks his Experiencesexperiences harmonize with his own. And if besides all this, in giving his Relationrelation, he speaks with much Affectionaffection; and above all, if in speaking, he seems to shewshow much Affectionaffection to him, to whom he speaks, such an Affectionaffection as the Galatians did to the Apostleapostle Paul; these Thingsthings will naturally have a powerful Influenceinfluence, to affect and draw his Hearershearers Heartheart, and open wide the Doorsdoors of his Charitycharity towards him. David speaks as one who had felt Ahithophel's Talktalk, and had once a sweet Savoursavorsavour and Relishrelish of it. And therefore exceeding great was his Surprisesurprise and Disappointmentdisappointment, when he fell; it was almost too much for 〈◊〉 him. Psal.Ps 55.: 12, 13, 14. It was not an Enemyenemy—then I could have borne it,—but it was thou, a Manman, mine Equalequal, my Guideguide, and my Acquaintanceacquaintance; we took sweet Counselcounsel together, and walked unto the Househouse of God in Companycompany.

It is with Professorsprofessors of Religionreligion, especially such as become so in a Timetime of out-pouring of the Spirit of God, as it is with the Blossomsblossoms in the Springspring A Timetime of out-pouring of the Spirit of God, reviving Religionreligion, and producing the pleasant Appearancesappearances of it, in new Convertsconverts, is in Scripture compared to this very Thingthing, viz. theThe spring Seasonseason, when the benign Influencesinfluences of the Heavensheavens, cause the Blossomsblossoms to put forth. Cant.Song 2.: 11, 12.; there are vast Numbersnumbers of them upon the Treestrees, which all look fair and promising; but yet very many of them never come to any Thingthing. And many of those, that in a little Timetime wither up, and drop off, and rot under the Treestrees; yet for a while, look as beautiful and gay as others; and not only so, but smell Sweetsweet, and send forth a pleasant Odourodorodour: Soso that we can't, by any of our Sensessenses, certainly distinguish those Blossomsblossoms which have in them that secret Vertuevirtue, which will afterwards appear in the Fruitfruit, and that inward Soliditysolidity and Strengthstrength which shall enable them to bear, and cause them to be perfected by the hot Summersummer Sunsun, that will dry up the others. 'Tis the mature Fruitfruit which comes afterwards, and not the beautiful Colourscolorscolours and Smellsmell of the Blossomblossom, that we must judge by. So new Convertsconverts, (professedly so) in their Talktalk about Thingsthings of Religionreligion, may appear fair, and be very savourysavory, and the Saintssaints may think
they talk feelingly. They may relish their Talktalk, and imagine they perceive a divine Savoursavorsavour in it; and yet all may come to nothing.

'Tis strange how hardly Menmen are brought to be contented with the Rulesrules and Directionsdirections Christ has given them, but they must needs go by other Rulesrules, of their own inventing, that seem to them wiser and better. I know of no Directionsdirections or Counselscounsels which Christ ever delivered more plainly, than the Rulesrules he has given us, to guide us in our judging of others Sinceritysincerity; viz. thatThat we should judge of the Treetree chiefly by the Fruitfruit: Butbut yet this won't do; but other Waysways are found out, which are imagined to be more distinguishing and certa 〈◊〉 incertain. And wofulwoeful have been the mischievous Consequencesconsequences, of this arrogant 〈◊◊〉 setting up Men'smen's Wisdomwisdom above the Wisdomwisdom of Christ. I believe many Saintssaints have gone much out of the Wayway of Christ's Wordword, in this Respectrespect: Andand some of them have been chastised 〈◊〉 with Whipswhips, and (I had almost said) Scorpionsscorpions, to bring them back again. But many Thingsthings which have lately appeared, and do now appear, may convince, that ordinarily, those who have gone furthest this Wayway, that have been most highly conceited of their Facultyfaculty of discerning, and have appeared most forward, peremptorily • and suddenly to determine the Statestate of Mensmen'smens Soulssouls, have been Hypocriteshypocrites, who have known nothing of true Religionreligion.

In the Parableparable of the Wheatwheat and Tarestares, it is said, Matth.Matt 13.: 26. When the Bladeblade was sprung up, and bro't forth Fruit, 〈…〉 then appeared the Tarestares also 〈◊〉 . As tho'though the Tares 〈◊〉 tares were not discerned, nor distinguishable from the Wheatwheat, 'tilltill then, as Mr. Flavel observes; Husbandry spiritualiz'dspiritualized, Chapchchap. 12. who 〈◊〉 mentions it as an Observationobservation of Jerom's, Thatthat Wheat and Tarestares are so much alike, 'tilltill the Bladeblade of the Wheatwheat comes to bring forth 〈◊〉 the Earear, that 'tis next to impossible to distinguish them. And then, Mr. Flavel adds, Howhow difficult so ever it be to discern the Differencedifference between Wheatwheat and Tarestares; yet doubtless the Eyeeye of Sensesense can much easier discriminate them, than the most quick and piercing Eyeeye of Manman, can discern the Differencedifference between special and common Gracegrace. For all saving Gracesgraces in the Saints 〈◊〉 saints, have their Counterfeitscounterfeits in Hypocriteshypocrites; there are similar Worksworks in those, which a spiritual and very judicious Eyeeye may easily mistake, for the saving and genuine Effectseffects of a sanctifying Spiritspirit.

As 'tis the Earear or the Fruitfruit which distinguishes the Wheatwheat from the Tarestares, so this is the true Shibboleth, that he who stands as Judgejudge at the Passagespassages of Jordan, makes use of to distinguish those that shall pass over Jordan into the true Canaan, from those that should be slain at the Passagespassages. For the Hebrew Wordword Shibboleth, signifies an Earear of Corncorn. And perhaps the more full Pronounciationpronunciationpronounciation of Jepthah's
Friendsfriends, Shibboleth, may represent a full Earear with Fruitfruit in it, typifying the Fruitsfruits of the Friendsfriends of Christ, the Antitypeantitype of JephtbabJephthah; and the more lean Pronounciationpronunciationpronounciation of the Ephraimites his Enemiesenemies, may represent their empty Earsears, typifying the Showshow of Religionreligion in Hypocriteshypocrites, without Substancesubstance and Fruitfruit. This is agreableagreeable to the Doctrinedoctrine we are abundantly taught in Scripture, viz. That he who is set to judge those that pass through Deathdeath, whether they have a Rightright to enter into the heavenly Canaan or no, or whether they should not be slain, will judge every Manman according to his Worksworks.

We seem to be taught the same Thingsthings, by the Rulesrules given for the Priestspriests discerning the Leprosyleprosy. In many Casescases it was impossible for the Priestpriest to determine whether a Manman had the Leprosyleprosy, or whether he were clean, by the most narrow Inspectioninspection of the Appearancesappearances that were upon him, 'tilltill he had waited to see what the Appearancesappearances would come to, and had shut up the Personperson who shewedshowed himself to him, one seven Daysdays after another; and when he judged, he was to determine by the Hairhair, which grew out of the Spotspot that was shewedshowed him, which was as it were the Fruitfruit that it brought forth.

And here, before I finish what I have to say under this Headhead, I would say something to a strange Notionnotion some have of late been led away with, of certainly knowing the good Estateestate that others are in, as tho'though it were immediately revealed to 'emthem from Heavenheaven, by their Lovelove flowing out to 'emthem in an extraordinary Mannermanner. They argue thus, that their Lovelove being very sensible and great, it may be certainly known by them who feel it, to be a true christian Lovelove: Andand if it be a true christian Lovelove, the Spirit of God must be the Authorauthor of it: Andand inasmuch as the Spirit of God, who knows certainly, whether others are the Childrenchildren of God or no, and is a Spiritspirit of Truthtruth, is pleased, by an uncommon Influenceinfluence upon 'emthem, to cause their Lovelove to flow out, in an extraordinary Mannermanner, towards such a Personperson, as a Childchild of God; it must needs be that this infallible Spirit, who deceives none, knows that that Personperson is a Childchild of God. But such Personspersons might be convinced of the Falsenessfalseness of their Reasoningreasoning, if they would consider whether or no it be not their Dutyduty, and what God requires of 'emthem, to love those as the Childrenchildren of God, who they think are the Childrenchildren of God, and whom they have no Reasonreason to think otherwise of, from all that they can see in them.,

Tho' though God, who searches the Heartshearts, knows 'emthem not to be his Childrenchildren. If it be their Dutyduty, then it is Goodgood, and the Wantwant of it Sinsin; and therefore, surely the Spirit of God may be the Authorauthor of it: Thethe Spirit of God, without being a Spiritspirit of Falshoodfalsehoodfalshood, may in such a Casecase assist a Personperson to do his Dutyduty, and keep him from Sinsin. But then they argue from the uncommon Degreedegree and special Mannermanner, in which their Lovelove flows out to the Personperson; which they think the Spirit of God never would cause, if he did not know the Objectobject to be a Childchild of God.
But then I would ask them, whether or no it is not their Dutyduty to love all such as they are bound to think are the Childrenchildren of God, from all that they can see in them, to a very great Degreedegree, tho'though God, from other Thingsthings which he sees, that are out of Sightsight to them, knows 'emthem not to be so. 'Tis Men'smen's Dutyduty to love all whom they are bound in Charitycharity to look upon as the Childrenchildren of God, with a vastly dearer Affectionaffection than they commonly do. As we ought to love Christ to the utmost Capacitycapacity of our Naturenature, so 'tis our Dutyduty to love those who we think are so near and dear to him as his Membersmembers, with an exceeding dear Affectionaffection, as Christ has loved us; and therefore it is Sinsin in us not to love them so. We ought to pray to God that he would, by his Spirit keep us from Sinsin, and enable us to do our Dutyduty: Andand may not his Spirit answer our Prayersprayers, and enable us to do our Dutyduty, in a particular Instanceinstance, without lying? If he can't, then the Spirit of God is bound not to help his Peoplepeople to do their Dutyduty in some Instancesinstances, because he can't do it without being a Spiritspirit of Falshoodfalsehoodfalshood. But surely God is so sovereign as that comes to, that he may enable us to do our Dutyduty when he pleases, and on what Occasionoccasion he pleases. When Personspersons think others are his Childrenchildren, God may have other Endsends in causing their exceedingly endeared Lovelove to flow out to them, besides revealing to them whether their Opinionopinion of 'emthem be right or no: Hehe may have that merciful Endend in it, to enable them to do their Dutyduty, and to keep them from that dreadful infinite Evilevil, Sinsin. And will they say God shall not show 'emthem that Mercymercy in such a Casecase? If I am at a Distancedistance from Homehome, and hear, that in my Absenceabsence, my Househouse is burnt, but my Familyfamily have, in some extraordinary Mannermanner, all escaped the Flamesflames; and every Thingthing in the Circumstancescircumstances of the Storystory, as I hear it, makes it appear very credible; Itit would be Sinsin in me, in such a Casecase, not to feel a very great Degreedegree of Gratitudegratitude to God, tho'though the Storystory indeed be not true. And is not God so sovereign, that he may if he pleases, shewshow me that Mercymercy on that Occasionoccasion, and enable me to do my Dutyduty in a much further Degreedegree than I used to do it, and yet not incur the Chargecharge of Deceitfulnessdeceitfulness, in confirming a Falshoodfalsehoodfalshood?

'Tis exceeding manifest, that Errorerror or Mistakemistake may be the Occasionoccasion of a gracious Exerciseexercise, and consequently a gracious Influenceinfluence of the Spirit of God, by Rom.Romans 14.: 6. He that eateth to the Lord, he eateth, and giveth God Thanksthanks; and he that eateth not to the Lord, he eateth not, and giveth God Thanksthanks. The Apostleapostle is speaking of those, who thro'through erroneous and needless Scruplesscruples, avoided eating legally unclean Meatsmeats.—Byby this it is very evident, that there may be true Exercisesexercises of Gracegrace, a true Respectrespect to the Lord, and particularly, a true Thankfulnessthankfulness, which may be occasion'doccasioned, both by an erroneous Judgmentjudgment and Practicepractice. And consequently, an Errorerror may be the Occasionoccasion of those truly holy Exercisesexercises that are from the infallible Spirit of God.
And if so, 'tis certainly too much for us to determine, to how great a Degreedegree the Spirit of God may give this holy Exerciseexercise, on such an Occasionoccasion.

This Notionnotion, of certainly discerning another's Statestate, by Lovelove flowing out, is not only not founded on Reasonreason or Scripture, but it is anti-scriptural, 'tis against the Rulesrules of Scripture; which say not a Wordword of any such Wayway of judging the Statestate of others as this▪, but direct us to judge chiefly by the Fruitsfruits that are seen in them. And it is against the Doctrinesdoctrines of Scripture, which do plainly teach us that the Statestate of others Soulssouls towards God, cannot be known by us, as in Rev.Revelation 2.: 17. To him that overcometh, will I give to eat of the hidden Mannamanna; and I will give him a white Stonestone, and in the Stonestone a new Namename written, which no Manman knoweth, saving he that receiveth it. And Rom. 2.: 29. He is a Jew, which is one inwardly; and Circumcisioncircumcision is that of the Heartheart; in the Spiritspirit, and not in the Letterletter; whose Praisepraise is not of Menmen, but of God. That by this last Expressionexpression, whose Praisepraise is not of Menmen, but of God, the Apostleapostle has Respectrespect to the Insufficiencyinsufficiency of Menmen to judge concerning him, whether he be inwardly a Jew or no (as they could easily see by outward Marksmarks, whether Menmen were outwardly Jews) and would signify, that it belongs to God alone to give a determining Voicevoice in this Mattermatter, is confirmed by the same Apostle'sapostle's Useuse of the Phrasephrase, in 1 Cor.Corinthians 4.: 5. Therefore judge nothing before the Timetime, until the Lord come; who both will bring to Lightlight the hidden Thingsthings of Darknessdarkness, and will make manifest the Counselscounsels of the Heartshearts; and then shall every Manman have Praisepraise of God. The Apostleapostle, in the two foregoing Versesverses, says, But with me, it is a very small Thingthing, that I should be judged of you, or of Man'sman's Judgmentjudgment: Yeayea, I judge not mine own self, for I know nothing by my self, yet am I not hereby justified; but he that judgeth me is the Lord. And again, it is further confirmed, because the Apostleapostle in this second Chapterchapter to the Romans, directs his Speechspeech especially to those who had a high Conceitconceit of their own Holinessholiness, made their Boastboast of God, and were confident of their own Discerningdiscerning, and that they knew God's Willwill, and approved the Thingsthings which were excellent, or tried the Thingsthings that differ (as it is in the Marginmargin.) V.Verse 18. And were confident that they were Guidesguides of the Blindblind, and a Lightlight to them which are in Darknessdarkness, Instructorsinstructors of the Foolishfoolish, Teachersteachers of Babesbabes; and so took upon them to judge others, see V.Verse 1. andAnd 17, 18, 19, 20.

And how arrogant must the Notionnotion be, that they have, who imagine they can certainly know others Godlinessgodliness, when that great Apostleapostle Peter pretends not to say any more concerning Silv •• anus, than that he was a faithful Brotherbrother, as he supposed; 1 Pet. 5.: 12. Tho'Though this Sylvanus appears to have been a very eminent Ministerminister of Christ, and an Evangelistevangelist, and a famous Lightlight in God's Churchchurch at that Dayday, and an intimate Companioncompanion of the Apostlesapostles. See 2 Cor. 1.: 19. 1 Thes.Thess 1.: 1. andAnd 2 Thes.Thess 1: 1. 1.

div.head: PART III.
ShewingShowing what are distinguishing Signs of truly gracious and holy Affections.
div.p: I COMEcome now to the SECONDsecond Thingthing appertaining to the Trialtrial of religious Affectionsaffections, which was proposed, viz. To take notice of some Thingsthings, wherein those Affectionsaffections that are spiritual and gracious, do differ from those that are not so.
But before I proceed directly to the distinguishing Characterscharacters, I would previously mention some Thingsthings which I desire may be observed, concerning the Marksmarks I shall lay down.

1. That I am far from undertaking to give such Signssigns of gracious Affectionsaffections, as shall be sufficient to enable any certainly to distinguish true Affectionaffection from false in others; or to determine positively which of their Neighboursneighborsneighbours are true Professorsprofessors, and which are Hypocriteshypocrites. In so doing, I should be guilty of that Arrogancearrogance which I have been condemning. Tho'Though it be plain that Christ has given Rulesrules to all Christians, to enable 'emthem to judge of Professorsprofessors of Religionreligion, whom they are concerned with, so far as is necessary for their own Safetysafety, and to prevent their being led into a Snaresnare by false Teachersteachers, and false Pretenderspretenders to Religionreligion; Andand tho'though it be also beyond Doubtdoubt, that the Scriptures do abound with Rulesrules, which may be very serviceable to Ministersministers, in counsellingcounseling and conducting Soulssouls committed to their Carecare, in Thingsthings appertaining to their spiritual
and eternal Statestate; yet, 'tis also evident, that it was never God's Designdesign to give us any Rulesrules, by which we may certainly know, who of our Fellowfellow-Professorsprofessors are his, and to make a full and clear Separationseparation between Sheepsheep and Goatsgoats: Butbut that on the Contrarycontrary, it was God's Designdesign to reserve this to himself, as his Prerogativeprerogative. And therefore no such distinguishing Signssigns as shall enable Christians or Ministersministers to do this, are ever to be expected to the World'sworld's Endend: Forfor no more is ever to be expected from any Signssigns, that are to be found in the Wordword of God, or gathered from it, than Christ designed them for.

2. No such Signssigns are to be expected, that shall be sufficient to enable those Saintssaints certainly to discern their own good Estateestate, who are very low in Gracegrace, or are such as have much departed from God, and are fallen into a dead, carnal and unchristian Frameframe. It is not agreableagreeable to God's Designdesign (as has been already observed) that such should know their good Estateestate: Nornor is it desirable that they should; but on the contrary, every Wayway best that they should not; and we have Reasonreason to bless God, that he has made no Provisionprovision that such should certainly know the Statestate that they are in, any other Wayway, than by first coming out of the ill Frameframe and Wayway they are in.

Indeed it is not properly thro'through the Defectdefect of the Signssigns given in the Wordword of God, that every Saintsaint living, whether strong or weak, and those who are in a bad Frameframe, as well as others, can't certainly know their good Estateestate by them. For the Rulesrules in themselves are certain and infallible, and every Saintsaint has, or has had those Thingsthings in himself, which are sure Evidencesevidences of Gracegrace; for every, even the least Actact of Gracegrace is so. But it is thro'through his Defectdefect to whom the Signssigns are given. There is a twofold Defectdefect in that Saintsaint who is very low in Gracegrace, or in an ill Frameframe, which makes it impossible for him to know certainly that he has true Gracegrace, by the best Signssigns and Rulesrules which can be given him. First, A Defectdefect in the Objectobject, or the Qualificationqualification to be view'dviewed and examin'dexamined. I don't mean an essential Defectdefect; because I suppose the Personperson to be a real Saintsaint; but a Defectdefect in Degreedegree: Gracegrace being very small, cannot be clearly and certainly discerned and distinguished. Things that are very small, we can't clearly discern their Formform, or distinguish them one from another; tho'though, as they are in themselves, their Formform may be very different. There is doubtless a great Differencedifference between the Bodybody of Manman, and the Bodiesbodies of other Animalsanimals, in the first Conceptionconception in the Wombwomb: Butbut yet if we should view the different Embryosembryos, it might not be possible for us to discern the Differencedifference, by reason of the imperfect Statestate of the Objectobject; but as it comes to greater Perfectionperfection, the Differencedifference becomes very plain. The Differencedifference between Creaturescreatures of very contrary Qualitiesqualities, is not so plainly to be seen while they are very young, even
after they are actually brought forth, as in their more perfect Statestate. The Differencedifference between Dovesdoves and Ravensravens, or Dovesdoves and Vulturesvultures, when they first come out of the Eggegg, is not so evident; but as they grow to their Perfectionperfection, 'tis exceeding great and manifest. Another Defectdefect attending the Gracegrace of those I am speaking, is its being mingled with so much Corruptioncorruption, which clouds and hides it, and makes it impossible for it certainly to be known. Tho'Though different Thingsthings that are before us, may have in themselves many Marksmarks thoroughly distinguishing them one from another; yet if we see them only in a thick Smokesmoke, it may nevertheless be impossible to distinguish them. A fix'dfixed Starstar is easily distinguishable from a Cometcomet, in a clear Skysky; but if we view them thro'through a Cloudcloud, it may be impossible to see the Differencedifference. When true Christians are in an ill Frameframe, Guiltguilt lies on the Conscienceconscience; which will bring Fearfear, and so prevent the Peacepeace and Joyjoy of an assured Hopehope.

Secondly, Therethere is in such a Casecase a Defectdefect in the Eyeeye. As the Feeblenessfeebleness of Gracegrace and Prevalenceprevalence of Corruptioncorruption, obscures the Objectobject; so it enfeebles the Sightsight; it darkens the Sightsight as to all spiritual Objectsobjects, of which Gracegrace is one. Sin is like some Distempersdistempers of the Eyeseyes, that make Thingsthings to appear of different Colourscolorscolours from those which properly belong to them, and like many other Distempersdistempers, that put the Mouthmouth out of Tastetaste, so as to disenable from distinguishing good and wholesome Foodfood from bad, but every Thingthing tastes bitter. Men in a corrupt and carnal Frameframe, have their spiritual Sensessenses in but poor P • light for judging and distinguishing spiritual Thingsthings.

Therefore, tho'though good Rulesrules to distinguish true Gracegrace from Counterfeitcounterfeit, may tend to convince Hypocriteshypocrites, and be of great Useuse to the Saintssaints, in many Respectsrespects; and among other Benefitsbenefits, may be very useful to them to remove many needless Scruplesscruples, and establish their Hopehope; yet I am far from pretending to lay down any such Rulesrules, as shall be sufficient of themselves, without other Meansmeans, to enable all true Saintssaints to see their good Estateestate, or as supposing they should be the principal Meansmeans of their Satisfactionsatisfaction.

3. Nor is there much Encouragementencouragement, in the Experienceexperience of present or past Timestimes, to lay down Rulesrules or Marksmarks to distinguish between true and false Affectionsaffections, in Hopeshopes of convincing any considerable Numbernumber of that Sortsort of Hypocriteshypocrites, who have been deceived with great false Discoveriesdiscoveries and Affectionsaffections, and are once settled in a false Confidenceconfidence, and high Conceitconceit of their own supposed great Experiencesexperiences
and Privilegesprivileges. Such Hypocriteshypocrites are so conceited of their own Wisdomwisdom, & so blinded & harden'dhardened with a very great Selfself-Righteousnessrighteousness, (but very subtilsubtle and secret, under the Disguisedisguise of great Humilityhumility) and so invinceableinvincible a Fondnessfondness of their pleasing Conceitconceit, of their great Exaltationexaltation, that it usually signifies nothing at all, to lay before them the most convincing Evidencesevidences of their Hypocrisyhypocrisy. Their Statestate is indeed deplorable, and next to those that have committed the unpardonable Sinsin., Somesome of this Sortsort of Personspersons seem to be most out of the Reachreach of Meansmeans of Convictionconviction and Repentancerepentance. But yet the laying down good Rulesrules may be a Meansmeans of preventing such Hypocriteshypocrites, and of convincing many of other Kindskinds of Hypocriteshypocrites: Andand God is able to convince even this Kindkind, and his Gracegrace is not to be limited, nor Meansmeans to be neglected. And besides, such Rulesrules may be of Useuse to the true Saintssaints, to detect false Affectionsaffections, which they may have mingled with true. And be a Meansmeans of their Religion'sreligion's becoming more pure, and like Goldgold tried in the Firefire.

Dreamdream, or when he is awake, any outward Ideasideas of any of the Sensessenses, either Voicesvoices, or Shapesshapes and Colourscolorscolours, 'tis only exciting Ideasideas of the same Kindkind that he has by natural Principlesprinciples and Sensessenses.
