Thus the Spirit of God by his common Influencesinfluences may assist Men'smen's natural Ingeniosityingenuityingeniosity, as he assisted Bezaleel and Aholiab in the curious Worksworks of the Tabernacletabernacle: so he may assist Mensmen'smens natural Abilitiesabilities in political Affairsaffairs, and improve their Couragecourage, and other natural Qualificationsqualifications; as he is said to have put his Spiritspirit on the seventy Elderselders, & on Saul, so as to give him another Heartheart: so God may greatly assist natural Men'smen's Reasonreason, in their Reasoningreasoning about secular Thingsthings, or about the Doctrinesdoctrines of Religionreligion, and may greatly advance the Clearnessclearness of their Apprehensionsapprehensions and Notionsnotions of Thingsthings of Religionreligion in many Respectsrespects, without giving any spiritual Sensesense. So in those Awakeningsawakenings and Convictionsconvictions that natural Menmen may have, God only assists Conscienceconscience, which is a natural Principleprinciple, to do that Workwork in a further Degreedegree, which it naturally does. Conscience naturally gives Menmen an Apprehensionapprehension of Rightright and Wrongwrong, and suggests the Relationrelation there is between Rightright and Wrongwrong, and a Retributionretribution: Thethe Spirit of God assists Men'smen's Consciencesconsciences to do this in a greater Degreedegree, helps Conscienceconscience against the stupifyingstupefying Influenceinfluence of worldly Objectsobjects and their Lustslusts. And so there are many other Waysways might be mention'dmentioned wherein the Spirit acts upon, assists and moves natural Principlesprinciples; but after all, 'tis no more than Naturenature moved, acted and improved; here is nothing supernatural and divine. But the Spirit of God in his spiritual Influencesinfluences on the Heartshearts of his Saintssaints, operates by infusing or exercising new, divine and supernatural Principlesprinciples; Principlesprinciples which are indeed a new and spiritual Naturenature, and Principlesprinciples vastly more noble and excellent than all that is in natural Menmen.

From what has been said it follows, that all spiritual and gracious Affectionsaffections are attended with, and do arise from some Apprehensionapprehension, Ideaidea or Sensationsensation of Mindmind, which is in its whole Naturenature different, yea exceeding different from all that is or can be in the Mindmind of a natural Manman; and which the natural Manman discerns nothing of, and has no Mannermanner of Ideaidea of, (agreeable to 1 Cor. 2.: 14.) and conceives of no more than a Manman without the Sensesense of Tastingtasting can conceive of the sweet Tastetaste of Honeyhoney, or a Manman without the Sensesense of Hearinghearing can conceive of the Melodymelody of a Tunetune, or a Manman born Blindblind can have a Notionnotion of the Beautybeauty of the Rainbowrainbow.
But here two Thingsthings must be observed in order to the right Understandingunderstanding of this.

1. On the one Handhand it must be observed, that not every Thingthing which in any Respectrespect appertains to spiritual Affectionsaffections, is new and entirely different from what natural Menmen can conceive of, and do experience; some Thingsthings are common to gracious Affectionsaffections with other Affectionsaffections; many Circumstancescircumstances, Appendagesappendages and Effectseffects are common. It may be clearly illustrated by this: Wewe will suppose two Menmen; one is born without the Sensesense of Tastingtasting, the other has it; the latter loves Honeyhoney, and is greatly delighted in it because he knows the sweet Tastetaste of it; the other loves certain Soundssounds and Colourscolorscolours: Thethe Lovelove of each has many Thingsthings that appertain to it, which is common; it causes both to Desiredesire and Delightdelight in the Objectobject beloved, and causes Griefgrief when it is absent, &c.—: Butbut yet, that Ideaidea or Sensationsensation which he who knows the Tastetaste of Honeyhoney, has of its Excellencyexcellency and Sweetnesssweetness, that is the Foundationfoundation of his Lovelove, is entirely different from any Thingthing the other has or can have; and that Delightdelight which he has in Honeyhoney, is wholly diverse from any Thingthing that the other can conceive of; tho'though they both delight in their beloved Objectsobjects. delicious Tastetaste; not only because he has seen it'sits pleasant Colourscolorscolours, but knows it'sits sweet Tastetaste; the other, perfectly ignorant of this, loves it only for its beautiful Colourscolorscolours: Therethere are many Thingsthings seem, in some Respectrespect, to be common to both; both love, both desire, and both delight; but the Lovelove, and Desiredesire, and Delightdelight of the one, is altogether diverse from that of the other. 2. On the other Handhand, it must be observed, that a natural Manman may have those religious Apprehensionsapprehensions and Affectionsaffections, which may be in many Respectsrespects very new and surprising to him, and what before he did not conceive of; and yet what he experiences be nothing like the Exercisesexercises of a Principleprinciple of new Naturenature, or the Sensationssensations of a new spiritual Sensesense: Hishis Affectionsaffections may be very new, by extraordinarily moving natural Principlesprinciples, in a very new Degreedegree, and with a great many new Circumstancescircumstances, and a new Co-operation of natural Affectionsaffections, and a new Compositioncomposition of Ideasideas; this may be from some extraordinary powerful Influenceinfluence of Satan and some great Delusiondelusion; but there is nothing but Naturenature extraordinarily acted. Now therefore, to apply these Thingsthings to the Purposepurpose of this Discoursediscourse.

of a natural Gratitudegratitude. There is doubtless such a Thingthing as a gracious Gratitudegratitude, which does greatly differ from all that Gratitudegratitude which natural Menmen experience. It differs in the following Respectsrespects:

1. True Gratitudegratitude or Thankfulnessthankfulness to God for his Kindnesskindness to us, arises from a Foundationfoundation laid before, of Lovelove to God for what he is in himself; whereas a natural Gratitudegratitude has no such antecedent Foundationfoundation. before them. God's Lovelove to a particular elect Personperson, discovered by his Conversionconversion, is a great Manifestationmanifestation of God's moral Perfectionperfection and Gloryglory to him, and a proper Occasionoccasion of the Excitationexcitation of the Lovelove of holy Gratitudegratitude, agreeable to what was before said. And because the Joyjoy of Hypocriteshypocrites is in themselves, hence it comes to pass, that in their Rejoicingsrejoicings and Elevationselevations, they are wont to keep their Eyeeye upon themselves; having received what they call spiritual Discoveriesdiscoveries or Experiencesexperiences, their Mindsminds are taken up about them, admiring their own Experiencesexperiences: Andand what they are principally
taken and elevated with, is not the Gloryglory of God, or Beautybeauty of Christ, but the Beautybeauty of their Experiencesexperiences. Nor does the Pleasurepleasure and Sweetnesssweetness of his Mindmind at that Timetime, chiefly arise from the Considerationconsideration of the Safetysafety of his Statestate, or any Thingthing he has in Viewview of his own Qualificationsqualifications, Experiencesexperiences, or Circumstancescircumstances; but from the divine and supreamsupreme Beautybeauty of what is the Objectobject of his direct Viewview, without himself; which sweetly entertains, and strongly holds his Mindmind.

As the Lovelove and Joyjoy of Hypocriteshypocrites, are all from the Sourcesource of Selfself-Lovelove; so it is with their other Affectionsaffections, their Sorrowsorrow for Sinsin, their Humiliationhumiliation and Submissionsubmission, their religious Desiresdesires and Zealzeal: Everyevery Thingthing is as it were paid for before-hand, in God's highly gratifying their Selfself-love, and their Lustslusts, by making so much of them, and exalting them so highly, as Thingsthings are in their Imaginationimagination. III. Those Affectionsaffections that are truly Holyholy, are primarily founded on the Lovelinessloveliness of the moral Excellencyexcellency of divine Thingsthings. Or, (to express it otherwise) a Lovelove to divine Thingsthings for the Beautybeauty and Sweetnesssweetness of their moral Excellencyexcellency, is the first Beginningbeginning and Springspring of all holy Affectionsaffections.
Here, for the sake of the more illiterate Readerreader, I will explain what I mean by the moral Excellencyexcellency of divine Thingsthings.

And it may be observed that the Wordword Moralmoral is not to be understood here, according to the common and vulgar Acceptationacceptation of the Wordword, when Menmen speak of Moralitymorality, and a moral Behaviourbehaviorbehaviour meaning an outward Conformityconformity to the Dutiesduties of the moral Lawlaw, and especially the Dutiesduties of the second Tabletable; or intending no more at farthest, than such seeming Vertuesvirtues, as proceed from natural Principlesprinciples, in Oppositionopposition to those Vertuesvirtues that are more inward, spiritual, and divine; as the Honestyhonesty, Justicejustice, Generositygenerosity, Goodgood Naturenature, and publickpublic Spirit of many of the Heathenheathen, are called moral Vertuesvirtues, in Distinctiondistinction from the holy Faithfaith, Lovelove, Humilityhumility, and Heavenlymindednessheavenlymindedness of true Christians: I say the Wordword Moralmoral is not to be understood thus in this Placeplace.

But in order to a right understanding what is meant, it must be observed, that Divinesdivines commonly make a Distinctiondistinction between moral Goodgood and Evilevil, and natural Goodgood and Evilevil. By moral Evilevil, they mean the Evilevil of Sinsin, or that Evilevil which is against Dutyduty, and contrary to what is right and ought to be. By natural Evilevil, they don't mean that Evilevil which is properly opposed to Dutyduty; but that which is contrary to meermere Naturenature, without any Respectrespect to a Rulerule of Dutyduty. So the Evilevil of suffering is called natural Evilevil, such as Painpain, and Tormenttorment, Disgracedisgrace, and the like: Thesethese Thingsthings are contrary to meermere Naturenature, contrary to the Naturenature of both Badbad and Goodgood, hateful to wicked Menmen and Devilsdevils, as well as good Menmen and Angelsangels. So likewise natural Defectsdefects are called natural Evilsevils, as if a Childchild be monstrous, or a natural Foolfool; these are natural Evilsevils, but are not moral Evilsevils, because they han't properly the Naturenature of the Evilevil of Sinsin. On the other Handhand, as by moral Evilevil, Divinesdivines mean the Evilevil of Sinsin, or that which is contrary to what is right; so by moral Goodgood, they mean that which is contrary to Sinsin, or that Goodgood in Beingsbeings who have Willwill and Choicechoice, whereby, as voluntary Agentsagents, they are, and act, as it becomes 'emthem to be and to act, or so as is most fit, and suitable, and lovely. By natural Goodgood they mean that Goodgood that is entirely of a different Kindkind from Holinessholiness or Vertuevirtue, viz. That which perfects or suits Naturenature, considering Naturenature abstractly from any holy or unholy Qualificationsqualifications, and without any Relationrelation to any Rulerule or Measuremeasure of Rightright and Wrongwrong.

Thus Pleasurepleasure is a natural Goodgood; so is Honourhonorhonour; so is Strengthstrength; so is speculative Knowledgeknowledge, human Learninglearning, and Policypolicy. Thus
there is a Distinctiondistinction to be made between the natural Goodgood that Menmen are possessed of, and their moral Goodgood; and also between the natural and moral Goodgood of the Angelsangels in Heavenheaven: the great Capacitycapacity of their Understandingsunderstandings, and their great Strengthstrength, and the honourablehonorable Circumstancescircumstances they are in as the great Ministersministers of God's Kingdomkingdom, whence they are called Thronesthrones, Dominionsdominions, Principalitiesprincipalities, and Powerspowers, is the natural Goodgood which they are possessed of; but their perfect and glorious Holinessholiness and Goodnessgoodness, their pure and flaming Lovelove to God, and to the Saintssaints, and one another, is their moral Goodgood. So Divinesdivines make a Distinctiondistinction between the natural and moral Perfectionsperfections of God: Byby the moral Perfectionsperfections of God, they mean those Attributesattributes which God exercises as a moral Agentagent, or whereby the Heartheart and Willwill of God are good, right, and infinitely becoming, and lovely; such as his Righteousnessrighteousness, Truthtruth, Faithfulnessfaithfulness, and Goodnessgoodness; or, in one Wordword, his Holinessholiness. By God's natural Attributesattributes or Perfectionsperfections, they mean those Attributesattributes, wherein, according to our Wayway of conceiving of God, consists, not the Holinessholiness or moral Goodnessgoodness of God, but his Greatnessgreatness; such as his Powerpower, his Knowledgeknowledge whereby he knows all Thingsthings, and his being eternal, from everlasting to everlasting, his Omnipresenceomnipresence, and his awful and terrible Majestymajesty.

The moral Excellencyexcellency of an intelligent voluntary Beingbeing, is more immediately seated in the Heartheart or Willwill of moral Agentsagents. That intelligent Beingbeing whose Willwill is truly right and lovely, he is morally good or excellent.

This moral Excellencyexcellency of an intelligent Beingbeing, when it is true and real, and not only external, or meerlymerely Seemingseeming and Counterfeitcounterfeit, is Holinessholiness. Therefore Holinessholiness comprehends all the true moral Excellencyexcellency of intelligent Beingsbeings: Therethere is no other true Vertuevirtue, but real Holinessholiness. Holiness comprehends all the true Vertuevirtue of a good Manman, his Lovelove to God, his gracious Lovelove to Menmen, his Justicejustice, his Charitycharity, and Bowelsbowels of Merciesmercies, his gracious Meeknessmeekness and Gentlenessgentleness, and all other true christian Vertuesvirtues that he has, belong to his Holinessholiness. So the Holinessholiness of God in the more extensive Sensesense of the Wordword, and the Sensesense in which the Wordword is commonly, if not universally usedused concerning God in Scripture, is the same with the moral Excellencyexcellency of the divine Naturenature, or his Puritypurity and Beautybeauty as a moral Agentagent, comprehending all his moral Perfectionsperfections, his Righteousnessrighteousness, Faithfulnessfaithfulness and Goodnessgoodness. As in holy Menmen their Charitycharity, christian Kindnesskindness and Mercymercy, belongs to their Holinessholiness; so the Kindnesskindness and Mercymercy of God, belongs to his Holinessholiness. Holiness in Manman, is but the image of God's Holinessholiness: Therethere are not more Vertuesvirtues belonging to the Imageimage, than are in the Originaloriginal: Derivedderived Holinessholiness has not more in it, than is in that underived Holinessholiness, which is its Fountainfountain: Therethere
is no more than Gracegrace for Gracegrace, or Gracegrace in the Imageimage, answerable to Gracegrace in the Originaloriginal.

As there are two Kindskinds of Attributesattributes in God, according to our Wayway of conceiving of him, his moral Attributesattributes, which are sum'dsummed up in his Holinessholiness, and his natural Attributesattributes, of Strengthstrength, Knowledgeknowledge, &c. thatThat constitute the Greatnessgreatness of God; so there is a twofold Imageimage of God in Manman, his moral or spiritual Imageimage, which is his Holinessholiness, that is the Imageimage of God's moral Excellencyexcellency; (which Imageimage was lost by the Fallfall) and God's natural Imageimage, consisting in Men'smen's Reasonreason and Understandingunderstanding, his natural Abilityability, and Do ••• miniondominion over the Creaturescreatures, which is the Imageimage of God's natural Attributesattributes.

From what has been said, it may easily be understood what I intend, when I say that a Lovelove to divine Thingsthings for the Beautybeauty of their moral Excellencyexcellency, is the Beginningbeginning and Springspring of all holy Affectionsaffections. It has been already shown, under the former Headhead, that the first objective Groundground of all holy Affectionsaffections is the supreamsupreme Excellencyexcellency of divine Thingsthings as they are in themselves, or in their own Naturenature; I now proceed further, and say more particularly, that that Kindkind of Excellencyexcellency of the Naturenature of divine Thingsthings, which is the first objective Groundground of all holy Affectionsaffections, is their moral Excellencyexcellency, or their Holinessholiness. Holy Personspersons, in the Exerciseexercise of holy Affectionsaffections, do love divine Thingsthings primarily for their Holinessholiness: Theythey love God, in the first Placeplace, for the Beautybeauty of his Holinessholiness or moral Perfectionperfection, as being supreamlysupremely amiable in it self. Not that the Saintssaints, in the Exerciseexercise of gracious Affectionsaffections, do love God only for his Holinessholiness; all his Attributesattributes are amiable and glorious in their Eyeseyes, they delight in every divine Perfectionperfection; the Contemplationcontemplation of the infinite Greatnessgreatness, Powerpower, and Knowledgeknowledge, and terrible Majestymajesty of God, is pleasant to them. But their Lovelove to God for his Holinessholiness is what is most fundamental and essential in their Lovelove. Here it is that true Lovelove to God begins: Allall other holy Lovelove to divine Thingsthings flows from hence: Thisthis is the most essential and distinguishing Thingsthings that belongs to a holy Lovelove to God, with Regardregard to the Foundationfoundation of it. A Lovelove to God for the Beautybeauty of his moral Attributesattributes, leads to, and necessarily causes a Delightdelight in God for all his Attributesattributes; for his moral Attributesattributes can't be without his natural Attributesattributes: Forfor infinite Holinessholiness supposes infinite Wisdomwisdom, and an infinite Capacitycapacity and Greatnessgreatness; and all the Attributesattributes of God do as it were imply one another.

The true Beautybeauty and Lovelinessloveliness of all intelligent Beingsbeings does primarily and most essentially consist in their moral Excellencyexcellency or Holinessholiness. Herein consists the Lovelinessloveliness of the Angelsangels, without which, with all their natural Perfectionsperfections, their Strengthstrength, and their Knowledgeknowledge, they would have no more Lovelinessloveliness than Devilsdevils. 'Tis moral Excellencyexcellency alone, that is in it self, and on it'sits own Accountaccount, the
Excellencyexcellency of intelligent Beingsbeings: 'Tis'tis this that gives Beautybeauty to, or rather is the Beautybeauty of their natural Perfectionsperfections and Qualificationsqualifications. Moral Excellencyexcellency is the Excellencyexcellency of natural Excellenciesexcellencies. Natural Qualificationsqualifications are either excellent or otherwise, according as they are join'djoined with moral Excellencyexcellency or not. Strength and Knowledgeknowledge don't render any Beingbeing lovely, without Holinessholiness; but more hateful: Tho'Though they render them more lovely, when join'djoined with Holinessholiness. Thus the elect Angelsangels are the more glorious for their Strengthstrength and Knowledgeknowledge, because these natural Perfectionsperfections of their's, are sanctified by their moral Perfectionperfection. But tho'though the Devilsdevils are very strong, and of great natural Understandingunderstanding, they ben't the more lovely: Theythey are more terrible indeed, but not the more amiable; but on the contrary, the more hateful. The Holinessholiness of an intelligent Creaturecreature, is the Beautybeauty of all his natural Perfectionsperfections. And so it is in God, according to our Wayway of conceiving of the divine Beingbeing: Holinessholiness is in a pecularpeculiar Mannermanner the Beautybeauty of the divine Naturenature. Hence we often read of the Beautybeauty of Holinessholiness; Psal.Ps 29.: 2. Psal.Ps 96.: 9. andAnd 110. 3. This renders all his other Attributesattributes glorious and lovely. 'Tis the Gloryglory of God's Wisdomwisdom, that 'tis a holy Wisdomwisdom, and not a wicked Subtiltysubtletysubtilty and Craftinesscraftiness. This makes his Majestymajesty lovely, and not meerlymerely dreadful and horrible, that it is a holy Majestymajesty. 'Tis the Gloryglory of God's Immutabilityimmutability, that it is a holy Immutabilityimmutability, and not an inflexible Obstinacyobstinacy in Wickednesswickedness.

And therefore it must needs be, that a Sightsight of God's Lovelinessloveliness must begin here. A true Lovelove to God must begin with a Delightdelight in his Holinessholiness, and not with a Delightdelight in any other Attributeattribute; for no other Attributeattribute is truly lovely without this, and no otherwise than as (according to our Wayway of conceiving of God) it derives its Lovelinessloveliness from this; and therefore it is impossible that other Attributesattributes should appear lovely, in their true Lovelinessloveliness, 'tilltill this is seen; and it is impossible that any Perfectionperfection of the divine Naturenature should be loved with true Lovelove, 'tilltill this is loved. If the true Lovelinessloveliness of all God's Perfectionsperfections, arises from the Lovelinessloveliness of his Holinessholiness; then the true Lovelove of all his Perfectionsperfections, arises from the Lovelove of his Holinessholiness. They that don't see the Gloryglory of God's Holinessholiness, can't see any Thingthing of the true Gloryglory of his Mercymercy and Gracegrace: Theythey see nothing of the Gloryglory of those Attributesattributes, as any Excellencyexcellency of God's Naturenature, as it is in it self; tho'though they may be affected with them, and love them, as they concern their Interestinterest: Forfor these Attributesattributes are no Partpart of the Excellencyexcellency of God's Naturenature, as that is excellent in it self, any otherwise than as they are included in his Holinessholiness, more largely taken; or as they are a Partpart of his moral Perfectionperfection.

As the Beautybeauty of the divine Naturenature does primarily consist in God's Holinessholiness, so does the Beautybeauty of all divine Thingsthings. Herein consists the Beautybeauty of the Saintssaints, that they are Saintssaints, or holy Onesones: 'Tis'tis
the moral Imageimage of God in them, which is their Beautybeauty; and whichthat is their Holinessholiness. Herein consists the Beautybeauty and Brightnessbrightness of the Angelsangels of Heavenheaven, that they are holy Angelsangels, and so not Devilsdevils; Dan. 4.: 13, 17, 23. Matth.Matt 25.: 31. Mark 8.: 38. Acts 10.: 22. Rev. 14.: 10. Herein consists the Beautybeauty of the christian Religionreligion, above all other Religionsreligions, that it is so holy a Religionreligion. Herein consists the Excellencyexcellency of the Wordword of God, that it is so holy; Psal.Ps 119.: 140. Thy Wordword is very pure, therefore thy Servantservant lovethlovethloueth it. Verse 128. I esteem all thy Preceptsprecepts, concerning all Thingsthings, to be right; and I hate every false Wayway. Verse 138. Thy Testimoniestestimonies, that thou Lastlast commanded, are righteous, and very faithful. And 172. My Tonguetongue shall speak of thy Wordword; for all thy Commandmentscommandments are Righteousnessrighteousness. And Psal.Ps 19.: 7, 8, 9, 10. The Lawlaw of the Lord is perfect, converting the Soulsoul: Thethe Testimonytestimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the Simplesimple: Thethe Statutesstatutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the Heartheart: Thethe Commandmentcommandment of the Lord is pure, enlightningenlightening the Eyeseyes: Thethe Fearfear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever: Thethe Judgmentsjudgments of the Lord are true, and righteous altogether: Moremore to be desired are they than Goldgold, yea, than much fine Goldgold; sweeter also than Honeyhoney, and the Honeyhoney-comb. Herein does primarily consist the Amiablenessamiableness and Beautybeauty of the Lord Jesus, whereby he is the chief among ten Thousandsthousands and altogether lovely; even in that he is the holy Oneone of God, Acts 3.: 14. andAnd God's holy Childchild, Acts 4.: 27. andAnd he that is Holyholy, and he that is Truetrue, Rev. 3.: 7. All the spiritual Beautybeauty of his human Naturenature, consisting in his Meeknessmeekness, Lowlinesslowliness, Patiencepatience, Heavenlinessheavenliness, Lovelove to God, Lovelove to Menmen, Condescentioncondescensioncondescention to the Meanmean and Vilevile, and Compassioncompassion to the Miserablemiserable, &c. allAll is sum'dsummed up in his Holinessholiness. And the Beautybeauty of his divine Naturenature, of which the Beautybeauty of his humane Naturenature is the Imageimage and Reflectionreflection, does also primarily consist in his Holinessholiness. Herein primarily consists the Gloryglory of the Gospelgospel, that it is a holy Gospelgospel, and so bright an Emanationemanation of the holy Beautybeauty of God and Jesus Christ: Hereinherein consists the spiritual Beautybeauty of it'sits Doctrinesdoctrines, that they are holy Doctrinesdoctrines, or Doctrinesdoctrines according to Godlinessgodliness. And herein does consist the spiritual Beautybeauty of the Wayway of Salvationsalvation by Jesus Christ, that it so holy a Wayway. And herein chiefly consists the Gloryglory of Heavenheaven, that it is the holy Citycity, the holy Jerusalem, the Habitationhabitation of God's Holinessholiness, and so of his Gloryglory; Isai.Isa 63.: 15. All the Beautiesbeauties of the new Jerusalem, as it is described in the two last Chapterschapters of Revelationrevelation, are but various Representationsrepresentations of this: Seesee Chapchchap. 21.: 2, 10, 11, 18, 21, 27. Chap.Chapter 22.: 1, 3.

And therefore it is primarily on Accountaccount of this Kindkind of Excellencyexcellency, that the Saintssaints do love all these Thingsthings. Thus they love the Wordword of God, because it is very pure. 'Tis on this Accountaccount they love the Saintssaints; and on this Accountaccount chiefly it is, that Heavenheaven is lovely to them, and those holy Tabernaclestabernacles of God amiable in their
Eyeseyes: 'Tis'tis on this Accountaccount that they love God; and on this Accountaccount primarily it is, that they love Christ, and that their Heartshearts delight in the Doctrinesdoctrines of the Gospelgospel, and sweetly acquiesce in the Wayway of Salvationsalvation therein revealed To the right closing with Christ's Personperson, this is also required, to taste the Bitternessbitterness of Sinsin, as the greatest Evilevil: Elseelse a Manman will never close with Christ, for his Holinessholiness in him, and from him, as the greatest Goodgood. For we told you, that that is the right Closingclosing with Christ for himself, when it is for his Holinessholiness. For ask a whorish Heartheart, what Beautybeauty he sees in the Personperson of Christ; he will, after he has looked over his Kingdomkingdom, his Righteousnessrighteousness, all his Worksworks, see a Beautybeauty in them, because they do serve his Turnturn, to comfort him only. As in Marriagemarriage, it is the personal Beautybeauty draws the Heartheart. And hence I have thought it Reasonreason, that he that loves the Brethrenbrethren for a little Gracegrace, will love Christ much more. Shepard's Parableparable, P. I. pP. 84..

Under the Headhead of the first distinguishing Characteristickcharacteristiccharacteristick of gracious Affectionaffection, I observed that there is given to those that are regenerated, a new supernatural Sensesense, that is as it were a certain divine spiritual Tastetaste, which is in its whole Naturenature diverse from any former Kindskinds of Sensationsensation of the Mindmind, as Tastingtasting is diverse from any of the other five Sensessenses, and that something is perceived by a true Saintsaint in the Exerciseexercise of this new Sensesense of Mindmind, in spiritual and divine Thingsthings, as entirely different from any Thingthing that is perceived in them by natural Menmen, as the sweet Tastetaste or Honeyhoney is diverse from the Ideasideas Menmen get of Honeyhoney by looking on it or feeling of it; now this that I have been speaking, viz. The Beautybeauty of Holinessholiness is that Thingthing in spiritual and divine Thingsthings, which is perceived by this spiritual Sensesense, that is so diverse from all that natural Menmen perceive in them: Thisthis Kindkind of Beautybeauty is the Qualityquality that is the immediate Objectobject of this spiritual Sensesense: Thisthis is the Sweetnesssweetness that is the proper Objectobject of this spiritual Tastetaste. The Scripture often represents the Beautybeauty and Sweetnesssweetness of Holinessholiness as the grand Objectobject of a spiritual Tastetaste, and spiritual Appetiteappetite. This was the sweet Foodfood of the holy Soulsoul of Jesus Christ, John 4.: 32, 34. I have Meatmeat to eat, that ye know not of;—Mymy Meatmeat is to do the Willwill of him that sent me, and to finish his Workwork. I know of no Partpart of the holy Scriptures, where the Naturenature and Evidencesevidences of true and sincere Godlinessgodliness, are so much of set Purposepurpose, and so fully and largely insisted on and delineated,
as the 119th Psalm; the Psalmistpsalmist declares his Designdesign in the first Versesverses of the Psalm, and he keeps his Eyeeye on this Designdesign all along, and pursues it to the Endend: Butbut in this Psalm the Excellencyexcellency of Holinessholiness is represented as the immediate Objectobject of a spiritual Tastetaste, Relishrelish, Appetiteappetite and Deli •• ghtdelight, God's Lawlaw, that grand Expressionexpression and Emanationemanation of the Holinessholiness of God's Naturenature, and Prescriptionprescription of Holinessholiness to the Creaturecreature, is all along represented as the Foodfood and Entertainmententertainment, and as the great Objectobject of the Lovelove, the Appetiteappetite, the Complais ••• ancecomplacence and Rejoicingrejoicing of the gracious Naturenature, which prizes God's Commandmentscommandments above Goldgold, yea, the finest Goldgold, and to which they are sweeter than the Honeyhoney, and Honeyhoney-comb; and that upon Accountaccount of their Holinessholiness, as I observed before. The same Psalmistpsalmist declares, that this is the Sweetnesssweetness that a spiritual Tastetaste relishes in God's Lawlaw, Psal.Ps 19.: 8, 9, 10. The Lawlaw of the Lord is perfect:—Thethe Commandmentcommandment of the Lord is pure: Thethe Fearfear of the Lord is clean: Thethe Statutesstatutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the Heartheart:—Thethe Judgmentsjudgments of the Lo • raLord are true, and righteous altogether: Moremore to be desired are they than Goldgold, yea than much fine Goldgold; sweeter also than Honeyhoney and the Honeyhoney comb.

A holy Lovelove has a holy Objectobject: Thethe Holinessholiness of Lovelove consists especially in this that it is the Lovelove of that which is holy, as holy, or for it'sits Holinessholiness; so that 'tis the Holinessholiness of the Objectobject, which is the Qualityquality whereon it fixes and terminates. An holy Naturenature must needs love that in holy Thingsthings chiefly, which is most agreableagreeable to itself; but surely that in divine Thingsthings, which above all others is agreeable to holy Naturenature, is Holinessholiness; because Holinessholiness must be above all other Thingsthings agreableagreeable to Holinessholiness; for nothing can be more agreableagreeable to any Naturenature than itself; holy Naturenature must be above all Thingsthings agreableagreeable to holy Naturenature: Andand so the holy Naturenature of God and Christ, and the Wordword of God, and other divine Thingsthings, must be above all other Thingsthings, agreableagreeable to the holy Naturenature that is in the Saintssaints.

And again, an holy Naturenature doubtless loves holy Thingsthings, especially on the Accountaccount of that, for which sinful Naturenature has Enmityenmity against them: Butbut that for which chiefly sinful Naturenature is at Enmityenmity against holy Thingsthings, is their Holinessholiness; it is for this, that the carnal Mindmind is Enmityenmity against God, and against the Lawlaw of God, and the Peoplepeople of God. Now 'tis just arguing from Contrariescontraries; from contrary Causescauses, to contrary Effectseffects; from opposite Naturesnatures, to opposite Tendenciestendencies. We know that Holinessholiness is of a directly contrary Naturenature to Wickednesswickedness: Asas therefore 'tis the Naturenature of Wickednesswickedness chiefly to oppose and hate Holinessholiness; so it must be the Naturenature of Holinessholiness chiefly to tend to, and delight in Holinessholiness.

The holy Naturenature in the Saintssaints and Angelsangels in Heavenheaven (where the true Tendencytendency of it best appears) is principally engaged by the Holinessholiness of divine Thingsthings. This is the divine Beautybeauty which chiefly engages
the Attentionattention, Admirationadmiration and Praisepraise of the bright and burning Seraphimseraphim; Isai.Isa 6.: 3. One cried unto another, and said, Holyholy, Holyholy, Holyholy is the Lord of Hostshosts; the whole Earthearth is full of his Gloryglory. And Rev. 4.: 8. They rest not Dayday and Nightnight, saying, Holyholy, Holyholy, Holyholy, Lord God almighty, which was, and is, and is to come. So the glorified Saintssaints, Chapchchap. 15.: 4. Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and glorify thy Namename, for thou only art Holyholy?

And the Scriptures represent the Saintssaints on Earthearth as adoring God primarily on this Accountaccount, and admiring and extolling all God's Attributesattributes, either as deriving Lovelinessloveliness from his Holinessholiness, or as being a Partpart of it. Thus when they praise God for his Powerpower, his Holinessholiness is the Beautybeauty that engages them; Psal.Ps 98.: 1. O sing unto the Lord a new Songsong, for he hath done marvellousmarvelous Thingsthings; his right Handhand and his HOLYholy Arm hath gotten him the Victoryvictory. So when they praise him for his Justicejustice and terrible Majestymajesty; Psal.Ps 99.: 2, 3. The Lord is great in Zion, and he is high above all PeeplePeople: Letlet them praise thy great and terrible Namename, for it is HOLYholy. Verse 5. Exalt ye the Lord our God, and worship at his Footstoolfootstool, for he is HOLYholy. Verse 8, 9. Thou wast a God that forgavest them, tho'though thou tookest Vengeancevengeance of their Inventionsinventions. Exalt ye the Lord our God, and worship at his holy Hillhill; for the Lord our God is HOLYholy. So when they praise God for his Mercymercy and Faithfulnessfaithfulness; Psal.Ps 97.: 11. 12. Rejoice in the Lord ye Righteousrighteous, and give Thanksthanks at the Remembranceremembrance of his HOLINESSholiness. 1 Sam. 2.: 2. There is none HOLYholy as the Lord; for there is none beside thee; neither is there any Rockrock like our God.

By this therefore all may try their Affectionsaffections, and particularly their Lovelove and Joyjoy. Various Kindskinds of Creaturescreatures shewshow the Differencedifference of their Naturesnatures, very much, in the different Thingsthings they relish as their proper Goodgood, one delighting in that which another abhors. Such a Differencedifference is there between true Saintssaints, and natural Menmen: Naturalnatural Menmen have no Sensesense of the Goodnessgoodness and Excellencyexcellency of holy Thingsthings; at least for their Holinessholiness; they have no Tastetaste of that Kindkind of Goodgood; and so may be said not to know that divine Goodgood, or not to see it; it is wholly hid from them: Butbut the Saintssaints, by the mighty Powerpower of God, have it discovered to them: Theythey have that supernatural, most noble and divine Sensesense given them, by which they perceive it: Andand it is this that captivates their Heartshearts, and delights them above all Thingsthings; 'tis the most amiable and sweet Thingthing to the Heartheart of a true Saintsaint, that is to be found in Heavenheaven or Earthearth; that which above all others attracts and engages his Soulsoul; and that wherein, above all Thingsthings, he places his Happinesshappiness, and which he lots upon for Solacesolace and Entertainmententertainment to his Mindmind, in this Worldworld, and full Satisfactionsatisfaction and Blessednessblessedness in another. By this you may examine your Lovelove to God, and to Jesus Christ,
and to the Wordword of God, and your Joyjoy in them, and also your Lovelove to the Peoplepeople of God, and your Desiresdesires after Heavenheaven; whether they be from a supreamsupreme Delightdelight in this Sortsort of Beautybeauty, without being primarily moved from your imagined Interestinterest in them, or Expectationsexpectations from 'emthem. There are many high Affectionsaffections, great seeming Lovelove and rapturous Joysjoys, which have nothing of this holy Relishrelish belonging to 'emthem.

Particularly, Byby what has been said you may try your Discoveriesdiscoveries of the Gloryglory of God's Gracegrace and Lovelove, and your Affectionsaffections arising from them. The Gracegrace of God may appear lovely two Waysways; either as Bonumbonum Utileutile, a profitable Goodgood to me, that which greatly serves my Interestinterest, and so suits my Selfself-Lovelove; or as Bonumbonum formosum, a Beautifulbeautiful Goodgood in itself, and Partpart of the moral and spiritual Excellencyexcellency of the divine Naturenature. In this latter Respectrespect it is that the true Saintssaints have their Heartshearts affected, and Lovelove captivated by the free Gracegrace of God in the first Placeplace.

Therefore truly gracious Affectionsaffections are attended with such a Kindkind of Convictionconviction and Perswasionpersuasion of the Truthtruth of the Thingsthings of the Gospelgospel, and Sightsight of their Evidenceevidence and Realityreality, as these and other Scriptures speak of.

Some Personspersons, under high Affectionsaffections, and a confident Perswasionpersuasion of their good Estateestate, have that, which they very ignorantly call a Seeingseeing the Truthtruth of the Wordword of God, and which is very far from it, after this Mannermanner; they have some Texttext of Scripture coming to their Mindsminds, in a sudden and extraordinary Mannermanner, immediately declaring to them (as they suppose) that their Sinssins are forgiven or that God loves them, and will save them; and it may be have a Chainchain of Scriptures coming one after another, to the same Purposepurpose; and they are convinced that it is Truthtruth; i. eE. theyThey are confident that it is certainly so, that their Sinssins are forgiven, and God does love them, &c.—; they say they know it is so; and when the Wordswords of Scripture are suggested to 'emthem, and as they suppose immediately spoken to 'emthem by God, in this Meaningmeaning, they are ready to cry out, Truth, Truthtruth! Whereas the Wholewhole of their Faithfaith amounts to no more, than only a strong Confidenceconfidence of their own good Estateestate, and so a Confidenceconfidence that those Wordswords are true, which they suppose tell 'emthem they are in a good Estateestate: Whenwhen indeed (as was shown before) there is no Scripture which declares that any Personperson is in a good Estateestate directly, or any other Wayway than by Consequenceconsequence. from Delusiondelusion, and not true Convictionconviction; and conseqentlyconsequently are themselves delusive and vain.

But if the religious Affectionsaffections that Personspersons have, do indeed arise from a strong Perswasionpersuasion of the Truthtruth of the christian Religionreligion; their Affectionsaffections are not the better, unless their Perswasionpersuasion be a reasonable Perswasionpersuasion or Convictionconviction. If it be so, that Thatthat is a spiritual Convictionconviction of the Divinitydivinity and Realityreality of the Thingsthings exhibited in the Gospelgospel, which arises from a spiritual Understandingunderstanding of those Thingsthings; I have shown already what that is, viz. aA Sensesense and Tastetaste of the divine, supreamsupreme and holy Excellencyexcellency and Beautybeauty of those Thingsthings. But if our Gospelgospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: Inin whom the God of this Worldworld hath blinded the Mindsminds of them that BELIEVE not, lest the Lightlight of the GLORIOUS GOSPELgospel of Christ, who is the Imageimage of God, should shine unto them. This Viewview or Sensesense of the divine Gloryglory, and unparallel'dunparalleled Beautybeauty of the Thingsthings exhibited to us in the Gospelgospel, has a Tendencytendency to convince the Mindmind of their Divinitydivinity, two Waysways; directly; and more indirectly, and remotely. 1. A Viewview of this divine Gloryglory directly, convinces the Mindmind of the Divinitydivinity of these Thingsthings, as this Gloryglory is in it self a direct, clear, and all-conquering Evidenceevidence of it; especially
when clearly discovered, or when this supernatural Sensesense is given in a good Degreedegree.

He that has his Judgmentjudgment thus directly convinced and assured of the Divinitydivinity of the Thingsthings of the Gospelgospel, by a clear Viewview of their divine Gloryglory, has a reasonable Convictionconviction; his Beliefbelief and Assuranceassurance is altogether agreableagreeable to Reasonreason; because the divine Gloryglory and Beautybeauty of divine Thingsthings is in it self, real Evidenceevidence of their Divinitydivinity, and the most direct and strong Evidenceevidence. He that truly sees the divine, transcendent, supreamsupreme Gloryglory of those Thingsthings which are divine, does as it were know their Divinitydivinity intuitively; he not only argues that they are divine, but he sees that they are divine; he sees Thatthat in them wherein Divinitydivinity chiefly consists; for in this Gloryglory, which is so vastly and inexpressibly distinguished from the Gloryglory of artificial Thingsthings, and all other Gloryglory, does mainly consist the true Notionnotion of Divinitydivinity: God is God, and distinguished from all other Beingsbeings, and exalted above 'emthem, chiefly by his divine Beautybeauty, which is infinitely diverse from all other Beautybeauty. They therefore that see the Stampstamp of this Gloryglory in divine Thingsthings, they see Divinitydivinity in them, they see God in them, and so see 'emthem to be divine; because they see that in them wherein the truest Ideaidea of Divinitydivinity does consist. Thus a Soulsoul may have a Kindkind of intuitive Knowledgeknowledge of the Divinitydivinity of the Thingsthings exhibited in the Gospelgospel; not that he judges the Doctrinesdoctrines of the Gospelgospel to be from God, without any Argumentargument or Deductiondeduction at all; but it is without any long Chainchain of Argumentsarguments; the Argumentargument is but one, and the Evidenceevidence direct; the Mindmind ascends to the Truthtruth of the Gospelgospel but by one Stepstep, and that is its divine Gloryglory.

It would be very strange, if any professing Christian should deny it to be possible that there should be an Excellencyexcellency in divine Thingsthings, which is so transcendent, and exceedingly different from what is in other Thingsthings, that if it were seen, would evidently distinguish them. We can't rationally doubt, but that Thingsthings that are divine, that appertain to the supreamsupreme Beingbeing, are vastly different from Thingsthings that are humane; that there is a god-like, high, and glorious Excellencyexcellency in them, that does so distinguish them from the Thingsthings which are of Menmen, that the Differencedifference is ineffable; and therefore such, as, if seen, will have a most convincing, satisfying Influenceinfluence upon any one, that they are what they are, viz. divineDivine. Doubtless there is that Gloryglory and Excellencyexcellency in the divine Beingbeing, by which he is so infinitely distinguished from all other Beingsbeings, that if it were seen, he might be known by it. It would therefore be very unreasonable to deny that it is possible for God, to give Manifestationsmanifestations of this distinguishing Excellencyexcellency, in Thingsthings by which he is pleased to make himself known; and that this distinguishing Excellencyexcellency may be clearly seen in them. There are natural Excellenciesexcellencies that are very evidently distinguishing of the Subjectssubjects or Authorsauthors, to any one who beholds them. How
is the Speechspeech of an understanding Manman different from that of a little Childchild! And how greatly distinguished is the Speechspeech of some Menmen of great Geniusgenius, as Homer, Cicero, Milton, Locke, Addison, and others, from that of many other understanding Menmen! There are no Limitslimits to be set to the Degreesdegrees of Manifestationmanifestation of mental Excellencyexcellency, that there may be in Speechspeech. But the Appearancesappearances of the natural Perfectionsperfections of God, in the Manifestationsmanifestations he makes of himself, may doubtless be unspeakably more evidently distinguishing, than the Appearancesappearances of those Excellenciesexcellencies of Wormsworms of the Dustdust, in which they differ one from another. He that is well acquainted with Mankindmankind, and their Worksworks, by viewing the Sunsun, may know it is no human Workwork. And 'tis reasonable to suppose, that when Christ comes at the Endend of the Worldworld, in the Gloryglory of his Father, it will be with such ineffable Appearancesappearances of Divinitydivinity, as will leave no Doubtdoubt to the Inhabitantsinhabitants of the Worldworld, even the most obstinate Infidelsinfidels, that he who appears is a divine Personperson. But above all, do the Manifestationsmanifestations of the moral and spiritual Gloryglory of the divine Beingbeing (which is the proper Beautybeauty of the Divinitydivinity) bring their own Evidenceevidence, and tend to assure the Heartheart. Thus the Disciplesdisciples were assured that Jesus was the Son of God, for they beheld his Gloryglory, as the Gloryglory of the only Begottenbegotten of the Father, full of Gracegrace and Truthtruth, John 1.: 14. When Christ appeared in the Gloryglory of his Transfigurationtransfiguration to his Disciplesdisciples, with that outward Gloryglory, to their bodily Eyeseyes, which was a sweet and admirable Symbolsymbol and Semblancesemblance of his spiritual Gloryglory, together with his spiritual Gloryglory it self, manifested to their Mindsminds; the Manifestationmanifestation of Gloryglory was such, as did perfectly, and with good Reasonreason, assure them of his Divinitydivinity; as appears by what one of them, viz. theThe Apostleapostle Peter, says concerning it, 2 Pet. 1.: 16, 17, 18. For we have not followed cunningly devised Fablesfables, when we made known unto you the Powerpower and Comingcoming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were Eyeeye-witnesses of his Majestymajesty: Forfor he received from God the Father, Honourhonorhonour and Gloryglory; when there came such a Voicevoice to him from the excellent Gloryglory, Thisthis is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased. And this Voicevoice which came from Heavenheaven, we heard, when we were with him in the holy Mountmount. The Apostleapostle calls that Mountmount, the holy Mount, because the Manifestationsmanifestations of Christ which were there made to their Mindsminds, and which their Mindsminds were especially impress'dimpressed and ravished with, was the Gloryglory of his Holinessholiness, or the Beautybeauty of his moral Excellencyexcellency; or, as another of these Disciplesdisciples, who saw it, expresses it, Hishis Gloryglory, as full of Gracegrace and Truthtruth.

Now this distinguishing Gloryglory of the divine Beingbeing has it'sits brightest Appearanceappearance and Manifestationmanifestation, in the Thingsthings proposed and exhibited to us in the Gospelgospel, the Doctrinesdoctrines there taught, the Wordword there spoken, and the divine Counselscounsels, Actsacts and Worksworks there revealed. These Thingsthings have the clearest, most admirable, and distinguishing Representationsrepresentations
presentations and Exhibitionsexhibitions of the Gloryglory of God's moral Perfectionsperfections, that ever were made to the Worldworld. And if there be such a distinguishing, evidential Manifestationmanifestation of divine Gloryglory in the Gospelgospel, 'tis reasonable to suppose that there may be such a Thingthing as Seeingseeing it: Whatwhat should hinder but that it may be seen? 'Tis no Argumentargument that it can't be seen, that some don't see it; tho'though they may be discerning Menmen in temporal Mattersmatters. If there be such ineffable, distinguishing, evidential Excellenciesexcellencies in the Gospelgospel, 'tis reasonable to suppose that they are such as are not to be discerned, but by the special Influenceinfluence and Enlightningsenlighteningsenlightnings of the Spirit of God. There is need of uncommon Forceforce of Mindmind to discern the distinguishing Excellenciesexcellencies of the Worksworks of Authorsauthors of great Geniusgenius: Thosethose Thingsthings in Milton, which to mean Judgesjudges, appear tasteless and Imperfectionsimperfections, are his inimitable Excellenciesexcellencies in the Eyeseyes of those who are of greater Discerningdiscerning, and better Tastetaste. And if there be a Bookbook, which God is the Authorauthor of, 'tis most reasonable to suppose that the distinguishing Gloriesglories of his Wordword are of such a Kindkind, as that the Sinsin and Corruptioncorruption of Men'smen's Heartshearts, which above all Thingsthings alienates Menmen from the Deity, and makes the Heartheart dull and stupid to any Sensesense or Tastetaste of those Thingsthings wherein the moral Gloryglory of the divine Perfectionsperfections consists; I say, 'tis but reasonable to suppose, that this would blind Menmen from discerning the Beautiesbeauties of such a Bookbook; and that therefore they will not see them, but as God is pleased to enlighten them, and restore an holy Tastetaste, to discern and relish divine Beautiesbeauties.

This Sensesense of the spiritual Excellencyexcellency and Beautybeauty of divine Thingsthings, does also tend directly to convince the Mindmind of the Truthtruth of the Gospelgospel, as there are very many of the most important Thingsthings declared in the Gospelgospel, that are hid from the Eyeseyes of natural Menmen, the Truthtruth of which does in Effecteffect consist in this Excellencyexcellency, or does so immediately depend upon it and result from it; that in this Excellency'sexcellency's being seen, the Truthtruth of those Thingsthings is seen. As soon as ever the Eyeseyes are opened to behold the holy Beautybeauty and Amiablenessamiableness that is in divine Thingsthings, a Multitudemultitude of most important Doctrinesdoctrines of the Gospelgospel, that depend upon it, (which all appear strange and dark to natural Menmen) are at once seen to be true. As for Instanceinstance, hereby appears the Truthtruth of what the Wordword of God declares concerning the exceeding Evilevil of Sinsin; for the same Eyeeye that discerns the transcendent Beautybeauty of Holinessholiness, necessarily therein sees the exceeding Odiousnessodiousness of Sinsin: Thethe same Tastetaste which relishes the Sweetnesssweetness of true moral Goodgood, tastes the Bitternessbitterness of moral Evilevil. And by this Meansmeans a Manman sees his own Sinfulnesssinfulness and Loathsomnessloathsomenessloathsomness; for he has now a Sensesense to discern Objectsobjects of this Naturenature; and so sees the Truthtruth of what the Wordword of God declares concerning the exceeding Sinfulnesssinfulness of Mankindmankind, which before he did not see. But he whose Heartheart is under the Powerpower of christian Humilityhumility, is of a contrary Dispositiondisposition. If the Scriptures are at all to be relied on, such an one is apt to think his Attainmentsattainments in Religionreligion to be comparatively mean, and to esteem himself low among the Saintssaints, and one of the least of Saintssaints. Jer. 1.: 6.) tho'though they were such eminent Saintssaints, and of great Knowledgeknowledge. It is not natural to them to think that it belongs to them to teach, but to be taught: Theythey are much more eager to hear, and to receive Instructioninstruction from others, than to dictate to others; Jam.Jas 1.: 19.. Be ye swift 〈◊〉 to hear, slow to speak. And when they do speak, 'tis not •
natural to them to speak with a bold, masterly Airair; but Humilityhumility disposes 'emthem rather to speak trembling. HoseaHos 13.: 1. When Ephraim spake trembling, he exalted himself in Israel; but when he offended in Baal, he died. They are not apt to assume Authorityauthority, and to take upon 'emthem to be chief Managersmanagers and Mastersmasters; but rather to be subject to others. Jam.Jas 3.: 1, 2. Be not many Mastersmasters. 1 Pet. 5.: 5. All of you be subject 〈◊〉 one to another, and be cloathedclothed with Humilityhumility. Eph. 5.: 21. Submitting your selves one to another, in the Fearfear of God.

There are some Person'sperson's Experiencesexperiences that naturally work that Wayway, to make them think highly of their Experiencesexperiences; and they do often themselves speak of their Experiencesexperiences as very great and extraordinary, they freely speak of the great Thingsthings; they have met 〈◊〉 with.
