The Personspersons that talk thus about their Experiencesexperiences, when they give an Accountaccount of them, expect that others should admire 'emthem. Indeed they don't call it Boastingboasting to talk after this Mannermanner about their Experiencesexperiences, nor do they look upon it as any Signsign of Pridepride; because they say, they know that it was not they that did it, it was free Gracegrace, they are the great Thingsthings that God has done for them, they would acknowledge the great Mercymercy God has shown them, and not make light of it. But so it was with the Pharisee that Christ tells us of, Luke 18. He in Wordswords gave God the Gloryglory of making him to differ from other Menmen; God I thank thee, says he, that I am not as other Menmen
Calvin, in his Institutionsinstitutions, B. 3. Chap.Chapter 12. § 7. speakingSpeaking of this Pharisee, observes, Thatthat in his outward Confessionconfession he acknowledges that the Righteousnessrighteousness that he has is the Giftgift of God: Butbut (says he) because he trusts that he is Righteousrighteous, he goes away out of the Presencepresence of God, unacceptable and odious.. Their verbally ascribing it to
the Gracegrace of God, that they are holier than other Saintssaints, don't hinder their Forwardnessforwardness to think so highly of their Holinessholiness, being a sure Evidenceevidence of the Pridepride and Vanityvanity of their Mindsminds. If they were under the Influenceinfluence of an humble Spirit, their Attainmentsattainments in Religionreligion would not be so apt to shine in their own Eyeseyes, nor would they be so much in admiring their own Beautybeauty. The Christians that are really the most eminent Saintssaints, and therefore have the most excellent Experiencesexperiences, and are greatest in the Kingdomkingdom of Heavenheaven, humble themselves as a little Childchild, Matth.Matt 18.: 4. Because they look on themselves as but little Childrenchildren in Gracegrace, and their Attainmentsattainments to be but the Attainmentsattainments of Babesbabes in Christ, and are astonished at, and ashamed of the low Degreesdegrees of their Lovelove, and their Thankfulnessthankfulness, and their little Knowledgeknowledge of God. Moses when he had been conversing with God in the Mountmount, and his Faceface shone so bright in the Eyeseyes of others, as to dazzle their Eyeseyes, wist not that his Faceface shone. There are some Personspersons that go by the Namename of high Professorsprofessors, and some will own themselves to be high Professorsprofessors; but eminently humble Saintssaints, that will shine brightest in Heavenheaven, are not at all apt to profess high. I don't believe there is an eminent Saintsaint in the Worldworld that is a high Professorprofessor. Such will be much more likely to profess themselves to be the least of all Saintssaints, and to think that every Saint'ssaint's Attainmentsattainments and Experiencesexperiences are higher than his. Luther, as his Wordswords are cited by Rutherford, in his Display of the spiritual Antichrist, p. 143, 144. saysSays thus, Soso is the Lifelife of a Christian, that he that has begun, seems to himself to have nothing; but strives and presses forward, that he may apprehend. Whence Paul says, I count not my self to have apprehended. For indeed nothing is more pernicious to a Believerbeliever, than that Presumptionpresumption, that he has already apprehended, and has no further Needneed of seeking. Hence also many fall back, and pine away in spiritual Securitysecurity and Slothfulnessslothfulness. So Bernard says, To stand still in God's Wayway, is to go back. Wherefore this remains to him that has begun to be a Christian, to think that he is not yet a Christian, but to seek that he may be a Christian, that he may glory with Paul, I am not, but I desire to be; a Christian not yet finished, but only in his Beginningsbeginnings. Therefore he is not a Christian, that is a Christian, that is, Hehe that thinks himself a finished Christian, and is not sensible how he falls short. We reach after Heavenheaven, but are not in Heavenheaven. Woe to him that is wholly renewed that is, that thinks himself to be so. That Manman, without Doubtdoubt, has never so much as begun to be renewed, nor did he ever taste what it is to be a Christian.

Such is the Naturenature of Gracegrace, and of true spiritual Lightlight, that they naturally dispose the Saintssaints in the present Statestate, to look upon their Gracegrace and Goodnessgoodness little, and their Deformitydeformity great. And they that have the most Gracegrace and spiritual Lightlight, of any in this Worldworld, have most of this Dispositiondisposition. As will appear most clear and evident to any one that soberly and thoroughly weighs the Naturenature and Reasonreason of Thingsthings, and considers the Thingsthings following.

That Gracegrace and Holinessholiness is worthy to be called little, that is, little in Comparisoncomparison of what it ought to be. And so it seems to one that is truly gracious: Forfor such an one has his Eyeeye upon the Rulerule of his Dutyduty; a Conformityconformity to that is what he aims at; it is what his Soulsoul struggles and reaches after; and it is by that that he estimates and judges of what he does, and what he has. To a gracious Soulsoul, and especially to one eminently gracious, that Holinessholiness appears little, which is little of what it should be; little of what he sees infinite Reasonreason for, and Obligationobligation to. If his Holinessholiness appears to him to be at a vast Distancedistance from this, it naturally appears despicable in his Eyeseyes, and not worthy to be mentioned as any Beautybeauty or Amiablenessamiableness in him. For the like Reasonreason as a hungry Manman naturally accounts that which is set before him, but a little Foodfood, a small Mattermatter, not worth mentioning, that is nothing in Comparisoncomparison of his Appetiteappetite. Or as the Childchild of a great Princeprince, that is jealous for the Honourhonorhonour of his Fatherfather, and beholds the Respectrespect which Menmen shewshow him, naturally looks on that Honourhonorhonour and Respectrespect very little, and not worthy to be regarded, which is nothing in Comparisoncomparison of that, which the Dignitydignity of his Fatherfather requires.

But that is the Naturenature of true Gracegrace and spiritual Lightlight, that it opens to a Person'sperson's Viewview the infinite Reasonreason there is that he should be holy in a high Degreedegree. And the more Gracegrace he has, the more this is open'dopened to Viewview, the greater Sensesense he has of the infinite Excellencyexcellency and Gloryglory of the divine Beingbeing, and of the infinite Dignitydignity of the Personperson of Christ, and the boundless Lengthlength and Breadthbreadth, and Depthdepth and Heightheight, of the Lovelove of Christ to Sinnerssinners. And as Gracegrace encreasesincreases, the Fieldfield opens more and more to a distant Viewview, 'tilltill the Soulsoul is swallowed up with the Vastnessvastness of the Objectobject, and the Personperson is astonished to think how much it becomes him to love this God, and this glorious Redeemer, that has so loved Manman, and how little he does love. And so the more he apprehends, the more the Smallnesssmallness of his Gracegrace and Lovelove appears strange and wonderful: Andand therefore is more ready to think that others are beyond him. For wondringwondering at the Littlenesslittleness of his own Gracegrace, he can scarcely believe that so strange a Thingthing happens to other Saintssaints: 'Tis'tis amazing to him, that one that is really a Childchild of God, and that has actually received the saving Benefitsbenefits of that unspeakable Lovelove of Christ, should love no more: Andand he is apt to look upon it as a Thingthing peculiar to himself, a strange
and exempt Instanceinstance; for he sees only the outside of other Christians, but he sees his own inside.

Here the Readerreader may possibly object, that Lovelove to God is really increased, in Proportionproportion as the Knowledgeknowledge of God is increased; and therefore how should an Increaseincrease of Knowledgeknowledge in a Saintsaint, make his Lovelove apearappear less, in Comparisoncomparison of what is known? To which I answer, that altho'although Gracegrace and the Lovelove of God in the Saintssaints, be answerable to the Degreedegree of Knowledgeknowledge or Sightsight of God; yet it is not in Proportionproportion to the Objectobject seen & known. The Soulsoul of a Saintsaint, by having something of God open'dopened to Sightsight, is convinced of much more than is seen. There is something that is seen, that is wonderful; and that Sightsight, brings with it a strong Convictionconviction of something vastly beyond, that is not immediately seen. So that the Soulsoul, at the same Timetime, is astonished at it'sits Ignoranceignorance, and that it knows so little, as well as that it loves so little. And as the Soulsoul, in a spiritual Viewview, is convinced of infinitely more in the Objectobject, yet beyond Sightsight; so it is convinced of the Capacitycapacity of the Soulsoul, of knowing vastly more, if Cloudsclouds and Darknessdarkness were but removed. Which causes the Soulsoul, in the Enjoymentenjoyment of a spiritual Viewview, to complain greatly of spiritual Ignoranceignorance, and Wantwant of Lovelove, and long and reach after more Knowledgeknowledge, and more Lovelove.

Grace and the Lovelove of God in the most eminent Saintssaints in this Worldworld, is truly very little in Comparisoncomparison of what it ought to be. Because the highest Lovelove, that ever any attain to in this Lifelife, is poor, cold, exceeding low, and not worthy to be named in Comparisoncomparison of what our Obligationsobligations appear to be, from the joint Considerationconsideration of these two Thingsthings; viz. 1. The Reasonreason God has given us to love him, in the Manifestationsmanifestations he has made of his infinite Gloryglory, in his Wordword, and in his Worksworks; and particularly in the Gospelgospel of his Son, and what he has done for sinful Manman by him. And 2. The Capacitycapacity there is in the Soulsoul of Manman, by those intellectual Facultiesfaculties which God has given it, of seeing and understanding these Reasonsreasons, which God has given us to love him. How small indeed is the Lovelove of the most eminent Saintsaint on Earthearth, in Comparisoncomparison of what these Thingsthings jointly considered do require! And this Gracegrace tends to convince Menmen of; and especially eminent Gracegrace: for Gracegrace is of the Naturenature of Lightlight, and brings Truthtruth to Viewview. And therefore, he that has much Gracegrace, apprehends much more than others, that great Heightheight to which his Lovelove ought to ascend; and he sees better than others, how little a Wayway he has risen towards that Heightheight. And therefore, estimating his Lovelove by the whole Heightheight of his Dutyduty, hence it appears astonishingly little and low in his Eyeseyes.

And the eminent Saintsaint, having such a Convictionconviction of the high Degreedegree in which he ought to love God, this shewsshows him, not only the Li •• ttlenesslittleness of his Gracegrace, but the Greatnessgreatness of his remaining Corruptioncorruption.
In order to judge how much Corruptioncorruption or Sinsin we have remaining in us, we must take our Measuremeasure from that Heightheight to which the Rulerule of our Dutyduty extends: Thethe whole of the Distancedistance we are at from that Heightheight, is Sinsin: Forfor failing of Dutyduty is Sinsin; otherwise our Dutyduty is not our Dutyduty; and by how much the more we fall short of our Dutyduty, so much the more Sinsin have we. Sin is no other than Disagreablenessdisagreeablenessdisagreableness, in a moral Agentagent, to the Lawlaw, or Rulerule of his Dutyduty. And therefore the Degreedegree of Sinsin is to be judged of by the Rulerule: Soso much Disagreablenessdisagreeablenessdisagreableness to the Rulerule, so much Sinsin, whether it be in Defectdefect or Excessexcess. Therefore if Menmen, in their Lovelove to God, don't come up half way to that Heightheight which Dutyduty requires, then they have more Corruptioncorruption in their Heartshearts than Gracegrace; because there is more Goodnessgoodness wanting, than is there; and all that is wanting is Sinsin: it is an abominable Defectdefect; and appears so to the Saintssaints, especially those that are eminent; it appears exceeding abominable to them, that Christ should be loved so little, and thanked so little for his dying Lovelove; it is in their Eyeseyes hateful Ingratitudeingratitude.

And then the Increaseincrease of Gracegrace has a Tendencytendency another Wayway, to cause the Saintssaints to think their Deformitydeformity vastly more than their Goodnessgoodness: Itit not only tends to convince them that their Corruptioncorruption is much greater than their Goodnessgoodness; which is indeed the Casecase: Butbut it also tends to cause the Deformitydeformity that there is in the least Sinsin, or the least Degreedegree of Corruptioncorruption, to appear so great, as vastly to out-weigh all the Beautybeauty there is in their greatest Holinessholiness: Forfor this also is indeed the Casecase. For the least Sinsin against an infinite God, has an infinite Hatefulnesshatefulness or Deformitydeformity in it; but the highest Degreedegree of Holinessholiness in a Creaturecreature, has not an infinite Lovelinessloveliness in it: Andand therefore the Lovelinessloveliness of it is as nothing, in Comparisoncomparison of the Deformitydeformity of the least Sinsin. That every Sinsin has infinite Deformitydeformity and Hatefulnesshatefulness in it, is most demonstrably evident; because what the Evilevil, or Iniquityiniquity, or Hatefulnesshatefulness of Sinsin consists in, is the violating of an Obligationobligation, or the being or doing contrary to what we should be or do, or are obliged to. And therefore by how much the greater the Obligationobligation is that is violated, so much the greater is the Iniquityiniquity and Hatefulnesshatefulness of the Violationviolation. But certainly our Obligationobligation to love and honourhonor any Beingbeing, is in some Proportionproportion to his Lovelinessloveliness and Honourablenesshonorablenesshonourableness, or to his Worthinessworthiness to be loved and honouredhonored by us; which is the same Thingthing. We are surely under greater Obligationobligation to love a more lovely Beingbeing, than a less lovely: Andand if a Beingbeing be infinitely lovely or worthy to be loved by us, then our Obligationsobligations to love him, are infinitely great: Andand therefore, whatever is contrary to this Lovelove, has in it infinite Iniquityiniquity, Deformitydeformity and Unworthinessunworthiness. But on the other Handhand, with Respectrespect to our Holinessholiness or Lovelove to God, there is not an infinite Worthinessworthiness in that. The Sinsin of the Creaturecreature against God, is ill-deserving and hateful in
Proportionproportion to the Distancedistance there is between God and the Creaturecreature: Thethe Greatnessgreatness of the Objectobject, and the Meannessmeanness and Inferiorityinferiority of the Subjectsubject, aggravates it. But 'tis the reverse with Regardregard to the Worthinessworthiness of the Respectrespect of the Creaturecreature to God; 'tis worthless, and not worthy, in Proportionproportion to the Meannessmeanness of the Subjectsubject. So much the greater the Distancedistance between God and the Creaturecreature, so much the less is the Creature'screature's Respectrespect worthy of God's Noticenotice or Regardregard. The great Degreedegree of Superioritysuperiority, increases the Obligationobligation on the Inferiourinferior to regard the Superioursuperior; and so makes the Wantwant of Regardregard more hateful: Butbut the great Degreedegree of Inferiorityinferiority diminishes the Worthworth of the Regardregard of the Inferiourinferior; because the more he is inferiourinferior, the less is he worthy of Noticenotice, the less he is, the less is what he can offer worth; for he can offer no more than himself, in offering his best Respectrespect; and therefore as he is little, and little worth, so is his Respectrespect little worth. And the more a Personperson has of true Gracegrace and spiritual Lightlight, the more will it appear thus to him; the more will he appear to himself infinitely deformed by Reasonreason of Sinsin, and the less will the Goodnessgoodness that is in his Gracegrace, or good Experienceexperience, appear in Proportionproportion to it. For indeed it is nothing to it: Itit is less than a Dropdrop to the Oceanocean: Forfor finite bears no Proportionproportion at all to that which is infinite. But the more a Personperson has of spiritual Lightlight, the more do Thingsthings appear to him, in this Respectrespect, as they are indeed. Hence it most demonstrably appears, that true Gracegrace is of that Naturenature, that the more a Personperson has of it, with remaining Corruptioncorruption, the less does his Goodnessgoodness and Holinessholiness appear, in Proportionproportion to his Deformitydeformity; and not only to his past Deformitydeformity, but to his present Deformitydeformity, in the Sinsin that now appears in his Heartheart, and in the abominable Defectsdefects of his highest and best Affectionsaffections, and brightest Experiencesexperiences.

The Naturenature of many high religious Affectionsaffections, and great Discoveriesdiscoveries (as they are called) in many Personspersons that I have been acquainted with, is to hide and cover over the Corruptioncorruption of their Heartshearts, and to make it seem to them as if all their Sinsin was gone, and to leave them without Complaintscomplaints of any hateful Evilevil left in them; (tho'though it may be they cry out much of their past Unworthinessunworthiness) a sure and certain Evidenceevidence that their Discoveriesdiscoveries (as they call them) are Darknessdarkness and not Lightlight. 'Tis Darknessdarkness that hides Men'smen's Pollutionpollution and Deformitydeformity; but Lightlight let into the Heartheart discovers it, searches it out in its secret Cornerscorners, and makes it plainly to appear; especially that penetrating, all-searching Lightlight of God's Holinessholiness and Gloryglory. 'Tis true that saving Discoveriesdiscoveries may for the present hide Corruptioncorruption in one Sensesense; they restrain the positive Exercisesexercises of it, such as Malicemalice, Envyenvy, Coveteousnesscovetousnesscoveteousness, Lasciviousnesslasciviousness, Murmuringmurmuring, &c. butBut they bring Corruptioncorruption to Lightlight, in that which is privative, viz. thatThat there is no more Lovelove, no more Humilityhumility, no more Thankfulnessthankfulness.
Which Defectsdefects appear most hateful, in the Eyeseyes of those who have the most eminent Exercisesexercises of Gracegrace; and are very burdensome, and cause the Saintssaints to cry out of their Leannessleanness, and odious Pridepride and Ingratitudeingratitude. And whatever positive Exercisesexercises of Corruptioncorruption, at any Timetime arise, and mingle themselves with eminent acting of Gracegrace, Gracegrace will exceedingly magnify the Viewview of them, and render their Appearanceappearance far more heinous and horrible.

The more eminent Saintssaints are, and the more they have of the Lightlight of Heavenheaven in their Soulssouls, the more do they appear to themselves, at the most eminent Saintssaints in this Worldworld do, to the Saintssaints and Angelsangels in Heavenheaven. How can we rationally suppose the most eminent Saintssaints on Earthearth appear to them, if beheld any otherwise, than covered over with the Righteousnessrighteousness of Christ, and their Deformitiesdeformities swallowed up and hid in the Coruscationcoruscation of the Beamsbeams of his abundant Gloryglory and Lovelove? How can we suppose our most ardent Lovelove and Praisespraises appear to them, that do behold the Beautybeauty and Gloryglory of God with out a Veilveil? How does our highest Thankfulnessthankfulness for the dying Lovelove of Christ appear to them, who see Christ as he is, who know? asAs they are known, and see the Gloryglory of the Personperson of him that died, and the Wonderswonders of his dying Lovelove, without any Cloudcloud or Darknessdarkness? And how do they look on the deepest Reverencereverence and Humilityhumility, with which Wormsworms of the Dustdust on Earthearth approach that infinite Majestymajesty, which they behold? Do they appear great to them, or so much as worthy of the Namename of Reverencereverence and Humilityhumility, in those that they see to be at such an infinite Distancedistance from that great and holy God, in whose glorious Presencepresence they are? The Reasonreason why the highest Attainmentsattainments of the Saintssaints on Earthearth appear so mean to them, is because they dwell in the Lightlight of God's Gloryglory, and see God as he is. And it is in this Respectrespect with the Saintssaints on Earthearth, as it is with the Saintssaints in Heavenheaven, in Proportionproportion as they are more eminent in Gracegrace.

I would not be understood that the Saintssaints on Earthearth have, in all Respectsrespects, the worst Opinionopinion of themselves, when they have most of the Exerciseexercise of Gracegrace. In many Respectsrespects 'tis otherwise. With Respectrespect to the positive Exercisesexercises of Corruptioncorruption, they may appear to themselves freest and best when Gracegrace is most in Exerciseexercise, and worst when the Actingsactings of Gracegrace are lowest. And when they compare themselves with themselves, at different Timestimes, they may know, when Gracegrace is in lively Exerciseexercise, that 'tis better with them than it was before, (tho'though before, in the Timetime of it, they did not see so much Badnessbadness as they see now); and when afterwards they sink again in the Frameframe of their Mindsminds, they may know that they sink, and have a new Argumentargument of their great remaining Corruptioncorruption, and a rational Convictionconviction of a greater Vilenessvileness than they saw before; and may have more of a Sensesense of Guiltguilt, and a kind of legal Sensesense of their
Sinfulnesssinfulness, by far, than when in the lively Exerciseexercise of Gracegrace. But yet it is true, and demonstrable from the foremention'd Considerationsconsiderations, that the Childrenchildren of God never have so much of a sensible and spiritual Convictionconviction of their Deformitydeformity; and so great and quick and abasing a Sensesense of their present Vilenessvileness and Odiousnessodiousness, as when they are highest in the Exerciseexercise of true and pure Gracegrace; and never are they so much disposed to set themselves low among Christians as then. And thus he that is greatest in the Kingdomkingdom, or most eminent in the Churchchurch of Christ, is the same that humbles himself, as the least Infantinfant among them; agreeable to that great Sayingsaying of Christ, Matth.Matt 18.: 4.

A true Saintsaint may know that he has some true Gracegrace: Andand the more Gracegrace there is, the more easily is it known; as was observed and proved before. But yet it does not follow, that an eminent Saintsaint is easily sensible that he is an eminent Saintsaint, when compared with others.—I will not deny that it is possible, that he that has much Gracegrace, and is an eminent Saintsaint, may know it. But he won't be apt to know it: Itit won't be a Thingthing obvious to him: Thatthat he is better than others, and has higher Experiencesexperiences and Attainmentsattainments, is not a foremost Thoughtthought; nor is it Thatthat which, from Timetime to Timetime, readily offers it self: Itit is a Thingthing that is not in his Wayway, but lies far out of Sightsight: Hehe must take Painspains to convince himself of it: Therethere will be need of a great Commandcommand of Reasonreason, and a high Degreedegree of Strictnessstrictness and Carecare in arguing, to convince himself. And if he be rationally convinced, by a very strict Considerationconsideration of his own Experiencesexperiences, compared with the great Appearancesappearances of low Degreesdegrees of Gracegrace in some other Saintssaints, it will hardly seem real to him, that he has more Gracegrace than they: Andand he'll be apt to lose the Convictionconviction, that he has by Painspains obtained: Nornor will it seem at all natural to him to act upon that Suppositionsupposition. And this may be laid down as an infallible Thingthing, That the Personperson who is apt to think that he 〈◊〉 , as compared with others, is a very eminent Saintsaint, much distinguished in christian Experienceexperience, in whom this is a first Thoughtthought, that rises of it self, and naturally offers it self; he is certainly mistaken; he is no eminent Saintsaint; but under the great Prevailingsprevailings of a proud and self-righteous Spiritspirit. And if this be habitual with the Manman, and is statedly the prevailing Tempertemper of his Mindmind, he is no Saintsaint at all; he has not the least Degreedegree of any true christian Experienceexperience; so surely as the Wordword of God is true.

And that Sortsort of Experiencesexperiences that appears to be of that Tendencytendency, and is found from Timetime to Timetime to have that Effecteffect, to elevate the Subjectsubject of them with a great Conceitconceit of those Experiencesexperiences, is certainly vain and delusive. Those supposed Discoveriesdiscoveries that naturally blow up the Personperson with an Admirationadmiration of the Eminencyeminency of his Discoveriesdiscoveries, and fill him with Conceitconceit, that now he has seen, and
knows more than most other Christians, have nothing of the Naturenature of true spiritual Lightlight in them. All true spiritual Knowledgeknowledge is of that Naturenature, 'that the more a Personperson has of it, the more is he sensible of his own Ignoranceignorance; as is evident by 1 Cor.Corinthians 8.: 2. He that thinketh he knoweth any Thingthing, he knoweth nothing yet, as he ought to kno • w. Agur when he had a great Discoverydiscovery of God, and Sensesense of the wonderful Heightheight of his Gloryglory, and of his marvellousmarvelous Worksworks, and cries out of his Greatnessgreatness and Incomprehensiblenessincomprehensibleness; at the same 〈◊〉 Timetime, had the deepest Sensesense of his bruitishbrutish Ignoranceignorance, and look d upon himself the most ignorant of all the Saintssaints; Prov. 30.: 2, 3, 4. Surely I am more brutish than any Manman, and have not the Understandingunderstanding of a Manman: I neither learned Wisdomwisdom, nor have the Knowledgeknowledge of the Holyholy. Who hath ascended up into Heavenheaven, or descended? Who hath gathered the Windwind in his Fistsfists? Who hath bound the Waterswaters in a Garmentgarment? Who hath established all the Endsends of the Earthearth? What is his Namename? And what is his Son's Namename? If thou canst tell.

For a Manman to be highly conceited of his spiritual and divine Knowledgeknowledge, is for him to be wise in his own Eyeseyes, if any Thingthing is. And therefore it comes under those Prohibitionsprohibitions, Prov. 3.: 7. Be not wise in thine own Eyeseyes. Rom. 12.: 16. Be not wise in your own Conceitsconceits. And brings Menmen under that Wo, Isai.Isa 5.: 21. Wo unto them that are wise in their own Eyeseyes, and prudent in their own Sightsight. Confidenceconfidence enough in God, to dare to trust him with a little of their Estatesestates, bestowed to pious and charitable Usesuses: I say, when it is thus • with Personspersons, their Pretencespretensespretences are manifestly vain. Dr. Owen (on the Spirit, Bookbook III. The most eminent divine Favoursfavorsfavours that the Saintssaints obtained, that we read of in Scripture, were in their Retirementretirement. But here some may object and say▪, Howhow is this consistent with what all allow, Thatthat spiritual Enjoymentsenjoyments are of a Soulsoul-satisfying Naturenature?

I answer, It'sIts being so, will appear to be not at all inconsistent with what has been said▪, if it be considered in what Mannermanner spiritual Enjoymentsenjoyments are said to be of a Soulsoul-satisfying Naturenature. Surely the Beggar'sbeggar's looking on the Moneymoney he has in his Handshands, as a Signsign of the Kindnesskindness of him who gave it to him, is in no Respectrespect, inconsistent with the Freenessfreeness of that Kindnesskindness. 'Tis his having Moneymoney in his Handhand as the Priceprice of a Benefitbenefit, that is the Thingthing which is inconsistent with the free Kindnesskindness of the Givergiver. The Notionnotion of the Freenessfreeness of the Gracegrace of God to Sinnerssinners, as that is revealed and taught in the Gospelgospel, is not that no holy and amiable Qualificationsqualifications or Actionsactions in us shall be a Fruitfruit, and so a Signsign of that Gracegrace; but that it is not the Worthinessworthiness or Lovelinessloveliness of any Qualificationqualification or Actionaction of ours which recommends us to that Gracegrace; that Kindnesskindness is shown to the Unworthyunworthy and Unlovelyunlovely; that there is great Excellencyexcellency in the Benefitbenefit bestowed, and no Excellencyexcellency in the Subjectsubject as the Priceprice of it; that Goodnessgoodness goes forth and flows out, from the Fulnessfullnessfulness of God's Naturenature, the Fulnessfullnessfulness of the Fountainfountain of Goodgood, without any Amiablenessamiableness in the Objectobject to draw it. And this is the Notionnotion of Justificationjustification without Worksworks (as this Doctrinedoctrine is taught in the Scripture) that it is
not 〈◊〉 the Worthinessworthiness or Lovelinessloveliness of our Worksworks, or any Thingthing in us 〈◊◊〉 , which is 〈◊〉 any wise 〈◊〉 accepted with God, as a Balancebalance for the Guiltguilt of Sinsin or a 〈◊◊〉 Recommendationrecommendation of Sinnerssinners to his 〈◊〉 Acceptanceacceptance as Heirs of Life 〈…〉 ▪. Thus 〈◊〉 Thusthus we are justified only by the Righteousnessrighteousness of Christ, and not by our 〈◊◊〉 Righteousnessrighteousness. And when Worksworks are opposed to Faithfaith i • n this Affairaffair, and it is said that we are justified by Faithfaith and 〈◊〉 not by Worksworks; thereby is meant, that it is not the Worthinessworthiness or Amiablenessamiableness of our Worksworks, or any Thingthing in us, which recommends us to an Interestinterest in Christ and his Benefitsbenefits; but that we have this Interestinterest only by Faithfaith, or by our Soulssouls receiving Christ, or adhering to, and closing with him. But that the Worthinessworthiness or Amiablenessamiableness of nothing in us recommends and brings us to an Interestinterest in Christ, is no Argumentargument that nothing in us is a Signsign of an Interestinterest in Christ.

If the Doctrinesdoctrines of free Gracegrace, and Justificationjustification by Faithfaith alone, be inconsistent with the Importanceimportance of holy Practicepractice as a Signsign of Gracegrace; then they are equally inconsistent with the Importanceimportance of any Thingthing whatsoever in u • s as a Signsign of Gracegrace, any Holinessholiness, or any Gracegrace that is in us, or any of our Experiencesexperiences or Religionreligion: for 'tis as contrary to the Doctrinesdoctrines of free Gracegrace and Justificationjustification by Faithfaith alone, that any of these should be the Righteousnessrighteousness which we are justified by, as that holy Practicepractice should be so. 'Tis with holy • Worksworks, as it is with holy Qualificationsqualifications: 'Tis'tis inconsistent with the Freenessfreeness of Gospelgospel Gracegrace, that a Titletitle to Salvationsalvation should be given to Menmen for the Lovelinessloveliness of any of their holy Qualificationsqualifications, as much as that it should b • e given for the Holinessholiness of their Worksworks. It is inconsistent with the Gospelgospel Doctrinedoctrine of free Gracegrace, that an Interestinterest in Christ and his Benefitsbenefits should be given for the Lovelinessloveliness of a Man'sman's true Holinessholiness, for the Amiablenessamiableness of his renewed, sanctified, heavenly Heartheart, his Lovelove to God, and being like God, or his Experienceexperience of Joyjoy in the Holyholy Ghost, Selfself-emptiness, a Spiritspirit to exalt Christ above all, and to give all Gloryglory to him, and a Heartheart devoted unto him: I say, it is inconsistent with the Gospelgospel Doctrinedoctrine of free Gracegrace, that a Titletitle to Christ's Benefitsbenefits should be given out of Regardregard to the Lovelinessloveliness of any of these, or that any of these should be our Righteousnessrighteousness in the Affairaffair of Justificationjustification. And yet this don't hinder the Importanceimportance of these Thingsthings as Evidencesevidences of an Interestinterest in Christ. Just so it is with Respectrespect to holy Actionsactions and Worksworks. To make light of Worksworks, because we ben't justified by Worksworks, is the same Thingthing in Effecteffect, as to make light of all Religionreligion, all Gracegrace and Holinessholiness, yea, true evangeli •• cal Holinessholiness, and all gracious Experienceexperience: Forfor all is included, when the Scripture says, we are not justified by Worksworks: Forfor by Worksworks in this Casecase, is meant all our own Righteousnessrighteousness, Religionreligion, or Holinessholiness, and every Thingthing that is in us, all the Goodgood we do, and all the Goodgood which we are conscious of, all external Actsacts, and all internal Actsacts and Exercisesexercises of Gracegrace, and all Experiencesexperiences, and all those holy and heavenly Thingsthings wherein the Lifelife and Powerpower, and the very Essenceessence of
Religionreligion do consist, all those great Thingsthings which Christ and his Apostlesapostles mainly insisted on in their Preachingpreaching, and endeavouredendeavored to promote▪, as of the greatest Consequenceconsequence in the Heartshearts and Liveslives of Menmen, and all good Dispositionsdispositions, Exercisesexercises and Qualificationsqualifications of every Kindkind whatsoever; and even Faithfaith it self, consider'dconsidered as a Part of our Holinessholiness. For we are justified by none of these Thingsthings: Andand if we were, we should, in a Scripture Sensesense, be justified by Worksworks. And therefore if it ben’t 〈◊〉 legal, and contrary to the evangelical Doctrinedoctrine of justification without Worksworks, to insist on any of these, as of great Importanceimportance, as Evidencesevidences of an Interestinterest in Christ; then no more is it thus, to i • nsist on the Importanceimportance of holy Practicepractice. It would be legal to suppose that holy Practicepractice justifies by bringing us to a Titletitle to Christ's Benefitsbenefits, as the Priceprice of it, or as recommending to it by its Preciousnesspreciousness or Excellenceexcellence; but it is not legal to suppose, that holy Practicepractice justifies the Sinceritysincerity of a Believerbeliever, as the proper Evidenceevidence of it. The Apostleapostle James did not think it legal to say, that Abraham our Father was 〈◊〉 Justifiedjustified by Worksworks in this Sensesense. The Spirit that indited the Scripture did not think the great Importanceimportance and absolute Necessitynecessity of holy Practicepractice, in this Respectrespect, to be inconsistent with the Freenessfreeness of Gracegrace; for it commonly teaches 'emthem both together; as in Rev.Revelation 21.: 6, 7. God says, I will give unto him that is Athirstathirst, of the Fountainfountain of the Waterwater of Lifelife freely: Andand then adds, in the very next Wordswords, He that overcometh 〈◊〉 shall inherit all Thingsthings. As tho'though behaving well in the christian Racerace and Warfarewarfare, were the Conditioncondition of the Promisepromise. So in the next Chapterchapter, in the 14th, and 15th Versesverses, Christ says, Blessed are they that do his Commandmentscommandments, that they may have Rightright to the •• Treetree of Lifelife, and enter in thro'through the Gatesgates, into the Citycity: Andand then declares in the 15th Verseverse, how they that are of a wicked Practicepractice shall be excluded; and yet in the two Versesverses next following, does with very great Solemnitysolemnity, give forth an Invitationinvitation to all to come and take of the Waterwater of Lifelife freely; I am the Rootroot and the Off-spring of David •• ▪, the bright and Morningmorning▪- Starstar: Andand the Spirit and the Bridebride say, Comecome, and let him that heareth say, Comecome, and let him that is Athirstathirst, Comecome, and whosoever will, let him come and take of the Waterwater of Lifelife freely. So Chapchchap. 3.: 20 • , 21. Behold I stand at the Doordoor and knock: Ifif any Manman hear my Voicevoice, and open the Doordoor, I will come in to him, and sup with him, and he with me: Butbut then it is added in the next Wordswords, To him that overcometh, will I grant to sit with me on my Thronethrone. And in that great Invitationinvitation of Christ, Matth.Matt 11, latter Endend, Come unto me, all ye that Labourlaborlabour and are heavy Ladenladen, and I will give you Restrest; Christ adds in the next Wordswords, Take my Yokeyoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly of Heartheart, and ye shall find Restrest unto your Soulssouls: Forfor my Yokeyoke is easy, and my Burdenburden is light: Asas tho'though taking the Burdenburden of Christ's Serviceservice, and imitating his Exampleexample, were necessary in order to the promis'dpromised Restrest. So in that great Invitationinvitation to Sinnerssinners
to accept of free Gracegrace, Isai.Isa 55, Ho • , every one that thirs • teth! comeCome ye to the Waterswaters: Andand he that hath no Moneymoney, come ye, buy and eat▪; yea, co • me, buy Winewine and Milkmilk, without Moneymoney and without Priceprice▪: Eveneven there, in the Continuationcontinuation of the same Invitationinvitation, the Sinnerssinners forsaking his wicked Practicepractice is spoken of as necessary t • o the obtaining Mercymercy: Verseverse 7, Let the Wickedwicked forsake his Wayway, and the unrighteous 〈◊〉 Manman his Thoughtsthoughts, and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have Mercymercy upon him, and to our God, and he will abundantly pardon •• . So the Richesriches of divine Gracegrace, in the Justificationjustification of Sinnerssinners, is set forth, with the Necessitynecessity of holy Practicepractice, Isai.Isa 1.: 15, &c. Wash y • e, m • ake you clean; put away the Evilevil of your Doingsdoings, from before mine 〈◊〉 Eyeseyes: Ceasecease to do evil, learn to do well; seek Judgmentjudgment, relieve the Oppressed 〈◊〉 , judge the Fatherlessfatherless, plead for the Widowwidow: Comecome now, let us Reasonreason together, saith the Lord, tho'though your Sinssins be as Scarletscarlet, they shall be as white as Snowsnow; tho'though they be red like Crimsoncrimson, they shall be as Woolwool. And in that most solemn Invitationinvitation of Wisdomwisdom, Prov. 9, after it is represented what great Provisionprovision is made, and how that all Thingsthings were ready, the Househouse built, the Beastsbeasts killed, the Wi • newine mingled▪, and the Tabletable furnished, and the Messengersmessengers sent for •• th to invite the Guestsguests; then we have the free Invitationinvitation, Vervvver. 4, 5, 6, Whoso is Simplesimple, let him turn in hither; as for him that wanteth Understandingunderstanding, (i. eE. hasHas no Righteousnessrighteousness) she saith to him, Comecome, eat of my Breadbread, and drink of the Winewine which I have mingled: Butbut then in the next Breathbreath it follows, Forsake the Foolishfoolish, and live, and go in the Wayway of Understandingunderstanding▪: Asas tho'though forsaking Sinsin, and going in the Wayway of Holinessholiness, were necessary in order to Lifelife. So that the Freenessfreeness of Gracegrace, and the Necessitynecessity of holy Practicepractice, which are thus from Timetime to Timetime join'djoined together in Scripture, are not inconsistent one with another. Nor • does it at all diminish the Honourhonorhonour and Importanceimportance of Faithfaith, that the Exercisesexercises and Effectseffects of Faithfaith in Practicepractice, should be esteem'desteemed the chief Signssigns of it; any more than it lessens the Importanceimportance of Lifelife, that Actionaction and Motionmotion are esteemed the chief Signssigns of that.

So that in what has been said 〈◊〉 of the Importanceimportance of holy Practicepractice, as the main Signsign of Sinceritysincerity; there is nothing legal, nothing derogatory to the Freedomfreedom and Sovereigntysovereignty of Gospelgospel Gracegrace, nothing in the least Clashingclashing with the Gospelgospel Doctrinedoctrine of Justificationjustification by Faithfaith alone, without the Worksworks of the Lawlaw, nothing in the least tending to lessen the Gloryglory of the Mediator, and our Dependancedependencedependance on his 〈◊〉 Righteousnessrighteousness, nothing infringing on the special Prerogativesprerogatives of Faithfaith in the Affairaffair of our Salvationsalvation, nothing in any wis •• e detracting from the Gloryglory of God and his Mercymercy, or exalt •• ing Manman, or diminishing his Dependancedependencedependance and Obligationobligation. So that if any are against such an Importanceimportance of holy Practicepractice as has been spoken of, it must be only from a senseless Aversionaversion to the Lettersletters and Soundsound of the Wordword Worksworks; when there is no Reasonreason in the Worldworld to be given for it, but what
may be given with equal Forceforce, why they should have an Aversionaversion to the Wordswords Holinessholiness, Godlinessgodliness, Gracegrace, Religionreligion, Experienceexperience, and even Faithfaith it self: Forfor to make a Righteousnessrighteousness of any of these, is as legal, and as inconsistent with the Wayway of the new Covenantcovenant, as to make a Righteousnessrighteousness of holy Practicepractice. You say you know Christ, and the Lovelove and Goodgood-will of Christ towards you, and that he is the Propitiationpropitiation for your Sins 〈◊〉 sins. How do you know this? He that saith I know him, and keepeth not his Commandmentscommandments, is a Liarliar, 1 John 2.: 4. True, might some reply, he that keeps not the Commandscommands of Christ, hath thereby a sure Evidenceevidence that he knows him not, and that he is not united to him; but is this any Evidenceevidence that we do know him, and that we are united to him, if we do keep his Commandmentscommandments? Yes verily, s • aith the Apostleapostle, Hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his Commandmentscommandments. And again, Vervver. 5. Hereby know we that we are in him. What can be more plain? What a Vanityvanity is it to say, that this is running upon a Covenantcovenant of Worksworks?—O Belovedbeloved, it is a sad Thingthing to hear such Questionsquestions, and such cold Answersanswers also, that Sanctificationsanctification possibly may be an Evidenceevidence. May be? Is it not certain? Assuredly to deny it, is as bad as to affirm that God's own Promisespromises of Favourfavorfavour are not sure Evidencesevidences thereof, and consequently that they are Lieslies and Untruths • untruths.—Our SaviourSavior, who was no legal Preacherpreacher, pronounceth ••• ▪, and consequently evidenceth Blessednessblessedness, by eight or nine Promisespromises, expreslyexpressly made to such Personspersons, as had inherent Grace • sgraces, Matth.Matt 5.: 3, 4, &c. Shepard's Soundsound Believerbeliever. pP. 221, 222, 223.

'Tis greatly to the Hurthurt of Religionreligion, for Personspersons to make light of, and insist 〈◊〉 little on • , tho • se • Thingsthings which the Scripture insist most upon, as of most Importanceimportance in the Evidenceevidence of our Interestinterest in Christ; (under a Notio ••• nnotion that to lay Weightweight on these Thingsthings is legal, and an old Covenantcovenant Wayway) and so to neglect the Exercisesexercises, and effectual Operationsoperations of Gracegrace in Practicepractice, and insist almost wholly on Discoveriesdiscoveries, and the Methodmethod and Mannermanner of the immanent Exercisesexercises of Conscienceconscience and Gracegrace in Contemplationcontemplation; depending on an Abilityability to make nice Distinctionsdistinctions in these Mattersmatters, and a Facultyfaculty of accurate Discerningdiscerning in them, from Philosophyphilosophy or Experienceexperience. It is in vain to seek for any better, or any further Signssigns, than those that the Scriptures have most expreslyexpressly mention'dmentioned, and most frequently insisted on▪, as Signssigns of Godlinessgodliness. They who pretend to a greater Accuracyaccuracy in giving Signssigns, or by their extraordinary Experienceexperience, or Insightinsight into the Naturenature of Thingsthings, to give more distinguishing Marksmarks, which shall more ••
thoroughly search out, and detect the Hypocritehypocrite; are but subtilsubtle to darken their own Mindsminds, and the Mindsminds of others; their Refiningsrefinings, and nice Discerningdiscerning, is in God's Sightsight, but refined Foolishnessfoolishness, and s • agacious Delusiondelusion. Here are applicable those Wordswords of Agur. Prov. 30 • .: 5. 6. Every Wordword of God is pure; he is a Shieldshield to them that put their Trusttrust in him: Addadd thou not unto his Wordswords, les • t he reprove thee▪, and thou b • e found a Liarliar. Our Wisdomwisdom and Discerningdiscerning, with Regardregard to the Heartshearts of Menmen, is not much to be trusted. We can see but 〈◊〉 a • little Wayway into the Naturenature of the Soulsoul, and the Depthsdepths of Mansman'smans Heartheart▪. TheThethe Waysways are so many whereby Personspersons Affectionsaffections may be moved without any supernatural Influenceinfluence, the natural Springssprings of the Aff ••• ectionsaffections are so various and so secret, so many Thingsthings have oftentimes a joint Influenceinfluence on the Affectionsaffections, the Imaginationimagination, (and that in Waysways innumerable and unsearchable) natural Tempertemper, Educationeducation, the common Influencesinfluences of the Spirit of God, a surprizingsurprising Concourseconcourse of affecting Circumstancescircumstances, an extraordinary Coincidencecoincidence of Thingsthings in the Coursecourse of Men'smen's Thoughtsthoughts, together with the subtilsubtle Managementmanagement of invisible mali •• cious Spiritsspirits; that no Philosophyphilosophy or Experienceexperience will ever be 〈◊〉 sufficient to guide us safely thro'through this Labyrinthlabyrinth and Mazemaze, without our • closely following the Clewclew which God has given us in his Wordword. God knows, his own Reasonsreasons why he insists on some Thingsthings, and plainly sets them forth as the Thingsthings that we should try our selves by, rather than others. It may be it is because he knows that these Thingsthings are attended with less Perplexityperplexity, and that we are less liable to be deceived by them than others. He best knows our Naturenature; and he knows the Naturenature and Mannermanner of his own Operationsoperations; and he best knows the Wayway of our Safetysafety: he knows what Allowancesallowances t • o make for different Statesstates of his Churchchurch, and different Temperstempers of particular Personspersons, and Varietiesvarieties in the Mannermanner of his own Operationsoperations, how far Naturenature may resemble Gracegrace, and how far Naturenature may be mix'dmixed with Gracegrace, what Affectionsaffections may arise from Imaginationimagination, and how far Imaginationimagination may be mix'dmixed with spiritual Illuminationillumination. And therefore 'tis our Wisdomwisdom not to take his Workwork out of his Handshands; but to follow him, and lay the Stressstress of the Judgmentjudgment of our selves there, where he has directed us. If we do otherwise, no wonder if • we are bewilder'dbewildered, confounded and fatally deluded. But if we had got into the Wayway of looking chiefly at those Thingsthings, which Christ and his Apostlesapostles and Prophetsprophets chiefly insisted on, and so in judging of our selves and others, chiefly regarding practical Exercisesexercises and Effectseffects of Gracegrace, not neglecting other Thingsthings; it would be of manifold happy Consequenceconsequence; it would above all Thingsthings tend to the Convictionconviction of deluded Hypocriteshypocrites, and to prevent the Delusiondelusion of those whose Heartshearts were never brought to a thorough Compliancecompliance with the strait and narrow Wayway which leads to Lifelife; it would tend to deliver us from innumerable Perplexitiesperplexities, arising from the various inconsistent
Schemesschemes there are about Methods 〈…〉 and Stepssteps of Experienceexperience; it would greatly tend to prevent 〈…〉 Professorsprofessors neglecting Strictnessstrictness of Lifelife, and tend to promote their 〈…〉 Engagednessengagedness and Earnestnessearnestness in their christian Walk 〈◊〉 walk▪; and 〈◊〉 it would become fashionable for Menmen to shewshow their Christianity •• , more by 〈◊〉 an amiable distinguished Behaviourbehaviorbehaviour, than by an abundant and 〈◊◊〉 exce • ssive declaring their Experiencesexperiences; and we should get into the Way •• way of appearing lively 〈◊〉 in Religionreligion, more by being lively in the Serviceservice of 〈◊〉 God and our 〈◊〉 Generationgeneration, than by the Livelinessliveliness and Forwardnessforwardness of • our To • nguestongues, and making a Businessbusiness of proclaiming on the Househouse Topstops, with our Mouthsmouths, the holy and eminent Actsacts and Exercisesexercises of our own Heartshearts; and Christians that are intimate Friendsfriends, would talk together of their Experiencesexperiences and Comfortscomforts, in a Mannermanner better becoming christian Humilityhumility and Modestymodesty, and more to each others Profitprofit; their Tonguestongues not running before, but rather going behind their •• Handshands and Feetfeet, after the prudent Exampleexample of the blessed Apostleapostle, 2 Cor. 12.: 6; and many Occasionsoccasions of spiritual Pridepride wou •• ld be cut off; and so a great Doordoor shut against the Devildevil; and a great many of the main stumbling Blocksblocks against experimental and powerful Religionreligion would be removed; and Religionreligion would be declared and manifested in such a Wayway, that instead of hardening Spectatorsspectators, and exceedingly promoting Infidelityinfidelity and Atheismatheism, would above all Thingsthings tend to convince Menmen that there is a Realityreality in Religionreligion, and greatly awaken t • hem, and win them, by convincing their Consciencesconsciences of the Importanceimportance and Excellencyexcellency of Religionreligion. Thus the Lightlight of Professorsprofessors would so shine before Menmen, that others seeing their good Worksworks, would glory their Father which is in Heavenheaven.

'Tis no Signsign that religious Affectionsaffections are gracious or otherwise, that they are great 31, &c. That they have great bodily Effectseffects 34, &c. That they cause Personspersons to abound in religious Talktalk 38, &c. That Personspersons did not make 'em themselves 40, &c. That they come with Textstexts of Scripture 44, &c.
